**Front Cover and Spine Description**

This volume is bound in a luxurious seventeenth or eighteenth-century style. The dark, mottled brown leather—likely calfskin—is decorated with an intricate gold-tooled border. This border features repeating "fleuron" motifs—small, stylized flower stamps—and pomegranate designs. The corners are further embellished with larger floral sprays.

The spine is divided into sections by raised bands. The labels on the spine identify both the author and the prestigious printing house responsible for the book.

->VALERIUS<-
->MAXIMUS<-
<note>original: "VALE MAXI MUS". Valerius Maximus was a Roman author from the 1st century AD. His work, a collection of historical anecdotes, was a standard textbook for students of rhetoric and morality for centuries.</note>

---

->ELZEVIR<-
<note>original: "ELZE VIR". The Elzevirs were a famous dynasty of Dutch printers and booksellers based in Leiden and Amsterdam. They were renowned for producing high-quality, small-format editions of classical texts during the 17th century.</note>

<summary>This page describes the ornate, gold-tooled leather binding of a book containing the works of the Roman historian Valerius Maximus, printed by the famous Elzevir family.</summary>

I well believe that men of greater gifts and experience would not have found this such a difficult task, but I speak according to my own circumstances and ability. It was also no small motivation for me to begin this work seeing that the four Evangelists—who described these things so holily and with such great certainty—are held in suspicion by some for inconsistency, or at least for obscurity. This is because certain stories, sayings, and events seem to differ somewhat due to variations in timing and circumstances. # PREFACE,
->to the<-
# CHRISTIAN READER.

The sweetness found in investigating the life of our Savior <term>Savior: a translation of 'Salighmaker,' literally 'one who makes blessed,' referring to Jesus Christ</term> was a constant encouragement and sustenance to me in this work; and just as those who labor in the gold mines surely face great hardships, yet are so comforted by the finding of those precious treasures that they hold their labor in low esteem, so it was also with me in this matter. Thus, the Apostle spoke quite rightly in 2 Timothy 2:6: **The farmer who tills the field shall be the first to enjoy its fruits.** I well believe that men of greater gifts and experience would not make such a great task of it, but I speak according to my own circumstances and ability. 

It was also no small reason for me to begin this work, seeing that the four Evangelists <term>Evangelists: the traditional authors of the four Gospels—Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John</term>, who so holily and with such great assurance described these things, are held in suspicion by some of disagreement, or at least of obscurity, because some stories, sayings, and events seem to differ somewhat through variety of times and circumstances; which in this work shall be found entirely innocent. One shall find nothing else in them but a sweet, clear, and melodious Harmony <term>Harmony: a 'Gospel Harmony' is a work that attempts to merge the four different Gospel accounts into a single, chronological narrative</term>, when one brings each thing to its proper order and time. Such that these four Evangelists are with great reason compared in Ezekiel Chapter 1 to four Wheels, which are to be seen as one wheel, being driven by a living wind; where one stands, there stands the other also; where one turns, there the other turns also; where one is raised or lowered, that always happened together with one another, just as did the four accompanying Living Creatures <note>The 'Living Creatures' or Tetramorph from Ezekiel’s vision are traditionally used in Christian art to symbolize the four Evangelists.</note>, having four different faces: the one like a **Man**, the second like a **Lion**, the third like an **Ox**, and the fourth like an **Eagle**,

<summary>In this preface, the author describes the spiritual joy of studying the life of Christ and explains his goal to resolve perceived contradictions between the four Gospels by creating a chronological "Harmony."</summary>
<keywords>Gospel Harmony, four Evangelists, Ezekiel's vision, biblical interpretation, Savior, 2 Timothy 2:6</keywords>

--- Page 13 ---
<meta>This page continues the author's preface to the reader. It picks up mid-sentence from the previous page, where the author was comparing the four Evangelists to the four living creatures/wheels described in the Book of Ezekiel.</meta>

*her*, expressing the nature and manner of writing of our four Evangelists, Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John; of whom the first has as his focus the genealogy and lineage of Christ according to his humanity, the second his powers <note>original: "krachten," referring here to the miracles and divine authority of Jesus</note>, the third his suffering, and the fourth his high Divinity. Yet they all four have these qualities together, just as these faces appear on each of these same creatures. Thus, this work of ours is nothing other than a proof that these four wheels are one wheel, and these four Creatures belong to one body, which provides great delight as well as no less certainty in investigating the Gospel Histories. 

For further reinforcement, foreign histories <note>original: "uytheemse geschiedenissen," referring to secular or non-biblical historical accounts from the same era</note> have also been added here, matching the Histories of the four Evangelists, which are followed until the passing of the Apostles. Likewise, the cities, places, mountains, rivers, and waters concerning the travels of our Lord have also been described. Furthermore, the entire Work consists of this arrangement:

1. Nothing is omitted of everything that the four Evangelists describe; however, only one speaks at a time—namely, the one who describes the matter in the greatest detail. If any others testify to the same with him, they are noted on the margin with Chapter and verse; and if these others have anything else regarding the same matter, it is handled in our observations.

2. To maintain the chronological order of time <term>chronological order: 't' onderhouden de ordening des tijts,' the practice of arranging events in the exact sequence they occurred</term>, some things that the Evangelists describe one after another are placed specifically.

3. Above each page, the speaking Evangelist or Evangelists are placed on the right-hand side, and those who are meanwhile silent on the left, with the chapter in which they rest.

4. The observations are of various types: sometimes explaining, sometimes Paraphrasing, and sometimes meditating, as the subject requires.

5. The entire work has eight parts, with a short summary of each provided beforehand to better understand the entire dealings of the book. 

May it please the God-fearing reader to interpret everything for the best and for his own instruction, and to receive it from our hand with such a heart as we offer it to him out of a favorable love. May it serve and be useful for the common edification and progress in Godliness. May God, to whom alone praise, laud, and honor belong, give His grace to that end, so that we may not only read the life of His beloved Son, but also contemplate it; which is the heartfelt wish of your servant and devoted friend,

->**J. P. SCHABAELIE.**<-

# Introduction to the Work, Described Historically.

The holy, unique, eternal Divine being, which is the origin of all things, beholding through the mirror of His Divine wisdom the entire world in its darkness and covered with the mists of sin: foresaw, therefore, through His merciful love, a means by which the fallen human race might be set right again, and the gate of life be opened; which was: namely, that He would send down His *Eternal Word*, the light of His wisdom, in a human form, and through the same not only teach and instruct, but also, through His very life and conduct, set an exemplary image <note>original: "exemplaer beelt," meaning a perfect model or archetype to be imitated</note> of all holiness and perfect virtues; furthermore, through His sacrifice, provide an eternal reconciliation <note>original: "versoeningh," referring to the theological concept of atonement</note> and certain entrance into life for those who would believe in His name.

### Prophecies of the Sibyls.

Augustine, in the eighteenth book of the *City of God*, Chapter 23, says of the *Erythraean Sibyl* that she composed a verse in the Greek language, the initial letters of which form these words: *Jesus Christ the Son of God, the Savior, the cross* <note>This refers to a famous acrostic poem where the first letter of each line spells out "ICHTHYS," the Greek word for fish and a shorthand for Christ's titles</note>, which verse, according to the testimony of the aforementioned *Onuphrius*, is also found in the books of *Cicero*, who lived some years before the birth of Christ. It is further testified by some that this *Erythraean Sibyl* spoke these words: *In the final Age, God shall be humbled, and that Divine lineage or seed shall be made human, and the Godhead shall be united with humanity; that lamb shall lie in the hay and be fed with virginal care.*

### Prophecies of Hermes Trismegistus.

This Hermes, who is also called *Mercury* <note>Known as Hermes Trismegistus or "Thrice-Greatest Hermes," a legendary figure combining the Greek god Hermes and the Egyptian god Thoth, regarded as the author of the Hermetic Corpus</note>, lived before the times of *Moses*—some believe around the times of *Abraham*. He was a priest in Egypt, a father of many sciences, and a man of great enlightenment. The fine writings attributed to him speak of great mysteries and clearly indicate that a great light had shone upon him. In his books named *The Perfect Word* <note>Original: "het volmaeckte woort," likely referring to the *Asclepius*, a dialogue in the Hermetic Corpus</note>, as *Augustine* in his oration on the five heresies and likewise *Lactantius* in the fourth book of the *Divine Institutes* testify, he says thus: *The Lord and Creator of all Gods has made a second Lord; because he made this one first, alone, and as one, he was God in his eyes, and full of all good; he rejoiced over him, and loved him dearly as his only-begotten.* The same writer says a little further: *The cause of this cause is the will of God's goodness, which has brought forth a God whose name cannot be spoken by a human mouth.* And further to his Son he says: *There is (my Son) a hidden word of wisdom, holy before the only Lord of all things, foreseen and prepared for him, who...*

### Letter of Lentulus to the Emperor Tiberius: which is read in Eutropius, in the Year-books of the Roman Senators.
<note>The "Letter of Lentulus" is a widely circulated medieval forgery. It purported to be an eyewitness report by Publius Lentulus, a fictional Governor of Judea, to the Roman Senate or Emperor Tiberius, providing a physical description of Jesus.</note>

AT this time there has arisen, and still lives today, a man of great and powerful works, named JESUS CHRISTUS, who is called a Prophet by the Gentiles, and whom his disciples call a Son of God. He raises the dead and heals all infirmities. He is a Man of moderate tall stature, distinguished, and with such a venerable countenance that the beholders may love and fear him for it. The hair of his head is of the color of a ripe hazelnut, and smooth down to the ears. From the ears down, it is somewhat curled, and of a yellowish hue, swaying slightly over the shoulders. Having his hair parted in the middle, after the manner of the Nazarenes <note>Original: "Nazarenen." Historically, this refers to the "Nazirite" tradition of letting hair grow long and parting it, which was frequently conflated with being from Nazareth.</note>. He has a broad and smooth forehead, as is his face, without any wrinkle or spot, all of which is adorned by a moderate redness <note>Referring to a healthy or ruddy complexion.</note>. Upon the nose and mouth nothing can be found to reproach. He has a full beard, though not on the chin <note>This likely suggests a short beard or a specific style where the point of the chin was visible between the forks of the beard.</note>, which is equal in color to the hair of his head; the beard is not long, but cleft in the middle. He has a very simple and stately expression, with bright eyes. In reproof he is earnest, in admonition sweet and friendly, also cheerful, yet always maintaining a sense of dignity. He has never been seen to laugh, but often seen to weep. In the stature of his body, he was straight and upright. His hands and feet were pleasant to behold. He engaged in few conversations, and was very modest therein, and distinguished among the children of men.

### Reflection.

<margin>Hebrews 11:3</margin>
Everything that is / or can be named / exists in two qualities / visible and invisible / the invisible is the root and origin of the visible / the visible an expression and image of the invisible. <note>The author uses a common 17th-century philosophical idea that the physical world is a mirror or "shadow" of a higher spiritual reality.</note> Therefore the invisible is the first / the visible is that which follows.

God is an invisible being / having within himself Omnipotence / wisdom / holiness / goodness / beauty / Eternity / and similar attributes / these are hidden within him / and would never become known or manifest / were it not through visible action / just as it stands clearly testified to the Romans: <margin>Romans 1:20</margin> That God’s invisible being, namely his eternal power and divinity, is made manifest through creation.

It is then certain that everything that exists / was created and emerged from the source of all things / namely from God’s invisible being / such that when we observe the Sun / the Moon / the Stars / the great architecture of the world / the order and movement of the same / together with all wonders of the Earth / that we then have before us firm witnesses / and sure signs of God’s Omnipotence / wisdom / providence / and furthermore whatever else is in him: except that there are still invisible things / hidden from our eyes / whether above in Heaven / or in the depth of the abyss / and a thousand other mysteries / of which we sense some within ourselves / some we believe to exist / some we consider and weigh through meditation / yet nonetheless for as many as there are / they are likewise witnesses of God’s invisible being.

Given the fact that there is a creation / it remains to be examined / how and in what manner that creation took place. The Holy Scripture says: That God did so through his Word: God spoke: let it be <margin>Genesis 1:3</margin> <note>original: "het worde", a reference to "Let there be light."</note>

# JOHN 1 <note>original: "JOAN. I."</note>

<margin>Gen. 19:4</margin>...surrounded the house in which this stranger stayed, groping with blind hands for the door, to abuse and violate him. <note>The author compares the rejection of Christ to the story of the men of Sodom surrounding Lot’s house to harm his guests.</note> Nevertheless, some received him and prepared unleavened cakes, opening the house of their hearts to him; to these he brought the rays of his light and gave power to become children of God, to take on the nature of God, to show themselves in all respects as newborn creatures, and to become like unto eternity. Having spoken of the eternal Word with some circumstances of the testimonies through John, the Evangelist <note>The author of the Gospel, John the Apostle.</note> now continues his reasoning to prove in what manner this Word—which is invisible and eternal in itself—has shown itself to mankind, and through which it is evident that this was the very same Word that had issued forth from God.

### JOHN CHAPTER 1 <note>original: "JOANNIS CAP. I."</note>

And that Word became **flesh**, and **dwelt** among us, and we saw his **glory**, a glory as of the only-begotten Son of the Father, full of grace and truth.

### Observation

He testifies to four things: First, that the same Word through which all things were created in the beginning has now become **flesh**, that is: that he has shown himself visibly in a human form according to the prophecies concerning this, which is confirmed with almost the <margin>1 Tim. 3:15 <note>The author refers to 1 Timothy 3:16: "God was manifest in the flesh."</note></margin> same words in another place: *God is revealed in the flesh*, this being a <term>godly mystery</term> <note>original: "Godtsalighe verholentheydt," referring to the Incarnation, which is hidden from human logic but revealed to faith.</note> that cannot be grasped by natural understanding, but only through the gifts of <margin>Heb. 11:2 <note>Likely referring to Hebrews 11:3: "By faith we understand that the world was created by the word of God."</note></margin> **faith**. Just as it is understood that visible things have come from the invisible, without being able to give a reason for it, so one also believes that the almighty Word has become a visible Man; but specifically how or in what manner, the Evangelist does not describe here; it is enough for him that we believe through his testimony that Jesus Christ is the only-begotten Son of God, which is why he wrote his Gospel. Secondly, he testifies that the same Word has **dwelt among them**, as he says in another place: <margin>1 John 1:1</margin> *We have seen the same, touched, and handled it.* That is to say, more than other common people who only heard, saw, and walked beside him occasionally; but we have associated with him daily, observed all things closely, and found in truth that which I shall describe, since we have been with him from the time of his revelation until the day he was taken up, continually...

...continually been upon him, around him, and about him. Thirdly, he indicates that they have seen his glory; for otherwise, nothing at all would have been proven, even if they had found him to be a man. A king who walks unknown among his subjects, if he does not display some sign or proof by which he can be recognized as the true king, then one need not acknowledge him as anything more <margin>Genesis 45:27</margin> than a common man. Jacob did not believe the words of his sons until he saw the wagons that Joseph had sent to fetch him; and this was a proof of his glory. <note>In the Book of Genesis, the patriarch Jacob only believes his son Joseph is alive and a ruler in Egypt when he sees the physical evidence of the Egyptian wagons.</note> Fourthly, he proves that the glory they found in Jesus was not common, such as one might find in the outward pomp of the kings or princes of this world, nor even such a glory as was seen in prophets, patriarchs, or holy men of God—who also spoke powerful words, predicted certain things, and even performed some signs like Moses, Elijah, Elisha, and the like—but that it was a glory such as had never been found in anyone else, nor could be, except in the only-begotten Son of the Father.

For he had not only, along with the powerful effect of his teaching, healed many kinds of illnesses, driven out demons, raised the dead, subdued the elements, walked upon the water against nature, and performed more such wonders; but beyond that, he had shown a never-before-heard patience in his passion. <note>The "Passion" refers to the period of suffering and the crucifixion of Jesus.</note> These miraculous signs convinced the hearts of men; also, after his burial, he had risen on the third day and was carried to Heaven in great glory, had abundantly distributed his spirit, and showed no less power than when he walked upon the earth. All the prophets were fulfilled through him, and there was not one part of his life nor of his suffering which did not entirely correspond with the prophecies <margin>Matthew 17:2</margin> from the beginning of the world. The very greatest miracle-workers, namely Moses and Elijah, honored him with their appearance, in the midst of whom he stood and shone like a sun on Mount Tabor; <note>This refers to the Transfiguration, where Jesus's divine nature was revealed to his disciples alongside the ancient prophets Moses and Elijah.</note> such that his glory was preeminent above all and proved itself to be a glory as of the only-begotten Son of the Father. His words came as from a fountain, overflowing with grace; his works consisted in truth, and there was nothing left to wish or desire for a broader testimony of his <margin>Baruch 3:38</margin> divine power. It appeared fully that he was the Word, and the wisdom, of which it was prophesied: *That one should see her upon the Earth, dwelling among Men.* <note>A reference to Baruch 3:37-38 in some versions of the Bible, where Divine Wisdom is said to appear on earth.</note>

Having thus far examined the eternal glory of Christ, let us now come to his humiliation and appearance in the world, which is described by the other Evangelists from the beginning; and first, we must note from which lineage he was born, which Matthew describes in the beginning of his Gospel.

### MATTHEW 1.

<margin>John 8</margin>
...the life and the miracles of Christ, and everything that serves to prove that he is the true Anointed One <note>original: "ghesalfden" — the Dutch equivalent of the Hebrew "Messiah" and Greek "Christos"</note>, [the Evangelist] has deemed it necessary above all things to begin with his descent and lineage according to the flesh. This certainly had to be demonstrated, because in the promises of the Savior <note>original: "Salighmaecker"</note> made to the Jews through both the Patriarchs and Prophets, it was clearly indicated and foretold that he would be born from the seed of Abraham and David. By this, it was also proven that he must come forth from the tribe of Judah, since it was certain that David was born from the tribe of Judah. Therefore, when the Evangelist calls Christ **A Son of David, the Son of Abraham**, he emphasizes that these are the Fathers to whom the promises were made, and from whose tribe the Messiah would surely come.

This can also have a higher meaning: namely, that being a "Son of Abraham" also means being a child of faith and a <margin>Luke 19:9</margin> descendant of a holy and pious Father. Such is the case with Zacchaeus, who is so named after he had turned away from his sinful life, <margin>John 8:44</margin> for through this he was grafted into the godly tribes; conversely, because the Jews had strayed from the footsteps of faith, they were called children of the Devil and not children of Abraham. It was the same with David; whenever one reads of a pious King, it is commonly added: "he walked in the ways of his father David." The common people, seeing the miracles of Christ and wishing to grant him his proper honor, <margin>Matt. 12:23</margin> said: **Is this not David's Son?** As if they wanted to say: "May he not <margin>1 Kings 1:5</margin> rightfully be called David’s Son, who does so much good for the people of Israel and demonstrates such wonders?" In contrast, Adonijah, because of his ungodly conduct, was called a Son of Haggith <note>Haggith was one of David's wives; the text suggests his lineage is traced through his mother to distance him from David's virtue</note>, <margin>Susanna 56</margin> after his mother and not a Son of David after his father. Daniel, wishing to express the corrupted nature of the wicked judges who wrongly condemned Susanna, said to them: "you seed of Canaan and not of Judah." He denied that those who strayed from the virtues of the tribe of Judah were truly of Judah. Thus, in this way too, Christ is rightly called a Son of Abraham and David, as one descending from a holy and pious lineage.

The Evangelist, pursuing his purpose, recounts in an orderly fashion through which members and generations David descended from Abraham, and in turn, Christ from David. He rests finally on Joseph, the husband of Mary; regarding this order, and the differences he has with Lucas <note>the Gospel of Luke provides a different genealogy for Jesus</note>, more shall be said at the proper time.

But it is entirely useful for our purpose that we speak more broadly of the <margin>1 Pet. 1:20</margin> promises and pledges made to the Fathers which apply to this lineage. For God, having already decided before the foundation of the world to send his Son into the world to redeem the human race and to provide for them a cause for eternal Salvation, has done this from the begin-

<margin>MATTHEW 1.</margin>
<margin>JOHN 1.</margin>
...ning <note>Continuing from the previous page's catchword "begin".</note>, just as He occasionally let the Patriarchs who walked in His truth know, and revealed that same promise most clearly first to Abraham. <margin>GENESIS 12:2</margin> Having first called him out of the darkness of the Chaldeans <note>Ancient inhabitants of Mesopotamia; Abraham's departure from "Ur of the Chaldeans" marks the beginning of the biblical narrative of the Hebrews.</note> (who since the times of Noah had fallen away from the true worship of God into idolatry and vanity) and having led him through the paths of faith, He brought him into a foreign land, namely the land of Canaan. There He established a covenant with him and first enticed him with temporal blessings, proving that He was his God, whom he must fully trust and believe. He promised him that his seed <margin>GENESIS 15:5</margin> would be as the stars of heaven, despite the fact that he had no children, nor was it likely he would have any—at least not from Sarah <note>original: "Zara"</note>, in whom the promise was contained. After this promise was made through several appearances, Isaac was finally born to him, in whom he placed his comfort and hope.

But God, to further teach him that His promises had a higher meaning than he could grasp with human understanding, commanded him <margin>GENESIS 22</margin> to sacrifice this son of his. When he obeyed, God renewed the covenant with Abraham, saying: *through your seed all nations on Earth shall be blessed*. Isaac was a <term>figure: a person or event in the Old Testament seen as a symbolic foreshadowing of Christ</term> of this promise, as was his sacrifice and his carrying of the wood up the mountain; but essentially, this all pointed toward the coming Savior <note>original: "Salighmaecker"</note>, who was the true lamb of the sacrifice. Afterward, God renewed the same promise to Isaac, speaking to him as He had before to his father Abraham: *Through your seed all nations <margin>GENESIS 26:4</margin> on earth shall be blessed*. The same happened many years later <margin>GENESIS 28:12</margin> to Jacob, who had then come into his father’s inheritance and blessing.

There were also other events that served as images of Christ, such as the stories of Joseph, Moses, David, and others; but especially the sacrifices in the Law, which were full of beautiful mysteries. In addition, this was indicated here and there with clear words, as when Moses spoke: *The Lord God <margin>DEUTERONOMY 18:15</margin> will raise up for you a Prophet from among your brothers, like me; Him you shall hear*. Specifically, He would be like Moses in that He would bring forth a new teaching and confirm it with signs and wonders, and also share certain similarities with him in His birth. There were yet other figures <note>original: "Figueren"</note>, such as the blossoming staff of Aaron, the raised-up serpent, the manna, and the water-giving rock, which all signified Christ, though in a cloudy and shadowy time so that it could not be easily perceived. Meanwhile, the pious, observing the oppressions and the poor state of Israel, were waiting for a general redemption through the coming Savior, just as the Lord had proclaimed in the time of the High Priest Eli: *I will <margin>1 SAMUEL 2:35</margin> raise up for myself a faithful Priest, who shall do according to what is in my heart and my soul.* Some time after that, from the tribe of Judah, God raised up King David...

But when **David** was now King and noticed that the kingdoms of this world are very unstable and can quickly change—as the example of **Saul** and others could teach him—he persisted through his prayers to God to obtain a steadfast kingdom for himself and his seed, of which he received a promise

Other Prophets were also full of such and similar predictions, even during the **Babylonian captivity**, such as **Ezekiel**, and thereafter **Zechariah**, **Haggai**, and **Malachi**, which is not necessary to set down here in great length; let it only be noted that the comfort of the Jews rested solely upon this whenever they were in any burden or need, turning their eyes toward the coming of their Savior—and especially from the times of the **Maccabees** <note>A group of Jewish rebel warriors who took control of Judea and reasserted Judaism in the 2nd century BCE.</note> onward, when through the advancement of the **Romans** their power diminished more and more.

# Of the Life of Jesus Christ.

<margin>MATTHEW 1.</margin>
<margin>JOHN 1.</margin>
...and by means of Antipater and his son Herod the Great, their scepter had been trodden underfoot. Seeing no human means to recover it, they constantly sighed and longed for the Savior. Even though their perspective was varied and often focused on worldly matters <note>The author suggests the Jewish people of the time were often looking for a political or military liberator rather than a spiritual one.</note>, they nevertheless kept the tribe of **Judah** in their sights, seeking to obtain from it the long-promised **Messiah**.

This is why the Evangelist Matthew begins his account by proving that **Jesus** is descended from the direct line of **Abraham** and **David**, and consequently from **Judah**, just as the aforementioned and all other prophecies and promises from the time of Abraham until then had presented it. This was done so that the Jews who were expecting the **Messiah** might be satisfied in this regard. And although **Joseph**, Mary’s husband, was not the Father of **Christ**, he was nevertheless regarded as such among the common people. Since **Mary** was his lawful wife—of whom **Christ** was born—He was reckoned as part of Joseph's household. Thus, it was sufficient to satisfy the requirements of that nation that this lineage was proven as far as Joseph. The Evangelist also saw fit to divide the entire genealogical line into three periods or parts, assigning an equal number of generations to each, according to these words:

### MATTHEW CHAPTER I.

<margin>verse 17</margin>
> So all the generations from **Abraham** to **David** are fourteen generations; and from **David** until the **Babylonian captivity** are fourteen generations; and from the **Babylonian captivity** until **Christ** are fourteen generations.

### Observation.

Here, three eras are described. The first is the time of the **Patriarchs** and the **Judges** of the Jews, which one may well call the "Rise of the Jews." According to general calculation, if one counts from the birth of **Abraham** to the birth of **David**, it comprises 910 years. The second era is the supreme glory and power of the Jews under the reign of their own **Kings**, being a period of 596 years. The third era is the decline of the Jews under the reign of the **Princes** and **High Priests**, which, when taken until the birth of **Christ**, is 607 years. But why Matthew counts only exactly fourteen generations in the lineage of the kings—omitting three of them, namely **Ahaziah**, **Joash**, and **Amaziah**—one cannot know the exact reason. The common opinion is that he created these three divisions by totaling

The First Part /

### MATTHEW I.

<margin>John 1.</margin>
...wanted to present the generations in a balanced symmetry, as it does not hinder the calculation of the lineage, and the true descent of Christ—which he intends to describe—remains intact. There are also those who believe that Matthew, through these forty-two generations, wanted to create a correspondence with the forty-two encampments of Israel in the wilderness. One can also observe that he intends to testify that restorations in kingdoms usually occur after twice-seven generations; indeed, some kingdoms barely last that long before they either perish entirely or undergo significant 
<margin>Genesis 5:3, Genesis 11:10.</margin>
change. This also occurs in the human race in general: from Adam to Noah, when the Deluge <note>original: "Diluvie", referring to the Great Flood</note> covered the entire world, only ten generations are counted; and from Noah to Abraham—at which time the lifespans of men greatly diminished—likewise only ten generations. 
<margin>Johann Alsted, *Chronology*, 22 and 20</margin>
In the Egyptian Kingdom, one cannot count seven consecutive kings before Pharaoh Acherres <note>A name used by some early modern historians for the Pharaoh of the Exodus</note> drowned in the Red Sea. The seventh king reigned in Troy <note>original: "Tropen"</note> when that same kingdom and city perished; 
<margin>Titus Livius, Dionysius of Halicarnassus; Justin, Book 11.</margin>
likewise, in Rome there had been no more than seven kings when, with a great change of state, the Consuls began to rule; in the Persian Monarchy, no more than thirteen kings are counted before Alexander overpowered it and brought it under the Greeks; and in the Macedonian Kingdom there were about sixteen kings, of whom Perseus was the last, when that kingdom came under the rule of the Romans. These and similar examples prove that in a short time great things change and are brought onto a different footing than they were before, as can be seen in Judaism according to this arrangement by Matthew; for he seems to mean that by attributing an equal number of generations to these three periods. We also have this lesson to draw from here: 1. That the things of this world are very unstable and wavering, and not worthy of building upon. 2. That God fulfills His promise swiftly; for although the time seems long to us humans, it is not so to God. What are forty-two consecutive generations from Abraham to Christ? What are two thousand years
<margin>2 Peter 3:8</margin>
more than two days to God, in which He fulfills His promises and, according to Peter's word, does not delay as we count delay; which should teach us all patience and long-suffering.

It is also worthy to note that Matthew names certain women in the lineage of Christ, such as **Tamar**, **Rahab**, **Ruth**, and **Bathsheba**, by which he wishes to make known (according to the opinion of some) that even Gentiles and sinners would have a share in the fruit of Christ’s birth, and that it is furthermore a proof of His humiliation <note>This refers to Christ’s humility in being born into a lineage that included people of low social status or questionable reputation in that era.</note>.

### The Third Chapter.

### Regarding the times in which the conception of John the Baptist and subsequently also of Christ occurred, and concerning the conversation of the Angel with Zacharias the Priest.

### Luke Chap. 1.

<margin>verse 1</margin>
In the days of Herod, King of Judea, there was a Priest named Zacharias, of the division of Abijah <note>The "division of Abijah" refers to one of the twenty-four groups of priests who served in the Temple on a rotating basis</note>; and his wife was of the daughters of Aaron, and her name was Elizabeth.
<margin>2</margin>
And they were both righteous before God, walking blamelessly in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord.
<margin>3</margin>
And they had no children, because Elizabeth was barren, and they were both well advanced in years.

---

#### Observation.

<margin>Josephus, Antiquities 14, Chap. 2.</margin>
Luke begins his Gospel History with the events of John the Baptist, as he was a forerunner of Christ; first noting the time, namely in the days of Herod, King of Judea. This Herod was very famous and well-known; and to distinguish him from his other descendants and sons who bore the same name, he is also called **Herod the Great**, both because of the greatness of his dominion—which no one after him in the land of the Jews possessed to such an extent—as well as for his long reign and the particular deeds performed by him. His father was an Idumaean <note>An inhabitant of Edom, a region south of Judea; the Idumaeans were forced converts to Judaism</note> named Antipater, a particularly clever and cunning man. Observing the discord between the two brothers, Hyrcanus and Aristobulus, who were both fighting for the Kingdom, Antipater interjected himself, aligning with Hyrcanus, whom he noticed was of a gentle nature and somewhat weak. He hoped thereby to become master of the entire government himself, and to this end, he took the power of the Romans to his aid. This succeeded well for him; for Pompey the Great <note>original: "Pompeius Magnus", a leading Roman general and statesman</note>, having become the victor over all Asia, arrived at Jerusalem with a great army through the instruction of this Antipater. He deposed Aristobulus and ordained Hyrcanus as High Priest, further entrusting <note>original: "bevelen"</note> him with the care of the Land.

The First Part

->Luke 1. Matthew 1. John 1.<-

...entrusting matters to Antipater—who, under the pretext of defending the rights of Hyrcanus, steadily worked for his own profit—making his son Herod the governor of Galilee. Herod, acting with no less cunning and boldness, advanced further and further in his dominion over the Jews. Many of the Jewish nobility were greatly annoyed by this and supported Aristobulus, striving to restore his son Antigonus to the kingdom with the help of the Parthian King. This occurred in part after the death of Antipater; that King, taking Jerusalem, carried Hyrcanus away captive to his country and made Antigonus King of the Jews. Meanwhile, Herod fled to Rome <margin>Josephus, Antiquities 14, Chapters 26, 27, 28.</margin> and, having the favor of Antony—a powerful Roman general—he was declared King of Judea by the Senate there. With the help of the general Sosius and a large army, he entered the Jewish land, captured many cities, besieged Jerusalem, overpowered it, and took Antigonus prisoner. By order of Antony, Antigonus was executed with an ax. Thus, the entire kingdom fell into the hands of the aforementioned Herod. This was very painful for the Jews, yet it was so ordained by Divine Providence so that, toward the coming of His Son, the prophecy <margin>Genesis 49:10.</margin> of Jacob would be fulfilled, which had said: "The scepter shall not be taken from Judah, nor a ruler from his feet, until the Hero <note>original: "Heldt"; this refers to the Messiah, often translated elsewhere as "Shiloh"</note> comes." 

Now being in full possession of the throne, this Herod most cruelly oppressed the lineage of the Hasmoneans—who were descended from the Maccabees <note>The Hasmoneans or Maccabees were the Jewish royal dynasty that had ruled Judea before the Roman-backed Herodian era</note>—and finally brought them entirely to ruin. First <margin>Josephus, Antiquities Book 15, Chapters 3, 9, and 11; Book 16, Chapter 17.</margin> he killed Aristobulus, the grandson of Hyrcanus, who was then High Priest; thereafter Hyrcanus himself, who had returned to Jerusalem from Parthia; then his own wife Mariamne, the sister of Aristobulus; and then Alexandra, the mother of them both. Finally, he also had his own two sons, whom he had fathered with the aforementioned Mariamne, put to death under the pretext that they had sought his life. Thus, in the eyes of the Jews who had to endure this, the Hasmonean lineage perished like sheep for the slaughter through Herod's schemes, as he reigned over them as a powerful king.

It was during the time of his reign that those events occurred which Luke describes here regarding the promise of John the Baptist. Historians do not agree exactly on which year of his reign this took place, but they all agree it was in his old age—and as some calculate, in the 33rd year after he was declared king by the Roman Senate. So the Evangelist says that in that time there was a priest named Zacharias, further stating that he was of the division of Abijah, which was the eighth order of priests established by David to serve the priestly office by turn. He also describes his wife Elizabeth, that she was of the daughters of Aaron, and that they were both righteous and blameless in the Law, by which the Evangelist intends to teach that... <margin>1 Chronicles 24:10.</margin>

This was the first revelation of the **Divine purpose** <note>original: "Goddelick voornemen"</note> that He had decreed so many centuries ago. All things seemed quiet and still / Zacharias, standing under the High Priest and following the common order, entered the Temple. See how great a utility it has / to faithfully follow the common services of God (even if they seem nearly worn out and corrupted) / Zacharias is about to offer sacrifice according to the law of *Moses* / and unexpectedly this joyful and long-awaited message appears to him. However, to proceed in an orderly manner / we shall briefly observe these things here:

1. That God generally arranges great and high matters through the service of his **Angels** / such as the message of the birth of *Isaac* and of *Samson* / the instruction of *Daniel* and *Esdras* <note>Esdras refers to the prophet Ezra; in this context, it likely refers to the apocalyptic visions in the book of 2 Esdras.</note> / the guidance of the young *Tobias* / and the healing of the Elder: The punishment of ungodly men for the deliverance of the pious / as happened with *Sodoma* / and the army of *Sennacherib* / and more such examples / which is very comforting for the God-fearing who place their trust in God / for He does not allow His help to be absent / whether He rescues and fulfills His promises through ordinary means / or through other extraordinary means such as His **Angels** and messengers.

2. The appearance of the Angel **Gabriel**, from which arose the fear that seized Zacharias / he was not expecting such a glorious person / he found himself in a holy place / it may be that he did not deem himself worthy to behold that Divine appearance / *Abraham* acknowledged that he was but earth and ashes, unfit to speak with God / *Manoah* the father of *Samson* feared he must die / because he had seen God / so that it was not strange, nor unlike reverence / that Zacharias was overcome with fear.

3. The speech of the Angel, who first proclaims to him the hearing of his prayer / it is comforting to receive such assurance / and all prayers that are made according to the will of God / are thus received / and the soul receives a certain testimony of it. Secondly, he gives an account of the future Son / by whom he should be born / what he should be named / and what his birth would bring about / namely / joy for him and many other pious people / who, now sitting in sorrow / longed for some comfort in the miserable state of **Israel**. To her were spoken these glorious testimonies: *The Lord is with you. Blessed are you among women.* Oh, very beautiful things that belong to no one except those in whom God takes a special delight. Furthermore, the Angel takes away from her the fear that had seized her upon hearing such an unusual greeting—just as human weakness is subject to such when so great a Majesty approaches her—and he proclaims four things to her.

<margin>Isaiah 7:14.</margin>1. That she shall conceive and bear a Son, according to the prophecy foretold in Isaiah. 2. That his name shall be **Jesus**, which is **Savior**, **Preserver**, or **Redeemer** of his people. 3. What kind of person he shall be: namely great, excellent, and glorious; not as a common man but a **Son of the Most High**. 4. What he shall possess: namely the **throne of David** his father—not earthly, not temporary, but heavenly and eternal—of which the throne and scepter of David were nothing other than a prototype and figure. For the reign of David and his descendants had ended; the heathens <note>Referring to the Roman and preceding occupations of Judea.</note> had long since laid it waste, and there appeared to be no improvement nor any recovery at hand, except through a divine hand—which was also promised to David and his seed, and now God would fulfill it. Yet, this was not according to human judgment, whose thoughts are as far removed from His as the heavens are from the earth <margin>Isaiah 55:8.</margin>, but as it was foreseen by His wisdom: to establish an eternal and incorruptible Kingdom for the **house of Jacob**, which refers to all upright and pious Israelites. The holy Virgin, hearing these things and being caught up in wonder, sought further instruction on this unusual matter, as now follows.

### Reflection.

God gladly instructs those who humbly ask Him about things that are too high and too wondrous for them; and in turn, those who are of a good-willed heart to fulfill the will of God gladly allow themselves to be taught and instructed, easily submitting their understanding to the voice of the Lord. She asks, and with great reason: *How will this come to pass?* For such a wonder had never happened, that a Virgin without the involvement of a man should conceive and bear a Son. The Angel answers to satisfy this question, stating that such would happen through the **Holy Spirit**, who would descend into her from above, and that to this would be added the **power of the Most High**. And this was reason enough, for by that same power God had brought forth all visible things out of the invisible; so it was then no wonder that the Divine, invisible Being, without the involvement of a man, should bring forth a visible body, since all things are subject to His power. 

Furthermore, to strengthen his reasoning, the Angel brought forward an example which, although it was not as great a matter as this, nevertheless could not happen without an accompanying Divine power above the common order of nature: namely, that Elizabeth her kinswoman <note>The Dutch "nichte" here refers to Elizabeth, usually translated as cousin or kinswoman in English biblical tradition.</note> had also become pregnant in her old age, and was now already in her sixth month—a time that takes away all doubt and which Mary herself could easily investigate. From this, she could easily conclude, understand, and accept from the heart that with God no thing (however wondrous and strange it may seem to men) is impossible. 

The holy Virgin, hearing the Angel’s reasoning, set herself entirely at rest, subjecting herself to the will of the Lord. She did not exalt herself over such a great mystery and special fortune that was granted to her above all women on earth, but she presented herself as a **willing handmaid**, ready to suffer, to do, and to undergo everything that belonged to the service of the Lord. And in such people God takes a special delight—those who always subject their own choice and discretion to the will of God, even if it goes against their intentions, beyond their estimation, and far differently than they had set the course of their lives. Whether nature is somewhat suppressed, or whether other people wonder at them—even hating and persecuting them—as long as it is according to the will of God, that is reason enough for them to gladly endure everything that may happen to them on His behalf.

### Observation.

Observe with a mindful heart:

1. The coming together of these two holy women and their loving greeting; for this has been an ancient custom of the saints, arising from a heart full of love. Sometimes it occurred with embracing and kissing, as Jacob did to Rachel, Laban to Jacob, likewise Jacob to his brother Esau, and Joseph again to his father Jacob. Also, when Moses and Aaron met each other on the way, their wish for one another was "Peace," just as the Angel spoke to Gideon. Likewise, Christ himself, when coming to his disciples, wished them Peace. Remember that He—being now a child within his Mother’s body—offered this same greeting to the holy John, not with words but with his very essence. For just as the **Magnet-stone** <note>original: "Magneet-steen"; a lodestone. Here used as a metaphor for the soul's natural attraction to God.</note> is drawn by an invisible force toward the North, where its center lies, so the pious are drawn by an invisible force of the Spirit toward one another, and especially toward Jesus, who is the center of their souls and the moving force of the mind. Oh, how happy it is to be thus greeted by Jesus.

2. The igniting of the rays of the Spirit in both Mary and Elizabeth, for both of them, prophesying, spoke of things that were previously hidden from them. In them, this word is fulfilled: *You have the Anointing from him who is holy, and know all things, and it is not necessary that anyone teach you, but as the Anointing teaches you, so it is true.* <note>A reference to 1 John 2:20. The "Anointing" refers to the presence of the Holy Spirit providing direct spiritual understanding.</note>

The power of Mary’s Song of Praise <term>Magnificat: The Latin name for Mary's hymn of praise</term>, which is very similar in form to the Song of Hannah, the mother of Samuel. <note>Hannah’s song is found in 1 Samuel 2; it also celebrates God raising the lowly and humbling the proud.</note> The subject matter serves mostly to magnify God out of an admiration for His works, since He exalts the poor and the small and casts down the proud, scattering them in the thoughts of their hearts. Mary considers it a great mercy, that which **happens** <note>The catchword "schiet" is the conclusion of the Dutch word "gheschiet" (happens/occurs).</note> to her.

<margin>Sirach 34:5</margin>...address. This is an expression which natural dreams do not have, as they arise from the uncertain fantasies of men, and therefore no actual power comes from them, unlike this one, where obedience followed immediately. One cannot darken, ignore, or cast doubt upon the command of God. <note>The author contrasts ordinary dreams with divine revelation; the latter carries an unmistakable authority that compels the dreamer to act.</note>

So let us briefly observe something else noteworthy in this history. 1. Joseph was betrothed to Mary; it was the custom in those days among the Jews that parents promised their children to one another early on, such that the wedding day occurred long after. <note>Betrothal was a legally binding contract that preceded the actual moving-in and physical union, often by a year.</note> 2. Joseph her husband was righteous, specifically in that he did not want to hide the evil with a false cover, nor did he want to be an informer of his wife's shame, through which she might come into 
<margin>Leviticus 20:10</margin>great suffering; since the Law commanded that adultery be punished with death. <note>Under Mosaic Law, specifically Leviticus 20:10, the penalty for adultery was death, usually by stoning.</note> By reporting her, he would have appeared unfaithful and would not have acted according to the nature of love toward her. Therefore his concern was the greater, and his resolve the firmer to leave her secretly. For in doing so, he neither accused her nor covered up her misdeed; and this righteousness of his is praised. 3. Through this, he received a complete instruction of everything, apart from his wife, which made him much more certain than if he had received it through 
<margin>Isaiah 7:14</margin>her. The Angel adds to his speech the prophecy of Isaiah to assure him even better that it could be fulfilled in this way and no other. The name Emmanuel holds a great mystery, for all our complete salvation consists in this: that God is with us. Which was accomplished in Christ and is still daily accomplished through him in all those whose God is that God, who is a father of Christ and of all believers. These overcome all things; for as the Apostle says very well: If God is with us, who can be against us. 
<margin>Romans 8:31</margin>For He is everything. 4. Joseph showed obedience, and he bore himself so purely alongside this holy Virgin that he was worthy to bear the name of that holy Patriarch, who through the 
<margin>Genesis 39:7</margin>power of chastity overcame all the evil that came to oppose him and threatened death. <note>The author compares Joseph, the husband of Mary, to the Patriarch Joseph in Egypt, who famously resisted the advances of Potiphar's wife.</note> Some understand that he never in all his life "knew" <note>biblical idiom for sexual intimacy</note> Mary his wife; whatever the case may be, the text does not say this clearly, but it does indicate that he walked modestly, holily, and godly alongside her.

# Of the Life of Jesus Christ. Luke 1. Matt. 1. John 1.

[He] was in the desert until the day when he should be shown to the people of Israel.

### Observation.

Herein four things are made known. First, what the office of **John** should be / A Prophet of the Most High, that is: more than any other prophets had been / <margin>Matt. 11:9.</margin> as it is also testified of him in another place. For just as all stars are witnesses to the great light / yet none is as glorious as the **Morning Star** / <note>In Christian tradition, John the Baptist is the "Morning Star" who appears just before the "Sun" (Jesus) rises.</note> which is immediately followed by the great daylight with the **Sun**. And going before the Lord is the office of a mighty Prince and the foremost of the Realm / like those who go before the face of Kings / to prepare their place / and so to speak, to escort them / wherever they wish to go. Of lesser status are those who follow / or those who announce the coming of their King from a great distance away.

Second / for what purpose this should happen / namely to give the knowledge of salvation to his people: For they did not yet have this / since they still lay imprisoned under the shadows of the law. <note>The "shadows of the law" refers to the Old Testament rituals and ceremonies which, according to early modern theology, were only dim reflections of the truth brought by Christ.</note> They walked like the blind / and fell from one sin into another. Thus this knowledge could not come except through <margin>Isaiah 43:27.</margin> the forgiveness of their sins: which lay like veils upon their heart / and hindered the Divine sight. And this is still daily the obstacle why eternal salvation is not more loved / namely: because it is not known / and this knowledge does not come as long as man remains in sin / serving it / clinging to it / and giving it no leave to depart.

Third / by what means such should happen / namely through our God’s heartfelt mercy, for that is the only means: had God not taken pity on man / and that out of a fiery and heartfelt love / just as a father takes pity on his wandering <margin>Psalm 103:13.</margin> children / they would all have remained in death / and eternal oblivion / through which the dawn <note>Original: "op-ganck," referring to the rising sun or the "Dayspring" mentioned in Luke 1:78.</note> has sought us out. A parable taken from the rising of the Sun / which is a cause of joy for the whole Earth / for what creature is there / even to the smallest animals / yes, the trees / clap with their hands / <note>A reference to Isaiah 55:12: "the trees of the field shall clap their hands."</note> so to speak, when the Sun rises / why? because it comes to enlighten those who have sat so long in the dark night. They are unhappy lands where it is always night / they are poor people who are always blind / for they are as if in the shadow of death, death is darkness itself. These sat in the shadows / which prevented them from seeing any light / having no power to raise themselves up / for they held these shadows to be precious and great things / and alas! there followed nothing but death / all the kingdom / crown / glory / sanctuary / upon which they fixed their hope were but paths and ways of death / so

### Reflections.

To thoughtfully consider this history for our instruction, it is necessary that we observe therein: 1. **The providence of God**, which easily brings about inconvenient things—and those which do not seem likely to follow—through a sweet and harmonious order. This is done in such a way that one cannot say any violence is done to anyone in the course of their life, nor that they are drawn by some miraculous force to fulfill His will. It had been foretold by the Prophet
<margin>Micah 5:1.</margin>
**Micah** that the birth of **Christ** would occur within **Bethlehem** in **Judea**; yet nothing seemed less likely. **Joseph** and **Mary** lived in **Nazareth**, in **Galilee**; he was busy with his carpentry, and she calculated that her hour was approaching to bring this holy birth into the world in the place where she was. And in these circumstances, when no one had any thought of departing for **Bethlehem**, hear what happened! Quite suddenly, a command comes from the **Emperor Augustus**. Natural causes moved him; his empty treasuries <note>original: "Cantooren." Refers to the administrative offices or tax-collection centers of the Empire.</note>, exhausted by war, required a refilling. **Cyrenius** <note>Also known as Quirinius.</note> comes with orders for an enrollment for a tax for the Emperor; he knew as little of a divine mission or guidance as **Saul** did when he came to **Samuel** while seeking his father’s 
<margin>1 Samuel 9:15.
1 Samuel 23:27.
Esther 6:1.</margin>
donkeys. Or like that messenger who, by his news, delivered **David** from an extreme distress. Likewise, **Augustus** knew as little why he demanded his tax at exactly this time as **Ahasuerus** <note>The Persian King Xerxes I.</note> did when he had the Chronicles read before him in the night for the preservation of **Mordecai**. See how wonderfully the wheels of God's works run through one another, each in its own time, until the goal is reached. 2. **The obedience of Joseph**, proceeding from his godly spirit; for although every person traveled up to the city where he was assigned, **Joseph** nevertheless had ten-fold reasons to postpone his journey. He had a pregnant wife who was at her latest stage; the way was long, leading over mountainous places, sometimes surrounded by woods and wildernesses; the days were short, and it was toward winter; furthermore, he was a craftsman <note>original: "Ambachtsman." Referring to his trade as a carpenter.</note> of small means, for whom it was more fitting to earn something than to spend his money and time on travel. Notwithstanding all this, he hears the command; he understands that through faith one must trust in God, who knows the reason for all things; that one must be simply obedient, overcoming all inconveniences. He saddles his donkey, sets his wife upon it, and thus walks toward **Bethlehem**, which was some sixteen miles distant <note>The author likely refers to Dutch miles, which were significantly longer than modern English miles; 16 Dutch miles would be roughly 80–90 kilometers.</note>. 3. **The divine protection and preservation** over His own during this dangerous journey; the saying of **David** should be noted: The 
<margin>Psalm 34:8.</margin>
Angel of the Lord encamps round about those who fear Him. It seems to me that

# The First Part

<margin>Luke 2.</margin>
<margin>Matthew 1. John 1.</margin>
The shepherds [were acquainted] with a beautiful heavenly melody, and great joy was shown, and now they [the angels] ascend. This teaches us how God sometimes fills His own with great sweetness, and allows His presence to be enjoyed in a certain way, and then He departs again,
<margin>Matthew 17:4.</margin>
leaving man in his everyday reality; for without this departure, man might say with Peter: "It is good to be here; let us build tabernacles <note>Dutch: "Tabernakelen bauwen." A reference to the Transfiguration, where Peter wanted to stay in the divine presence rather than return to the world.</note> here." Who would desire to part from so perfect a Lord? Thus the shepherds did not go as long as the angels stayed with them, and yet it was necessary that they went, in order to make this joyful message known to others as well. This shall be the first thing to note for our instruction: the diligence of the shepherds in investigating the matter: "Let us go to Bethlehem
<margin>Acts 17:11.</margin>
and see that which has happened there." They held this message in great esteem; they did not let it pass by carelessly. Those of Thessalonica <note>The author likely refers to the Bereans mentioned in Acts 17:11, who were compared favorably to the Thessalonians for their diligence.</note> are praised because they diligently searched that which was told to them by Paul. God gives man understanding and knowledge so that he might put the same to work, specifically in heavenly things that concern the salvation of souls. Some people waste the powers of their understanding on that which is perishable; wherever they hear or perceive of temporal profit, they immediately exert themselves to chase it, but they esteem heavenly things lightly, and show no diligence to fathom them, so that these things completely die away within them. 2. The shepherds took this as being from the Lord. "Let us see what the Lord has made known to us." God deals with people in various ways, now by this means, then by that; and it must all be accepted as a word of the Lord, after the example of these shepherds. The third is their experience: They came in haste; joy drove them, and willing obedience helped in this. And should they not go in haste to such a worthy
<margin>2 Samuel 18:19.</margin>
cause, upon which the salvation of all the world depended? For if Ahimaaz <note>The son of Zadok, who ran to tell King David the news of the victory over Absalom.</note> had cause to announce with haste the death of Absalom, how much more these shepherds the message of life? 3. They found Mary and Joseph, and that Child laid in a manger—a humble <note>Dutch: "onnosele," meaning simple or innocent in this context.</note> appearance. Father and Mother stood there like cast-off strangers, without any further company, except for the beasts in the stable; the Child lay in a manger just like Moses in the basket of reeds <note>Dutch: "biesen kistken."</note>; it was to the Bethlehemites a trivial thing, but to the shepherds a great sign,
<margin>Exodus 2:3.</margin>
as the message of the angels agreed with the reality. When we see a truly humble heart that is cast off from the world, and desires nothing from it,
<margin>1 Timothy 3:9.</margin>
wherein the devout Mary and the chaste Joseph are found, there is the manger of Jesus, and the mystery of faith; let it dwell there in a pure conscience. ### Description of the City of Bethlehem.

<margin>Genesis 35:19.</margin>
The City of Bethlehem also has the surname of Ephrata, and that because of the fertility of the surrounding land <note>The name "Ephrata" is often interpreted as "fruitful" in Hebrew.</note>. It was also called Bethlehem Judah, because it lay in the tribe of Judah / as another Bethlehem was situated in the tribe of Zebulun. It lay upon a high mountain / stretching lengthwise East and West / one and a half miles <note>The Dutch "mijl" was roughly 6 kilometers, making this about 9 kilometers or 5.5 miles.</note> from Jerusalem toward the Southwest. Near this city, the Patriarch Jacob lived in former times. # Of the Life of Jesus Christ.
G 2
<meta>catchword: Christi</meta>

<margin>Luke 2.</margin>
<margin>Matthew 1. John 1.</margin>
[He] is first [placed] under the Law of circumcision; this had to be given on the eighth day to every male, according to the covenant established with Abraham. And this was the first proof of Christ's humility, teaching us obedience to the commandments of God, even if they are painful to fulfill according to the flesh. For this circumcision, which was performed with stone knives <note>Early biblical circumcisions were traditionally performed with flint or sharpened stone.</note>, was a painful work; Zipporah, the wife of Moses, while circumcising her son, called him a <term>Bridegroom of Blood</term> <note>original: "Bloedt-bruydegom"; see Exodus 4:25.</note>. And this name is not ill-suited to Christ, as He, through the shedding of His blood, has acquired a holy congregation as His Bride. Some, observing the blood-sheddings of Christ, count seven of them, of which this is the first. The second: when He sweated water and blood in the Garden of Gethsemane. The third: when He was scourged. The fourth: when the crown of thorns was forced onto His head. The fifth: when He was led out with the cross on His shoulders, by the weight of which the previous wounds were reopened. The sixth: when He was nailed to the cross through His hands and feet. The seventh: when a soldier thrust a lance through His side, from which flowed an abundance of water and blood. Thus, He is rightly said to be that <term>Bridegroom of Blood</term> whom Zipporah signified by her words. Furthermore, this circumcision is a representation of the spiritual circumcision which happens without hands upon the foreskin of the heart—which is the casting off of the sinful flesh—and it is called the "circumcision of Christ" because this is Christ's office, just as the other was the office of Moses or the Law.

<margin>Genesis 17:12.</margin>
<margin>Exodus 4:25.</margin>
<margin>Luke 22:44.</margin>
<margin>John 19:1, 2.</margin>
<margin>Luke 23:25.</margin>
<margin>Mark 15:25.</margin>
<margin>John 19:34.</margin>
<margin>Colossians 2:11.</margin>

In this circumcision, the Name was also given, according to the custom of the Law. Thus, this child was named **JESUS**. But this did not happen by chance, or by the good pleasure of men—as some named their children Jesus, Joshua, Jeshua, or Jason, either because that name pleased them or because someone among their relatives was so named. Rather, this name was given by foreordained counsel by the Angel before He was conceived in His mother’s womb; and this was because no other name truly suited Him, since He was the essential <term>Saviour</term> <note>original: "Salighmaecker"; literally "Salvation-maker."</note> of mankind. God names all things according to the truth of their essence, just as Adam also did when he was in his first state, being illuminated with knowledge. This knowledge was later darkened by the Fall, so that the naming of things is now given improperly according to human whim. Thus, God in His wisdom named His Son with His proper name, just as He did with His forerunner, John. Some have observed that the four unreadable <note>The author refers to the Tetragrammaton (YHWH), the "ineffable" or unpronounceable name of God.</note> letters with which the Hebrews signify God—namely: Yod, He, Vav, He—contain within them the name "Jesus," so that the Jews unknowingly use the name "Jesus" within the Divine name, just as He was not a created being but was one with God in essence.

## Reflection

<margin>Exodus 13:1; Leviticus 12:4</margin>
Joseph and Mary then traveled from Bethlehem to Jerusalem to offer the firstborn according to the Law of Moses; and this occurred after a stay of forty days, which were the days of her purification. Ponder with what joy this procession took place, and in what wonder their thoughts were held—both in considering the Divine providence that this birth had occurred in Bethlehem, and the words of the shepherds who, coming to them in the night, had given such testimony. Mary, hastening to the Temple, might well have said with the holy David: <margin>Psalm 122:1</margin> I rejoiced when it was said to me, let us go into the house of the Lord, and our feet shall stand within your gates, O Jerusalem. But as yet she did not know what would be revealed there. She came and brought, according to her state of poverty, two small turtledoves, expressing the purity and the firm bond of faithfulness between God and the believing soul. Her hand could not afford a lamb <note>Under Mosaic Law, a lamb was the standard offering for purification, but a pair of birds was permitted for those who were poor.</note>; yet she brought the true Lamb in her arms, offering Him to God, and two turtledoves to the priest. This Lamb had such power that He drew to Himself all that was like His nature, even as the <term>lodestone</term> <note>original: "Magneet-steen"; a naturally occurring magnet.</note> draws iron. The aged Simeon was already on his feet throughout the streets, and the prophetess Anna felt a new spiritual youth at the approach of this Magnet, as is evident from what follows.

The first Part / Luke 2. Matthew 1. John 1.

### Reflections.

<margin>Josephus, *Antiquities of the Jews*: Book 15, Chapter 13; Book 14, Chapter 17; Book 17, Chapter 12.</margin>That in these corrupt times there were people who excelled in godliness and were filled with the spirit of prophecy is also testified by Josephus, <note>Flavius Josephus (c. 37–100 AD) was a Romano-Jewish historian whose works provide historical context for the New Testament era.</note> when he speaks of one Manahem the Essene, who predicted to Herod his future kingdom, tyranny, and subsequent punishment; also one Sameas <note>Likely Shammai or Shemaiah, a prominent Pharisaic scholar.</note> who, while sitting in the Council and seeing Herod’s boldness, prophesied the same. And also one Simon who interpreted the dream of Glaphyra, the wife of Archelaus, regarding her downfall, just as it later occurred; these men were held in very high esteem in their time. And of such a kind was this Simeon of whom Luke writes, who not only, along with others, was awaiting the consolation of Israel, but had received a promise from God to see the same with his own eyes before he died, for which he now longed just as Abraham longed for the promised Isaac. He was righteous and God-fearing, a glorious testimony, through which he was worthy to be a dwelling place for the Holy Spirit, just as God always assists and dwells within such people in a special way.

When he had now walked long in faith and reached an extreme old age, seeing no human way by which to reach his desire, he receives a fiery movement of the mind <note>original: "beweghingh des ghemoets"</note> that he must immediately go to the Temple; he does not delay but is obedient to the spiritual Teacher, who leads his own on certain paths. Being there and waiting for the outcome, he sees a holy, God-fearing couple enter with a young Son in their arms. His spirit leaps for joy; the testimony spoke within him just as it did in Samuel when he looked upon David: <margin>1 Samuel 16:12.</margin> *This is he; arise and anoint him.* Immediately those old arms spread open, the child was received therein, and his eyes were turned to Heaven, desiring his release: *Lord, now let your servant depart in peace according to your word.* "There is not an hour more that I desire to live." Jacob wished to die once he had seen Joseph, <margin>Genesis 46:30.</margin> and so it was here as well. Mary and Joseph look at him with great wonder, remembering all that had come before, and they feel great comfort; it did them well to hear him called: the salvation of all peoples, and moreover a light and a glory <note>original: "prijs," meaning honor or glory in this context</note> of Israel.

As they meditated on the power of these words, it bore an exceptional fruit in their souls, but soon after followed a thunderclap: *Behold, this child is set for the fall and rising of many in Israel,* and after that, something even heavier: *And for a sign which shall be spoken against.* O Simeon! we have already experienced this in part; for this happy child was by necessity born in a stable, and no one would receive him in the Inn; what else shall happen to us with this same child? So hear further: *A sword shall pierce through your own soul.* This sword began its work through the persecution of Herod and the flight into Egypt, but it was fully drawn and, as it were, twisted in the heart during the Passion and bitter suffering...

"Piercing" <note>original: "Dringen," suggesting a forceful, agonizing pressure</note> is a word for a powerful pressure, applied as if with a screw, or like someone trying to force themselves through a narrow opening where they cannot easily pass; experience teaches what kind of pain this is. These words might have saddened Mary and Joseph somewhat, but new comfort arrived. An old and very devout woman, who served God in the Temple with constant fasting and prayer and possessed the Spirit of Prophecy, came at that very time. Beholding this newborn child with great devotion, she acknowledged Him to be a Lord; despite the poor and humble status of the parents, she confirmed everything Simeon had said and spoke of great things regarding this child. <margin>Deuteronomy 33:24.</margin> The blessing of her father Asher rested upon her: *may your old age be as your youth.* She was indeed old in days, having been born in the time of Alexander, King of the Jews <note>Alexander Jannaeus, who ruled from 103 to 76 BC.</note>, the father of Hyrcanus and Aristobulus; thus, she had lived through all the uprisings and miseries under these rulers, as well as the conquest of Jerusalem under Pompey, with all the bloodshed and destruction under Herod. Yet, in all these troubles, she had preserved the youth of the Spirit. She looked forward to the Savior, embraced Him now, and as a prophetess, spoke of Him to all who waited for redemption in Jerusalem. This caused some stir, though most of it was triggered by the arrival of the Wise Men from the East, which followed later.

### Reflection.

They did not omit anything of what they were bound to do according to the Law of Moses. And it was fitting for the Son of God to have such parents, guardians, and precursors who were faithful and righteous in all that they knew to be pleasing and acceptable to God. They did not remain within the borders of the Judean countryside but returned to Galilee where they lived; they had come from Nazareth to Bethlehem because of the census, as the Evangelist Luke has said before. In this way, there are commonly occurring causes by which the godly, along with others, change their dwelling and place. For the sake of <margin>Genesis 12:10.</margin> a time of famine <note>original: "dieren tijdts," literally 'expensive time' or period of scarcity</note>, Abraham traveled into Egypt; Elimelech into the...

The First Part / Luke 2. Matthew 1. John 1.

<margin>Ruth 1:1; 2 Kings 8:1</margin>
...the land of the Moabites; the Shunammite woman <note>A woman from Shunem who, according to 2 Kings 8, left her home during a famine to live among the Philistines for seven years.</note> among the Philistines; and that for a certain time, returning thereafter again to their old dwelling place, just as Joseph and Mary have done here.

### Historical continuation.

<margin>Alsted, Chronology 11; Baronius, Year 1, number 6; Calvin in the Harmony of Matthew 2; Eusebius in his Chronology; Epiphanius in Panarion, Book 1, volume 1 at the end, and against Heresy 30; Bunting in Travelogue of the New Testament.</margin>
Luke does not mention the story of the Wise Men from the East, which took place at Bethlehem and is described at length by Matthew; now there is a difference of opinion regarding the time when this occurred. Some believe that the Wise Men followed immediately upon the birth of Christ, namely thirteen days thereafter. Others argue that it required more time and was not feasible to arrive there so quickly from Persia—which was over two hundred miles away—adding as a reason that during the presentation of Christ in the Temple, it was not evident that they were provided with any rich gifts; otherwise, they would have sacrificed a lamb instead of two pigeons <note>Under Mosaic Law, a lamb was the standard offering, but those who could not afford it were permitted to offer two turtledoves or pigeons.</note>. And this also seems the most likely to us, but then there is a difficulty: since Luke testifies above that they returned to Nazareth after fulfilling the requirements of the Law, how could the Wise Men have found the child Jesus in Bethlehem? 

To this, an answer is given: that they either returned there of their own accord to live, or were directed there by divine providence, just as the census had been previously arranged so that the birth would occur there. For it is evident that the killing of the Bethlehemite children <note>The Massacre of the Innocents ordered by King Herod.</note> occurred little less than two years after the birth of Christ, according to Herod’s calculation from the mouth of the aforementioned Wise Men; wherefore it would not be strange that their arrival had also been delayed for some time, both due to the long journey they had to make and due to the time they spent in Jerusalem searching for the child. Indeed, this latter opinion, which seems most probable to us, is what we have followed in the description of our history. Meanwhile, we leave everyone free to their own opinion.
