### Historical continuation.

<margin>Alsted, *Chronology* 11; Baronius, *Annals* 1, num. 6; Calvin in *Harmony of Matthew 2*; Eusebius in *Chronicles*; Epiphanius in *The Panarion* <note>original: "in Panar." — A Greek work by Epiphanius of Salamis refuting heresies.</note> Book 1, vol. 1; Bunting in *Travels of the New Testament*.</margin>Luke does not mention the history of the Wise Men from the East, which occurred at Bethlehem and is described at length by Matthew; now there is a dispute over the time when this happened. Some believe that the Wise Men followed immediately upon the birth of Christ / namely thirteen days thereafter <note>This refers to the Feast of the Epiphany, traditionally celebrated on January 6th.</note>. Others [believe] that it required more time / and [it was] not very feasible to be there so quickly from Persia, which was over two hundred miles away <note>The author likely refers to German leagues or "long miles," as the actual distance from Persia to Bethlehem is much greater than 200 modern miles.</note>; they add as a reason: That in the offering of Christ in the Temple <note>The Presentation in the Temple, 40 days after birth.</note> it did not appear that they were provided with any rich gifts, otherwise they would surely have offered a lamb instead of two young pigeons <note>Under Mosaic Law (Leviticus 12), those who could not afford a lamb were permitted to sacrifice two turtledoves or pigeons.</note>. And this also seems to us the most probable: but then the difficulty is: since Luke testifies above that they returned to Nazareth / after fulfilling the requirements of the Law / how the Wise Men could have found the child Jesus at Bethlehem. To this, the answer is given / that they either returned there of their own accord to live / or were directed there by some Divine arrangement / just as the census was previously arranged so that the birth would occur there. For it is evident that the killing of the children of Bethlehem <note>Commonly known as the Massacre of the Innocents.</note> happened little less than two years after the birth of Christ / according to Herod's calculation from the mouths of the aforementioned Wise Men / it would then not be strange that their arrival had also been delayed for some time / both by the long journey they had to make / as well as by the time they spent in Jerusalem seeking the child. Indeed, we have followed this latter opinion, which seems most probable to us, in the description of our History. Leaving, meanwhile, everyone to their own opinion.

The First Part / MATTHEW 2. Luke 2. John 1.

### Observation.

Luke, having recounted at length the birth of Christ; the causes by which it occurred in Bethlehem, and other circumstances serving the matter: Matthew now comes and relates another worthy and exceptional story which followed the birth of Christ. This history was not only prefigured in the Old Testament <margin>1 Kings 10:1 <note>original: "1. Reg. 10. 1." referring to 1 Regum, the Latin title for 1 Kings.</note></margin> by the Queen of Sheba, who came from distant lands to honor the wisdom of Solomon: but it was also foretold through clear prophecies. Let us now take up the text for a moment.

When Jesus was born. The Evangelist does not describe the time precisely, but indicates that this happened in the times of Herod: a King who was very famous for his power and raging tyranny. Just as Moses was also born in the times of a great tyrant, namely: King Pharaoh in Egypt, who sought the life of the newborn child, just as this Herod did. <margin>Josephus, *Antiquities of the Jews*, Book 2, Chapter 5 <note>original: "Ioseph. Antiq lib. 2. Cap. 5."</note></margin> [Pharaoh] was also no less fearful, jealous, and tormented by unease over the rumors and prophecies of the Egyptian Sages, who made it known that one would arise from the Hebrews to the great detriment of his realm and royal dominion.

See how wondrously God works in the minds of men; he also lets his secrets and hidden counsel be known among the Gentiles. To their Priests, their Sages, and their Scribes—who are the eyes of the people—he makes known what he intends, and that according to the measure of their understanding and according to the light bestowed upon them. He intends to show that he is a universal God over all nations of men, just as he is their creator and sustainer.

<margin>Baronius, *Annals*, Year 1, Number 3; Chrysostom, *Homily 6 on Matthew* <note>original: "Baron. An. 1. num 3. Chryfost. Hom. 6. in Math."</note></margin> 1. These Wise Men or Magi, whom the Evangelist Matthew describes here, were high, wise, and intelligent men in the Kingdom of the Persians; very learned in astrology <note>original: "Sterre-konst", literally "star-craft." In the 17th century, astronomy and astrology were often treated as a single discipline involving the study of celestial omens.</note>, such that they took very close note of the course of the stars, knowing sometimes how to foretell certain things from their positions. This was because these heavenly bodies have some connection with earthly ones and can give some indication of their events to those who are very experienced in them. <margin>Daniel 2:2; Daniel 5:7 <note>original: "Dan 2. 2. Dan. 5. 7."</note></margin> These Magi or star-gazers have always been held in high regard from of old by the Chaldeans and reckoned among their nobility, as can be noted in various places from the Prophet Daniel. Afterwards, they were in such high esteem among the Persians that they were the teachers of their Kings; indeed, Kings were even sometimes chosen from their number, <margin>Justin, Book 1 <note>original: "Iustin. Lib. 1." referring to the Roman historian Marcus Junianus Justinus.</note></margin> as the example of Darius Hystaspis can prove. From this it has arisen that some give these Magi the name of Kings, adding that they were three in number; though this is based on a misunderstanding and without any certainty from Holy Scripture or credible histories.

Besides the fact that these Magi were very experienced in Astrology, they had—

### Reflection.

<margin>MATTHEW 2.</margin>
Herod was deceived according to his own thinking, but in truth, it is no deception when a false deceiver—intent on murder and the shedding of blood—is himself thwarted. For such a deceiver deceives himself far more and is led captive into his own snares when the false command he relied upon is not obeyed. Yet men of this nature reveal themselves to be far more violent than reasonable and sensible people; they take offense at the conduct of the godly as if their own honor had been diminished and their Majesty grievously wounded. 

1. Anger found a greater place in him because, in his old age, like a cruel Saturn <note>In Roman mythology, Saturn (or the Greek Cronus) famously devoured his own children to prevent them from usurping him. The author compares this to Herod's historical executions of his own family members.</note>, he had recently killed his sons Alexander and Aristobulus. Having gained no peace thereby, he was increasingly disturbed, and now, driven to a frenzy by the Magi's report of this newborn King, he hardly knew what to do in his wickedness. It was not enough for him to conduct a narrow search for this child and kill him; all of Bethlehem and the surrounding countryside had to mourn for it, <margin>ESTHER 3:6.</margin> just as Haman <note>The antagonist of the Book of Esther who plotted a genocide against the Jewish people.</note> sought to destroy not only Mordecai but the entire Jewish nation.

2. He could not be moved by the weeping of the children or the lamentation of the mothers as they saw the naked swords approaching and, still bloody from one child, being pressed into another. The piteous wailing on the mountains of Rachel, the wringing of hands and tearing of hair that was heard in all the surrounding borders, could not restrain his tyrannical mind. <margin>GENESIS 35:17.</margin> 

3. Rachel seemed to feel a foretaste of this in the birthing of Benjamin, when she spoke mournfully: *A Son of my sorrows* <note>original: "Een Sone mijnder pijnen"—referring to the Hebrew name Ben-oni, which Rachel gave her son as she died.</note>, and thereafter gave up her spirit with deep sighs. She, still mourning through the Prophet Jeremiah, wept for this sorrowful slaughter of children which followed about 600 years later, renewing those bleak voices once more, amplifying them through the echoing of the mountains which called this tragedy out to one another. Stones are sooner moved to receive the complaints of the innocent than are the stony hearts which are deadened by cruelty and robbed of all humanity. 

<margin>MACROBIUS, Saturnalia, Book 2, Chapter 4. PHILO, Book 2 on Time. EXODUS 2:1. JOSEPHUS, Antiquities, Book 2, Chapter 5.</margin>

### Historical Continuation.

<margin>Josephus, Antiquities, Book 17, Chapters 6, 7.</margin> Not long after this, divine vengeance—which follows the wicked on woolen feet <note>A Dutch idiom meaning that justice approaches silently and stealthily before striking.</note>—overtook Herod, making him feel divine justice even in this life. <margin>Chapter 8.</margin> Thereupon followed Herod’s illness, which seized him violently in every part of his body. At times he sought to regain his health through medicines; at other times he sought to vent his anger upon the Council of the Jews, <margin>Chapter 9.</margin> whom he ordered to be locked inside a racecourse <note>Herod’s plan was to have these leaders executed the moment he died, so that the Jewish nation would be forced to mourn at the time of his passing.</note>. At yet other times, he sought to end his own suffering by his own hand, calling for a knife for that purpose, which he intended to plunge into his throat, had he not been prevented. Thus he was driven by a thousand fears and distractions; he was grieved that the Jews looked forward to his death, and yet he could not endure the long-lasting suffering which threatened him with death through ever-increasing pangs. ### Reflection.

The Evangelist Luke follows in good order the chronology of the youth of Christ; for although he does not recount many specific events, he nevertheless makes known in brief words the manner of Christ’s upbringing: that it was highly exceptional and fruitful. <margin>Genesis 37:3.</margin>
the children of Jacob, Joseph was the most exceptional, bearing signs of his future glory, and for that reason was hated by them all. The young boy Samuel grew in the presence of the Lord. Solomon, 

<margin>2 Samuel 12:24.</margin>
having been raised under the hand of Nathan, was beloved of the Lord and gifted with wisdom above his other older brothers,

When he reached his third year, God gave him such a countenance that there was no one so wild that they did not stare at him when they saw his beautiful appearance. And it often happened when he was carried across the street, that people were so amazed by him that they forgot their work and left it, so that they might look at him enough. He was such a lovely, beautiful child that no one could gaze upon him enough.* These examples teach us that in Jesus there were no fewer signs of his wisdom and grace, since the "images" <note>The author uses "af-beeldinghen" (images) to refer to biblical typology—the idea that Old Testament figures like Moses or Isaac serve as "types" or previews of Christ.</note> do not surpass the one who is being portrayed.

For everyone knows well through experience how little natural understanding there is in a child of twelve years, and especially one raised under such parents / being more practiced in daily manual labor for the support of the house / than in any learning or deep investigation of <term>Theological things</term> <note>matters concerning the study of God and religious doctrine</note> / in which even ingenious men, spending their whole lives, find enough to do just to understand some of the first principles. So then, this worthy History that Luke describes here shows us six remarkable things. The first is the willing obedience that Jesus showed to his Parents in going up to Jerusalem / a place situated so far away / and for his youth very difficult for travel / for it is well known that he did not do this for his own sake, since the supreme wisdom has no need of the lesser: And this journeying should also teach us / that we should not always maintain the gathering of the pious for our own sake / but out of a devoted love / to promote the general edification / which otherwise easily falls away and vanishes / if we despise the little ones / and because of some defect we might perceive, withdraw ourselves from those of lower status than us. The second is the sweet company that his Parents had with him on the road / for it is very much to be believed that his innate wisdom showed no small signs to his Parents / whether through wise questioning / teachings from natural things / willing help on the road / and whatever else is becoming of a modest and intelligent youth. The third is / his secret withdrawal within the city of Jerusalem / in which he seemed, contrary to his habit, to act against the Law of obedience / yet meanwhile showed the greatest submission to his Heavenly Father / to whom he was most bound. Herewith setting an example that in matters of Religion one must not look so much to the will of the Parents / that one should surrender the freedom of one's <term>Conscience</term> <note>the inner sense of right and wrong, especially regarding religious duty</note> and lie imprisoned as if in slavery under the discretion of others / even if they are wise and understanding / and take the matter most to heart. ## Remark.

In these short words the Evangelist makes known / the further upbringing of Jesus in his youth / just as he had spoken before of his childhood. *Jesus increased in wisdom.* That is: he proceeded thus / and took on yet more and more of that same wisdom / of which he had now given proof in Jerusalem. It was no human wisdom / which was poured into him through instruction / or School-learning <term>School-geleertheydt</term> <note>Refers to formal academic or rabbinical training as opposed to innate divine knowledge.</note> / but a Divine one / which sprang from the nature of his Spirit. For in him was the Spirit of the Lord, the Spirit of wisdom, <margin>Isaiah 11:2.</margin> and of understanding: the Spirit of counsel, and of strength: the Spirit of knowledge and of the fear of the Lord. Some have indeed a good beginning in their youth / appearing fiery and forward in virtue / yet the further they get in years / the more they slacken therein: indeed, they finally become children of a hundred years <note>A reference to Isaiah 65:20, implying those who grow old in age but remain spiritual infants or sinners.</note>. But in Jesus it was not so: He increased <margin>Isaiah 65:19.</margin> constantly / not only in wisdom / but also in age <note>The original "oudtheydt" refers to both physical age and the maturity associated with it.</note>: He did nothing foolishly in his time: his youth was even as a ripe old age: For true gray hair does not consist in a multitude of years, but in an unblemished life. That same thing makes one perfect in a short time / <margin>Wisdom 4:3 and 7. <note>original: "Sap. 4. 3. en 7." refers to the Book of the Wisdom of Solomon.</note></margin> and quickly fulfills many years. Others do not attain their old age / while the godless never brings his life even to the half <margin>Psalm 55:24.</margin>. So then Jesus was in the years of his youth; chosen as Joseph / beautiful as Moses / strong as Samson / wise as Solomon / understanding as Daniel; and obedient as Isaac. Carrying through a perfect example for the instruction of all states of people. He also increased in grace before God, that is: He had a gracious / pleasant / lovely nature / and that not made / or assumed hypocritically / for this or for that / but he was such in truth before God / just as the new man is described by the Apostle: that he is in all righteousness and holiness. One <margin>Ephesians 4:24.</margin> can also understand from these words / that he was revealed before God his Father to be such / although he was covered as with a cloud of humiliation / just like a common craftsman / or as a son of the same: And that he [kept] his hidden interaction and Divine

### Historical Continuation.

It shall not be unhelpful to our Gospel History / also to set down here / what happened in these years of Christ in the meantime / both in the Jewish lands as in other regions / especially of that which is worthy of note.

<margin>Josephus, *Antiquities*, Book 17, Chapter 15. Book 11, Chapter 1.</margin>
In the year of Christ 14, the 55th of the Emperor Augustus, King Archelaus <note>Son of Herod the Great, who ruled as ethnarch of Judea, Samaria, and Idumea.</note> was summoned to Rome / removed from his Kingdom / and sent into exile to the city of Vienne <note>original: "Wien in Vranckrijck" – This refers to Vienne in modern-day France, then part of Roman Gaul, not Vienna, Austria.</note> in France. Coponius was ordained Governor in Judea / Cyrenius <note>Quirinius</note> assessed the province of Syria for the second time and sold the property of Archelaus. Jeozarus was High Priest.

IN the fifteenth year of the reign of Emperor Tiberius, when Pontius Pilatus was governor <note>original: "rechter", literally judge or magistrate, referring to his role as governor of the province</note> in Judea, and Herod was a Tetrarch <term>Tetrarch: A ruler of a quarter-part of a province; from the Greek "tetrarchēs"</term> in Galilee, and his brother Philip a Tetrarch of the land of Iturea and Trachonitis: and Lysanias a Tetrarch of the land of Abilene. #### Observation.

<margin>Baronius: Annals, Book 3, Number 1. Luke 3:23. Luke 2:1.</margin>
Luke has carefully noted the time; namely: That in the fifteenth year of Emperor Tiberius, the word of God came to John. And in the Roman histories one finds that the Consuls <note>original: "Borgher-Meesters", meaning mayors or chief magistrates, a common early modern term for the Roman Consuls</note> were then Rubellius and Fufius, both with the surname of Geminus. From this description by Luke, and from what he says thereafter—that **Jesus** was nearly thirty years old—one calculates the time of his birth, and according to all the other Gospel Histories. He had previously spoken of Emperor Augustus, and now he mentions Tiberius, who succeeded him in the Empire; and how under the same, Pontius Pilatus was Governor in Judea; who now, according to our previous description, had entered into the third year of his office. All histories agree with this: and especially Josephus, who describes the histories of the Jews, <margin>Josephus: Antiquities, Book 17, Chapter 13.</margin> relating how after the death of Herod the Great the Kingdom was divided among his sons: as we have shown more broadly in its place. Now he mentions Herod the Tetrarch in Galilee, surnamed Antipas, and of Philip his brother, who [governed] Iturea and Trachonitis

### Reflection.

<margin>Luke 16:16.</margin>
That this was the very first beginning of the **Gospel** <term>Gospel: from the Greek 'Evangelium', meaning 'good news'</term>, the Lord testifies in another place, saying: *The Law and the Prophets prophesied until John, and from then on the Kingdom of God has been proclaimed through the Gospel.* The excellence of this beginning is confirmed here with two prophecies: one from **Malachi**, where John the Baptist is described as an **Angel** <note>original: 'Engel'; used here in the sense of a messenger or herald sent by God</note>; another from **Isaiah**, where he is called: *A voice crying in the wilderness*; just as he was in truth. This serves as a lesson to us: That the rough, unrefined person (who is nothing else than a wilderness full of vermin, Lions, Dragons, and Snakes) must be prepared through the **preaching of repentance** <term>preaching of repentance: 'boet-Predicatie', a call for internal change and sorrow for sins</term> by John, before the grace-filled word of Christ can find entry there: For the Lamb does not associate with the Wolf, nor does the Heavenly Bridegroom enter a place that is impure and stained with sin.

---

### LUKE CHAPTER III.

<margin>Verse</margin>
5 *Every valley shall be filled, and every mountain and hill shall be brought low: And what is crooked shall be made straight, and what is uneven shall become a smooth way.*
6 *And all flesh shall see the salvation of God.*

### Reflection.

When a King is about to travel, as one sees with advancing Armies, the path is made level for him, the heights are cast down, and the valleys filled. So also, for the coming of this great King, a preparation is necessary: The deep valleys of sorrowful and anxious hearts are filled with comfort; the high mountains of pride that puff themselves up through their own wisdom and vain conceit must be cast down and humbled, so that all may come to a state of equality, just as God is uniform and equal. Those who were despised and rejected by the Jews as people ignorant of God's Law were called by this **Herald** <term>Herald: 'Heraut', an official messenger announcing the arrival of a monarch</term> to prepare their hearts. Until then, the Jewish people had some cause for boasting, but now the **Salvation of God** has come to all People. Besides this, his calling voice, John had an exceptionally imposing presence, through which he was regarded by everyone as an envoy of the Most High: As the **Evangelists** <note>The writers of the four Gospels: Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John</note> further make known.

It emphasizes that Christ's message requires a foundation of repentance and humility, moving beyond Jewish exclusivity to offer salvation to all humanity.</summary>

The Evangelist intends to show that John was a man of an extraordinarily strict life, not unlike **Elijah the Tishbite** <term>Elijah the Tishbite: a major Old Testament prophet known for his asceticism and confrontation with kings</term> in his clothing, who wore a rough skin and was girded with a leather belt. It is thus that John, excelling in this manner of living, gained great respect among the people, and his word gained great power. So much so that they came to him in multitudes from the City of Jerusalem and the entire Judean Land, and all the land around the Jordan. **That is:** namely, a great and nearly countless number of people, not only to hear his preaching, but also to obey, coming with a moved heart: **Confessing their sins**, which is a thing that does not happen except from a great contrition of the mind, since man through **innate pride** <term>innate pride: 'in-ghebozen hooghmoet', the human tendency to hide faults to appear righteous</term> usually prefers to cover and minimize his sins rather than confess them. They let themselves be baptized by him: Which baptism was so famous that even **Josephus** <note>original: 'Joſephus'; a 1st-century Jewish historian who is one of the few non-biblical sources to mention John the Baptist</note> in his historical description makes mention of it, adding how he exhorted the people to earnest repentance, as is also seen in what follows.

### Observation.

The greatest wonder was that these stubborn Sects <note>referring to the Pharisees and Sadducees</note> were also moved in their hearts to come to John, desiring his baptism; the hand of God was clearly visible in this. For the nature and character of these men is well revealed by John’s address to them when he calls them: *Generations of Vipers*, <note>original: "Gheslachten der Slanghen"</note> that is, devious and wicked people who have the venom of adders under their lips.
<margin>Psalm 140:4. Romans 3:13.</margin>
He attributes this to the Pharisees as well as the Sadducees. By this, he signifies the perverse nature of humans, who in their animalistic state—outside of rebirth <term>rebirth: the spiritual transformation or "regeneration" required for salvation</term>—are no better than irrational creatures, who each live and move according to their own inclinations; and for this reason, they are frequently described in Holy Scripture not only as Serpents and Adders, but also as Lions, Wolves, Foxes, Dragons, and similar wild beasts.
<margin>Matthew 23:32. Ezekiel 19:2. Matthew 10:16. Luke 13:30.</margin>
Therefore, John exhorts them to produce the sincere fruits of repentance; <note>original: "vruchten van boete"</note> that is, a true turning of the heart, so that not only are outward behaviors restrained and controlled, but the inclinations and affections of the soul are also changed and made into "New Men." Alongside this, he strips away their vain refuge and deceptive delusion, which the Jewish nation and especially these sects boasted of and prided themselves on, namely: That they were children of Abraham, as if natural birth contributed anything toward Salvation.
<margin>John 8:33</margin>
For this reason, he demonstrates that God was able to turn the stony hearts of the Tax Collectors <term>Tax Collectors: often called Publicans, these were Jews who collected taxes for Rome and were socially and religiously marginalized</term> and Sinners—who were despised by the religious elite—into children of Abraham through faith. These would far exceed the religious leaders in number if there were any reason to boast; truly, this defect remains to this day, as many people boast of the Christian name, and how they were raised in it by parents and ancestors: Crying "here is the Temple of the Lord, here is the Temple of the Lord," <note>a reference to Jeremiah 7:4, critiquing those who rely on institutional religion rather than personal faith</note> just as the Jews did in former times; but John proves here how deceptive such a thing is.
<margin>Jeremiah 7:4.</margin>
He further declares: That the axe, which is the sharp judgment of God, is set to the root, not to the branches or leaves which could sprout again in greater numbers, but to the root of the heart's foundation. This is expressed more clearly elsewhere: That God's word is living and powerful, and sharper than any two-edged sword, cutting down and penetrating wherever it reaches.
<margin>Hebrews 4:12.</margin>
But this is also not inappropriately understood to refer to the eternal

### Observation.

One notices in the common people much more contrition and agitation of soul regarding the preaching of this heavenly messenger than in those who attributed light and wisdom to themselves; the common proverb is true here: *the more learned, the more perverse* <note>original: "hoe gheleerder hoe verkeerder", a traditional Dutch saying suggesting that intellectual pride often leads to spiritual error</note>. John, then, seeing these willing hearts asking "What shall we do?", counsels them to works of mercy <note>original: "barmhertigheydt"</note> as the only means to draw near to God and escape His punishment: He who has two <margin>Dan. 4:26</margin> coats, let him give to him who has none; for the withholding of the portion belonging to the poor creates inequality, and consequently the misery among the human race. The tax collectors, who are generally greedy and unshakeable people, also stood here contrite and confounded <note>original: "pessust", meaning perplexed or stunned</note>, asking counsel of this messenger who pierced hearts with his voice: "What shall we do?" He points them to the known path: to demand no more than what was set, for greed had driven them beyond these bounds, often bringing the people into many undeserved fines and penalties, assaulting and exhausting <note>original: "upt gemerghelt", literally "sucking the marrow out"</note> them by misusing the power of authority. The casting off of this injustice was the first step they had to climb in order to [come] to Christ.

<margin>Matthew 3. Mark 1. Luke 3. John 1.</margin>
...gathering the trees <note>The author uses trees here as a metaphor for people or the fruits of one's life</note> like Wheat: the ungodly and those who were mixed among the wheat under the appearance of godliness; and like Chaff: as
<margin>Psalm 1:5.</margin>
David also indicates in the first Psalm. These would now be made manifest through the stirring of the Gospel, and as if shaken with the winnowing fan <note>A "wan" or winnowing fan was a tool used to toss grain into the air so the wind would blow away the lighter, useless husks (chaff) while the heavy, valuable grain (wheat) fell back down</note>, tossed up and down by various trials, persecutions, and temptations. The Chaff, being unable to endure these, would be scattered by those gusts of wind, so that the Wheat—having been separated from the Chaos—might be gathered purely together in the Barn of eternal preservation.

The Evangelist further relates that John preached yet other things to the people: Of which Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus was a 1st-century Jewish historian whose works provide outside confirmation of biblical figures</note> makes some mention,
<margin>Josephus Antiquities Book 18. Chapter 6. <note>In modern editions, this is usually found in Book 18, Chapter 5, Section 2.</note></margin>
when he says: "John exhorted the people that their baptism would then be acceptable to God, when they did not merely abstain from one or two sins, but earnestly purified the heart through righteousness, and thereafter also the body." This agrees with the Evangelists, who testify that John first exhorted the people to true repentance before he gave them Baptism, which is according to the right order of God.

### Chapter Two.

->*Jesus coming from Galilee to the Jordan: Let him be Baptized by John, which was followed by a Heavenly testimony. Thereafter his lineage and age are described.*<-

### Historical Continuation.

<margin>Luke 2:52.</margin>
Until now, Jesus had kept himself quiet within the city of Nazareth, living as a common man. He was certainly outstanding in his life—in wisdom, piety, obedience, and all modest manners—but in such a way that no noteworthy thing has been described of him since his twelfth year; it did not yet appear that he was such a great person as he afterwards made himself known to be. And in this
<margin>Exodus 3:1.</margin>
he bore a resemblance to Moses, who was first hidden from the eyes of the children of Israel for a long time (first in the Court of Pharaoh, and thereafter with the Priest in Midian), only to later reveal himself suddenly like a flash of lightning.

### Observation.

<margin>Mark 1:9</margin>
Mark says clearly that Jesus did not only come from Galilee, but also from the city of Nazareth, where he had been raised and where he had stayed until now. The time is not precisely described, only that it was while John was baptizing the people with a great following. Some understand (and not inappropriately) that it was in the month of November, called <term>Casleu|The ninth month of the Hebrew religious calendar, usually falling in November or December.</term> by the Hebrews, understanding that Jesus was not yet fully thirty years old. Others hold it was in January when the thirtieth year was completed and the thirty-first had begun. Since little depends on this, we shall observe the things of which the text speaks and which can give us teaching.

# The Second Part /

<margin>John 1.</margin>
-> MATTHEW 3. MARK 1. LUKE 3. <-

The Jordan River flows from the Sea of Galilee and ends in the Dead Sea, where formerly the fertile and well-watered lands of the Sodomites <note>The "Sodomites" refers to the inhabitants of Sodom and Gomorrah; the Dead Sea was historically believed to have covered the site of these cities.</note> were located. It is a 
<margin>Joshua 3:13.</margin>
river where God in former times had shown many miracles, such as the stopping 
<margin>2 Kings 2:8.</margin>
of the current to bring the Ark across, as well as the dividing of the waters in the time of Elijah. But especially relevant to this 
<margin>2 Kings 5:10.</margin>
purpose is that Naaman of Syria, by the counsel of Elisha, washed himself seven times herein and was thereby delivered from his leprosy: so that it might serve in some way as a foreshadowing of this Baptism. 

2. Jesus requested Baptism from John, not because he had any leprosy of the body or of the soul—as did the other unclean multitude—nor because he was less than John and thus had to receive his baptism and mission from him; not at all, but as he himself testifies: to fulfill all righteousness. For if baptism had been despised by Jesus as an unnecessary thing for him to undergo—either because the water in itself was powerless, or because the person who baptized there was of less worth than he—then he would have brought his Father’s institution into contempt. The disciples of John themselves would have had reason to reject Jesus, or to accuse their Master of fickleness for recommending such a person to them who would not even submit himself to his baptism (which John said was from God).

It also belongs to the righteousness of a Lawgiver that he himself fulfills his own laws in deed, just as Lycurgus and Zaleucus <note>Lycurgus of Sparta and Zaleucus of Locri were legendary Greek lawgivers praised by ancient authors for living by the strict codes they established for their citizens.</note> are praised for 
<margin>Luke 11:46.</margin>
strengthening their laws through example. In contrast, the Pharisees are accused of being unrighteous Lawgivers because they pressed heavy burdens onto other people's necks, which they themselves would not touch with a single finger. So then Jesus obediently bowed himself under the law of his Father, with whom he was one, and thus fulfilled all righteousness. Seeing this, John turned away from his humble refusal, which had 
<margin>John 13:8</margin>
arisen out of reverence and self-deprecation; just as Peter did during the washing of the feet. He acknowledged, and with reason, that he indeed needed to be baptized by him—namely, with the Holy Spirit, which is properly the baptism of Christ—testifying hereby that he had some knowledge of the person of Christ, but not as complete and certain as afterward, when the descent of the Holy Spirit and the testimony from Heaven were added to it. 

3. See then Jesus standing here alongside the other common people, as if he too were a sinner, receiving the baptism of repentance from the hand of John. Through which humiliation he teaches us to lay aside presumptuous self-righteousness, and rather to bear guilt while innocent than to appear innocent while being guilty. He climbed out of the water where he had previously entered. From which it appears that the custom of that time 
<margin>Luke 3:21.</margin>
in those warm countries was to use an abundance of water in Baptism <note>The author suggests that baptism by immersion was the standard practice due to the climate and the phrasing "climbing out of the water."</note>. 4. After that (as Luke testifies) he betook himself to prayer,

# Of the Life of Jesus Christ
D 2

### MATTHEW 3. MARK 1. LUKE 3.
<margin>John 1.</margin>
...beginning most devovoutly this new way of life, in order to give himself entirely to the service of his Heavenly Father, to which he had been sent. And what happened then? The Heavens were opened; signifying the power of prayer mixed with a submissive obedience of life, even in the smallest things. That the Heavens now often remain closed above us is because we do not faithfully walk in his footsteps: upright obedience is the key to Heaven, as the Apostle John testifies in one place: *Whatever we ask we shall receive from him, because we keep his commandments and do what is pleasing to him.* <note>Reference to 1 John 3:22.</note> On the contrary, disobedience shuts the Heaven tight and makes prayers powerless. 

A certain Desert Father, <note>The Dutch "Oudt-Vader" refers to the early Christian hermits and monks of the Egyptian desert whose stories were popular moral examples.</note> having a disciple who lay deeply ensnared in sin, was requested by the same to pray to God for him. When this had happened several times and no benefit came of it, the disciple said: "Father, your prayers are not being heard." The elder, wishing to instruct him through an example, said: "Go and fill that sack with sand for me, and bring it here." The disciple, having filled the sack and wishing to lift it up, found the elder holding the sack fast by one corner, saying to him: "Why do you not lift it up?" To which he answered: "How should I do that, for you are holding it fast?" "That is true," said the elder, "and in the same way you also hold my prayers fast with your sins, so that they will not rise up before God." There are also various examples in Holy Scripture which sufficiently prove that sin is the partition wall between God and man.

<margin>1 John 3:22.</margin>
¶ 5. Furthermore, after the Heavens were opened, John saw the Holy Spirit descending like a dove upon Jesus. O noble expression! Of the pure, simple nature of the Divine being. O true anointing! How sweet-smelling and lovely you have descended upon the head of this Heavenly King and Priest. In this he has surpassed all his companions, for they have received the shadow, but he the true essence. What a joy this birthed in the heart of John, who besides this assurance also heard that glorious voice: *This is my beloved Son in whom I am well pleased.* Never was such a testimony given of anyone, for he was the only-begotten.

The Elders in the early Church held this example of Christ in great esteem; for besides understanding that they (according to the custom of the Apostles) first had to be catechumens <note>original: "Catechumenos"; Greek for "those being instructed." In the early church, converts underwent a long period of study before baptism.</note> and well-instructed in Christian doctrine before they received Baptism, some of them also [delayed] baptism...

->Of the life of Jesus Christ. Luke 1. Matthew 3. Mark 1. John 1.<-

...was the son of <term>Shem</term><note>A son of Noah, traditionally considered the ancestor of the Semitic peoples.</note>, who was the son of Noah, who was the son of Lamech. Who was the son of Methuselah, who was the son of Enoch, who was the son of Jared, who was the son of Mahalaleel, who was the son of Cainan. Who was the son of Enos, who was the son of Seth, who was the son of Adam, who was the son of God.

### Remark.

The <term>genealogy</term><note>original: "gheslachten Register"</note> which Matthew describes at the beginning of his book, Luke has saved until this time, when Jesus, having attained his manly age, begins to enter into his office. At this time, he may no longer be counted under the obedience of his parents as a son of Joseph, but as a Son of God, his Heavenly Father, into whose work he now entirely commits himself. Therefore, Luke, beginning from below, does not rest at Abraham as Matthew does, but climbing all the way up, he comes through all the first Patriarchs as if by steps unto Adam, and finally unto God, the origin of all things, from whom the <term>eternal Word</term><note>A theological reference to Jesus as the "Logos" or Word of God mentioned in John 1:1.</note> had descended.

Now there appears to be a difficulty in the difference of this Register between Matthew and Luke, specifically from the times of David until Christ. One traces the line from Solomon, the other from Nathan, also a son of David. But this can easily be resolved in several ways. First, some take it thus: that Joseph was a natural son of Jacob, and a legal son of Heli. That is to say, that Heli having died without children, he left his widow to his brother Jacob, according to the <term>Law</term><note>A reference to the Levirate law (Deuteronomy 25:5-6), where a man was required to marry his deceased brother's childless widow to provide an heir.</note>; and so Joseph was attributed to Jacob by Matthew, and to Heli by Luke. Others (which seems more fitting) understand that Matthew describes the lineage of Joseph, and Luke the lineage of Mary. Thus Joseph is called a son of Heli because he had married his daughter Mary as his wife. According to this, it is then not strange that these genealogies hold different courses, though both are descended from David; and therefore Jesus is rightly called a "Son of David" in various places of Scripture. Some object to this, arguing that Mary was of the tribe of Levi because Elizabeth is said to be her cousin, which would conflict with this latter opinion. However, others refute this, giving as a reason that Mary is descended from the tribe of Judah, since no families were permitted to marry outside their lines, except for the priests; and it is not probable that Joseph and Mary would have been married to one another outside the order of the Law. And as for the kinship between Mary and Elizabeth: They say that Mary...

And from that time on, the Maccabees, or Hasmoneans (beginning with Mattathias), held the scepter of the Jews until it was taken from them through the cunning of <term>Herod</term><note>Herod the Great, who achieved the kingship of Judea with Roman support, displacing the Hasmonean dynasty.</note>, as we have mentioned in its place.

### Reflection.

<margin>1 Samuel 16:13.</margin>
David, when he was anointed with the Holy Oil to be a King over Israel, was led by the impulse of his Spirit into the battle against the proud Giant Goliath, who had mocked and scorned the Host of Israel, making it known that there was no one who would be bound to combat against him. This Giant is a clear image of this chief Prince of Spirits <note>A reference to Satan/Lucifer</note> who rules in the air; for from the description of his weapons and the great length of his body, one finds a gruesome and formidable person in appearance, such that everyone who saw him took flight and did not dare to stand. And in this manner was this spiritual combatant <note>The Devil</note> also feared by everyone, as he had cut down many heroes. The strong Samson, the beautiful Absalom, the wise Solomon—yes, 
<margin>Genesis 3:6.</margin>
even our first parents in Paradise, the first creation of men that God had prepared—were cast down early on, as if he wanted to destroy and cast off the entire work of God. He mocked, he boasted, and seemed to care for no one. But this Spiritual David <note>A typological name for Jesus</note>, who wished to lay down his life for his flock, felt himself driven by the Holy Spirit to tame this pride of his: so that he might show how little his cunning attacks could do against the one who was armed within with an immovable strength. In order then to avoid this highly-famed Spirit in no part; So he went from the Jordan, from the midst of the people, far from the company of John the Baptist and all other Saints from whom any assistance could have been given to him, into a wilderness. Some hold it to have been the wilderness of Zin <note>original: "Sin"</note>, where formerly Moses and Elijah had been: others think it was the wilderness of Quarentena <note>Mount Quarantania, the traditional site of the temptation</note>, situated by Jericho; yet however it was, it was a place prepared for all temptations: desolate, wild, lonely, full of the gruesome howling of wild beasts,

And it was then that the Devil principally roused himself, as having now found right causes and great advantages to make his temptation strike home; where the garden wall is lowest, there he wants to cross over; where the city is weakest, there he wants to climb it; and where he finds the innate nature inclined, there he attacks. Seeing then Christ now in hunger and lack of necessities, he arrived with his
<margin>1 Samuel 17:40.</margin>
cunning; yet he found a David who already had his sling ready. A Joseph who paid no heed to his false song.

The tempter came to him. He came like a roaring lion to devour: he came like a murderer to destroy: he came like a Goliath to become glorious. The Devil hid under a cloak of teachableness <note>original: "leersaemheydt"—here meaning the Devil pretends to be a student or a seeker of truth to mask his malice</note>. *Are you the Son of God?* as if he wanted to say: by some signs it seems so, by others again not; for how would God leave his Son, whom he loves, to fall into such lack? See, such a manner of temptation these words contained; for it is temptation when one seeks to move someone by reason to a matter that seems very profitable and necessary, and yet in itself is not good.

### MATTHEW 4. MARK 1. LUKE 4. John 1.

## Reflection.

<margin>Num. 23:14.</margin>
When Balak, the King of the Moabites, saw that he could not curse Israel, he said to Balaam: "Come, let us go to another vantage point, where you do not see all of Israel, and curse them for me from there." For he spared no diligence to achieve his purpose. The Devil did the same with Jesus, a method he maintains daily to bring the members of Christ <note>meaning the body of believers or the faithful</note> to a fall. Those whom he cannot overcome through suffering, poverty, distress, lack, or persecution, he leads in another way, so that he might bring them to a great presumption and spiritual pride. He leads them to the very top of the pinnacle of the Temple in the holy city, which is a place of great height, as if they were worthy through their strong faith to be set above all things, even above the Sanctuary itself. And not only that, but that God himself must be subject to their will, serving them as they desire, sending the Angels down from Heaven—not out of necessity, but to satisfy their pleasure and pastime. Into this temptation he has now led Jesus, saying: "If you are the Son of God, whom the Angels (like the attendants of a King) stand ready to serve, then throw yourself down from here; for it is written: He shall <margin>Psal. 91:11.</margin> give his Angels charge over you, and they shall bear you up in their hands, lest you dash your foot against a stone." In this proposal of the Devil, several things are to be noted:

1. That he seeks a thing that is entirely unnecessary, and first concocted by him, which served no purpose other than as a temptation and torment, wishing to move Christ to the confession he demanded and to his obedience, so as to triumph over him.

2. That he brings forth the Scripture for his defense, to create an appearance of truth.

3. That he repeats it falsely and not purely; for he leaves out and keeps silent those words *in all your ways*. For God the Lord has indeed promised to protect and preserve his own in their ways—those paths they must travel out of necessity and according to God's ordinance—but not in those ways that the Devil proposes to them, as he did here to Christ. And through this, many also fall into the snare: they follow their own perverse mind, throwing themselves into various perils, not according to God's prescription, but by the Devil's advice, and they think God will help them and the Angels will watch over them; but they end up deceived. As long as God provides means for human help, no miracles are needed. When the dough of the children of Israel that they brought out of <margin>Exod. 16:5.</margin> Egypt was finished, Manna fell from Heaven, and it did so as long as they were in a wilderness; but when they came into a fruitful land that they could cultivate themselves to provide for their needs, the Manna ceased, as it was no longer <margin>Joshua 5:12.</margin> necessary. Therefore Jesus answers Satan very well: "Again it is written: You <margin>Deut. 6:16.</margin> shall not tempt the Lord your God." That is called tempting or putting God...

->### Reflection.<-

<margin>Genesis 3:5.</margin>Satan, who is a cunning deceiver and well knows with what snares he can best catch and undermine man, has kept this for the very last. For it is the manner of a clever military commander to save the most fearsome assault until the very end, in order to then bring to bear all the forces he knows he can muster. Thus this rogue <note>original: "schalck"; here used to describe Satan's malicious trickery</note> knew that he had made Adam forget his God through the desire for glory, casting the commandment behind his back and intoxicating the heart with that foolish hope of being like God. He knew that he had conquered so many <margin>Genesis 6:2.</margin>children of God in the first world <note>a reference to the era before the Great Flood, where the "sons of God" were said to be tempted by the "daughters of men"</note> through the lusts and vain pleasures of visible things, catching them in his net, notwithstanding that some had struggled and resisted him for a long time. He knew that he had overwhelmed many wise men of this world through this, bringing them to a pure apostasy from God—not only the entire mass of the Heathens, who sought nothing but status, dominion, and the pleasures of the flesh—but even those who had already climbed some steps toward Heaven, whom he pulled down and, <margin>Micah 3:5; Isaiah 9:23; Psalm 82:2; Psalm 5:5.</margin>as if bound by a bridle, led wherever he wished. The Prophets he had turned into false deceivers; the Judges into the unjust; the Priests into persecutors of the pious; yes, the whole world was set in turmoil, so that men, driven as if by a foolish madness, corrupted and destroyed one another, casting themselves into the greatest perils to accomplish such things—and all for money, for status, for enjoyment and the pleasure of lust, which almost no one could resi- <note>The text cuts off mid-word "wederstaen," meaning "to resist."</note>

# Concerning the life of Jesus Christ.
## Matthew 4. Mark 1. Luke 4. John 1.
<sig>N 3</sig>

...stand, as soon as this temptation approached Him, and as these Sirens <note>The author uses the "Sirens" from Greek mythology as a metaphor for the seductive nature of temptation.</note> began to sing their sweet, gilded songs.

Thus he thought to hurl these arrows at Jesus’s person as well, and to present them as a deceitful lure. Leading Him up a high mountain—for this place was suitable for overseeing all things, just as <margin>Deuteronomy 34:1.</margin> Moses stood on Mount Pisgah to behold the Promised Land—there he showed Him all the kingdoms of the world, and their glory, as if he meant to say: See there, how happy is that King in his palace; see yonder what beautiful Duchies and Counties belong to him; see how the Princes and the mighty bow before that Prince; see this one’s treasuries stuffed full of money; this one does all he desires; no one can resist the other. Behold the luxury that riches bring: tables full of delicacies, wardrobes full of beautiful clothes, coffers full of jewels, and everything that can be wished for or desired for pleasure and a delightful life. This presentation occurred in the most appropriate manner and at its highest power, for it is stronger because these all appear to be lawful things, which can be used as creatures of God without hindering salvation—and especially where the wisdom of God accompanies them, as was perfectly present in Jesus. 

This being presented in the most beautiful light, he then came out with the great word: <margin>Luke 4:6.</margin> **All this I will give You, if You fall down and worship me.** That was what he sought: namely, to be held as the supreme God, and none other than him. Oh, great pride! He boasted of being a distributor of all these fortunes and earthly circumstances, and that everything went according to his pleasure, because they were his own, as Luke expresses it: *for they are given to me, and I give them to whom I will.* By this deceitful lie he enchants the whole world, so that they bow their knees before him, call upon him, and honor him, thinking they do so for the supreme God, and they deceive themselves miserably; and the Devil secretly laughs at this, that he takes them captive through such vain play.

These ruses found no entrance into Him whose breast was armed with the truth, by whom those things were regarded as dung and filth <note>A reference to Philippians 3:8, where the Apostle Paul considers worldly gains as loss for the sake of Christ.</note>; so that it was not worthy of Jesus to refute these lies of his, only answering that which concerned the honor of His Father, saying: **Go away, Satan; for it is written:** <margin>Deuteronomy 6:5, 6; Matthew 22:30.</margin> **You shall worship the Lord your God, and Him only shall you serve.** Thereby making it known that one must offer up to God the whole heart, with soul and spirit, and all the powers of the mind, without leaving any part to Satan or created creatures. This is what we must diligently consider and take to heart, so that the love of God remains unfading in our hearts, whatever storms may be raised against it: for the slightest hearing given to Satan can rob one of the whole treasure.

The kingdoms of the world were also presented to Him several times / offering to crown Him King. Thus Satan was often on his feet / to tempt Him / but in all this He suffered patiently / without giving him any hearing / until He had placed all things (even death itself) under His feet.

### Reflection.

<margin>Josephus, Antiquities, Book 13, Chapter 9</margin>
What kind of people the Pharisees were, Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus (c. 37–100 AD) was a Romano-Jewish historian whose works provide essential context for the New Testament era.</note> testifies at length; they arose around the times of the Maccabees, alongside the Sadducees and Essenes, who all differ in their opinions and way of life. The Pharisees, being the foremost and greatest in power, held the primary authority over religious matters, so that sometimes even the kings had to fear them. The Sadducees, being fewer in number, also had to bow under these and agree with their counsel, or they would not have been tolerated by the common people. They were interpreters of the Law according to their name, for *Pherusim* <note>The author connects the name "Pharisee" to the Hebrew *parash*, which can mean both "to separate" and "to explain" or "interpret."</note> means as much as "interpreters." Their way of life was moderate, not indulgent in eating or drinking; they lived strictly according to natural reason, held elderly people in great honor, not contradicting them but listening in respectful silence. Their view was: that Divine providence <term>Divine providence</term> <note>original: "Goddelicke schickinghe"; the belief that God actively guides the universe and human affairs.</note> operates in such a way that man, in choosing virtue or vice, retains his free will; they believed in the immortality of souls and that these were judged beneath the earth according to their merit. The Sadducees believed in neither angel nor spirit, much less the immortality of the soul, and even less in Divine providence in human affairs. The Essenes believed that nothing happened except through Divine providence; they also believed in the immortality of the soul, were excellent in their lives, living apart from others, solitary, holding their goods in common, mostly unmarried, maintaining a strict discipline, and lived long lives, just as Josephus describes all of this at length.

<margin>Book 13, Chapter 23.</margin>
<margin>Book 18, Chapter 2.</margin>
<margin>Acts 23:8.</margin>
<margin>Josephus, The Jewish War, Book 2, Chapter 12.</margin>

The Evangelist does not recount in vain, then: *That these messengers were sent from the Pharisees*, as from the most prominent of the people, including notable persons, Priests and Levites to whom the Law was entrusted. They showed that they took the actions of John to heart, for the common people had a high opinion of him. Some said he is the Christ, others he is Elijah or another Prophet, the more so because the Prophets had foretold that such a one would arise. Thus they came to examine John, asking him: whether he was the Christ or Elijah? Or that Prophet <margin>Deuteronomy 18:15.</margin> of whom it was said that he should come? John, as a very faithful servant of his Lord, confessed the truth plainly, seeking not his own honor nor fearing the status of the ambassadors. Thus he said: that he was none of these. And to show his own nothingness, he declared himself

# The Second Part /

JOHN 1. ->Matthew 4. Mark 1. Luke 4.<-

...himself to be nothing other than a voice crying in the wilderness, which is but an echo or a wind. Yet at the same time, according to Isaiah's prophecy, he had come to prepare the way of the Lord, thereby expressing the power of his service: that it also exists in the heart of man as a preaching of repentance <term>preaching of repentance</term> <note>original: "boet-predicatie"; a sermon or call intended to lead listeners to regret their sins and turn toward God.</note>, so that the grace of the Gospel may follow once the inner self is prepared; for without true preparation, the Lord does not make an entrance. The emissaries of the Pharisees, still not satisfied, asked: why then did he baptize? Since he did not do this according to the common washing and bathing of the Jews, but as one having received a Divine command for it. To this, he made known two things: First, that his Baptism was nothing other than with water. But that the one of whom he spoke had another Baptism of greater power and might. Second: That He stood in their midst without them knowing Him, which was either according to the flesh—because He did not stand out in human highness as they were expecting the Messiah <margin>Revelation 3:20. Luke 17:20. Song of Solomon 5:2.</margin> to be—or according to the Spirit, with which He, being in the hearts of men, speaks to them, invites, seeks, prays, and exhorts them to improvement; yet they do not know His voice, being, and condition, and consequently do not hear. This one has always been, in a spiritual manner, as a lover of mankind long before John, and comes after him in bodily form, such that He is the first and the last. John confesses himself not worthy to untie the strap of His shoes, or as is said in other places, to carry them—that is, to step into His office <note>In the ancient world, untying or carrying a master’s sandals was the task of the lowest slave; John uses this image to show his total humility before Jesus.</note>.

Not without reason does the Evangelist also recount the place where this happened, namely Bethabara, across the Jordan, which was very well situated both for the baptizing and for the gathering of the people, who came in multitudes from the Jewish lands, Galilee, and Samaria to hear the preaching of John and to take heed of this testimony; for Bethabara <note>The name Bethabara is traditionally translated as "house of the crossing" or "place of passage."</note> was a crossing point to come from the lands of the Moabites and Ammonites into the Jewish land, strengthening at once an image of the crossing of Christians from the Law to the Gospel.

Jesus having returned from the place of His temptation <note>Referring to the forty days Jesus spent in the wilderness being tempted by the devil.</note>, where He had first gone, has now also come near the Jordan where John was baptizing, so that He might begin there to gather disciples and become known through the pointing out of this holy man.

...who gladly wishes to give up his life, in order to win your love, and to offer it to his Heavenly Father, so that through him you might become one with that Heavenly happiness. Return <margin>Song of Solomon 6:13</margin> <note>original: "Cant. 6. 13"; the Latin "Cantica Canticorum" refers to the Song of Solomon.</note>, return, O Man! from your straying ways; see there your guide, examine him, visit him, and learn his ways; you shall find in him nothing else but the nature of a meek and kind Lamb. Andrew was ignited with a fiery zeal; he wanted to share that treasure with the first person he met. His <margin>Exodus 4:27</margin> brother Simon was filled with the same hunger; they were sent to each other like Moses and Aaron. And to be certain of it, come and see if you do not find it so yourself. [Follow] me; the heart was moved, and all the powers of the soul inclined toward him. The Pharisees could not be moved by all the testimonies of John, nor by the urging of his words, even though they were learned in the Law and knew the scripture by heart; theirs was a faith of memory <note>The author uses the term "memoriaels gheloove" to describe an intellectual belief that resides only in the head without affecting the heart.</note> without power. He is ignited with a fiery love, and this same love teaches him to share with his neighbor that which he had found so beneficial for himself. He comes to Nathanael, who sat under the Fig Tree, having his thoughts on Heavenly things; the Spirit of Christ was near there, though he did not know it. A good message is brought to him: We have found him <margin>Deuteronomy 18:15.</margin> of whom Moses wrote in the Law: who was signified through many shadows of the sacrifices. That Prophet whom God promised <margin>Isaiah 42:1. Jeremiah 33:15 Micah 5:1.</margin> to his people: That King of righteousness, of whom much was said by the Prophets. And what is most to be wondered at; he is not recognized or famous for it, the scribes know nothing of him; he is a man of little stature, but of great hidden powers, namely: Jesus of Nazareth, Joseph’s Son.

The good Nathanael listens with surprise; he is taken aback by the location, which was lowly and without fame in Galilee: can any good thing come from Nazareth? Had it been Jerusalem, or somewhere in the land of Judah—but what is Nazareth? Oh Nathanael! turn your eyes away from the person and the land; come and see for yourself. I hold myself certain that you shall find it so: experience must be believed above all opinion and fancy. Jesus saw Nathanael coming to him, like a Sheep to its Shepherd. He saw through the heart and the inner being of this man: He knew and recognized his upright intention, even though he still wandered somewhat in his understanding. Behold a true Israelite in whom there is no <margin>Psalm 73:1</margin> deceit. 

The man was astonished and immediately convicted within himself: How do you know me? For to my knowledge, I have never seen you (nor you me). Oh Nathanael! my eyes search the heart and the reins <note>A common biblical idiom referring to the innermost thoughts and emotions.</note>, and I am present everywhere among my own, especially when they are busy with Divine things and, being concerned for their salvation, sigh toward Heaven and wish for true enlightenment. I already saw you under the Fig Tree; that dark shadow blocked the light of the Sun from you, and it was not possible to come to a true vision while remaining under it. Then Philip came to call you, and that calling took some root in your heart. 

Nathanael acknowledged all these things; he thought no more of Nazareth or other places, but cried out: You are God’s Son: You <margin>Jeremiah 23:5. Daniel 2:44</margin> are the King of Israel, who was promised to appear in his time. This was indeed a beginning of faith in Nathanael, but Jesus set before his eyes that this was not yet such a great matter as they would later experience: now they saw as if through clouds, but then Heaven would stand open for them. They would recognize the great communion of the Son with the Father. The Angels, as ministering <margin>Genesis 24:21. <note>The original cites Gen 24:21, though the reference to the ladder is Gen 28:12.</note></margin> spirits, would climb up and down, just as was shown to Jacob in the vision.

### Observation.

Jesus, having arrived in Galilee with his first-chosen disciples, attended a wedding on the third day of his arrival. This was a uniquely fitting occasion to outwardly manifest the divine glory he carried within, providing great comfort and strengthening to those who had now followed him. Maria, the mother of Jesus, was also there, either due to kinship or because of a close acquaintance. Some believe that the bridegroom of this wedding
<margin>Baronius, Year 31, Number 12. Nicephorus, Book 8, Letter 30.</margin>
was John the Evangelist; others understand this to refer to Simon the Canaanite, who later <note>original: "vaderhant," likely a typo for "naderhand" (later)</note> became one of the twelve Apostles. However that may be, Jesus and the disciples accompanying him were also invited to the wedding. And let us note this as the first point: that Jesus came here not to make "good cheer" <note>to indulge in revelry</note>, nor to bolster the company with idle joy, nor to amuse himself with eating and drinking,
<margin>Luke 7:34.</margin>
as the Pharisees later slandered him. Rather, he came to honor the state of Matrimony with his presence, thereby proving that it was instituted by his Heavenly Father. And he, who was the true Bridegroom of souls, allowed himself to be found in this company, where a living image, expression, and figure was shown of the spiritual marriage and unchangeable Love
<margin>Song of Solomon 4:10</margin>
between God and the faithful soul, which is compared to a pure, undefiled Bride. 2. There was a lack of wine; and the mother of Jesus was concerned about this. She takes her refuge in her Son, whom she knew to be a helper in times of need and one who improved all things: *They have no wine.* This was either because there had been none due to poverty, or because what they had was insufficient for the company. Jesus, who was now entirely occupied with his Father's business, would acknowledge his mother in this situation no more than any other woman, saying that his hour had not yet come. Maria was not dismayed by this, nor was her hope in any way diminished, thereby teaching us that we should persevere through faith and trust in God, even if it seems that he disregards us and does not wish to hear us. Constant trust eventually overcomes; yet, in the meantime, we must do everything on our part that we know to be his will.
<margin>Judith 10:10.</margin>

The size of these jars is described variously; one says fifty or seventy-five *stoopen* <note>a "stoop" was a Dutch liquid measure approximately equal to 2.4 liters</note>, another says half an *aam* <note>an "aam" was a large cask containing about 150 liters</note> per jar. However, it matters little; they stood there for washing and purification according to the custom of the Jews. And see what happened? The Lord had them filled to the very brim. A matter worthy of notice: no one knew what it was meant to signify. Jesus sat there quietly, and his Divine power worked invisibly.

<margin>Exod. 15:23. 2 Kings 2:20.</margin>
Moses threw a piece of wood into the bitter water; Elisha put salt into it, and then it became flavorful and healthy to drink. But here, all things happened in silence and without any external means. O wonderful work of God! There was no time between the two: no sooner was it poured in than they stood ready to draw it out again. Shall we then prescribe any time or measure to God according to our human understanding when we are in need? Not at all: the less we worry about it, the readier the help is.

Taste and see how friendly the Lord is; and that through his deeds and works, which he performs so outwardly before our eyes and so inwardly in the soul. I have served many weddings, but never tasted the like, nor seen such an order maintained: Every man puts out the good wine first, and when the people are drunk, then that which is worse.

<margin>Prov. 9:16</margin>
So does the whole world and its Prince <note>referring to the devil or the spirit of the age</note>: They promise beautiful things until the senses are strayed and drunk; then they pay with base coin, and those who believed them come out deceived. But you have kept the best until now.

### Description of the city of Cana.

<margin>Travel Book Part 2. in con.</margin>Cana in Galilee, where the Lord Jesus turned the water into wine, is located in the territory of the tribe of Zebulun <note>original: "Sabulon"</note>, seventy miles from Jerusalem toward the North, and not far from Nazareth. It is also called *Cana minor*, or the Lesser Cana, to distinguish it from another Cana, formerly a Royal Capital, located in Upper Galilee near the borders of Tyre and Sidon. Near that place lived the famous race of the Canaanites, who derived their name (as did this city) from Canaan the son of Noah. Over this <margin>Judges 4:2.</margin>nation, Jabin was formerly King, whose general Sisera was killed by Jael. And it is believable that this Lesser Cana also had its origin from that same lineage. Toward the North of this city lies a beautiful round mountain, upon which Jesus often walked with his Disciples, as can be reasonably presumed; for it is evident from the Evangelists that he frequently took up his stay upon the heights of the mountains. Toward the South, it had a delightful green field, so that the countryside around this city was a pleasant landscape. From this city came Simon the Zealot <note>original: "Simon Zelotes"</note>, one of the twelve <margin>Mark 3:18.</margin>Apostles. And Jesus also performed another deed here (besides this great Miracle): the healing of the Son of the King’s Nobleman <note>See John 4:46-54</note>, as will be treated hereafter. Furthermore, this city held the honor above all other Galilean cities that Jesus performed his first miracle <note>original: "teeken," literally 'sign'</note> there, to strengthen his Disciples, who in their beginnings stood and grew like weak reeds and could easily have been broken by heavy storm-winds. And this corresponds well with the name of the city; for **Cana** is as much as to say a **Reed**. Happy are those who are called to the Wedding with Christ; for their weakness is helped and strengthened by the Heavenly wine.

His brothers also followed: some consider these to be children of Mary; others understand...

[Jesus was] here with his cousins or very close kin; as Holy Scripture has a custom of calling such relatives "brothers." These did not follow him with the same insight as Mary, seeing that they did not believe in him <margin>John 7:5</margin>, but whether it was out of curiosity or a desire to become famous through his powers—as the natural man is wonderfully inclined toward ambition <note>original: "Eergierighepdt," literally a greed for honor or status</note>—is unclear. Now, Jesus did not stay there long; for the feast of Passover <note>original: "Paesschen," which can refer to Easter or Passover; here it refers to the Jewish feast</note> was near, on which high feast days he was accustomed to come to Jerusalem. And now he had specifically intended to demonstrate the power of his mission there, as will follow in the next chapter.

---

### Description of the city of Capernaum.

The city of Capernaum, which is frequently mentioned by the Evangelists because Jesus lived there and performed many miracles, is located on the Lake of Gennesaret <note>original: "Meyr Genezareth"</note>, otherwise called the Sea of Galilee, across the Jordan, 14 miles <note>A "mile" in 17th-century Dutch geography was much longer than a modern mile, usually about 4.6 miles or 7.4 kilometers</note> from Jerusalem, belonging to the tribe of Issachar. Opposite it (on the other side of the flow of the Jordan) lay the city of Chorazin <note>original: "Corosin"</note>, and all around lay a beautiful fertile land, from which the city also takes its name; for Capernaum is as much as to say "Beautiful Village" <note>While the author translates this as "Schoondorp" or Beautiful Village, the name Capernaum traditionally derives from the Hebrew "Kfar Nahum," meaning "Village of Nahum" or "Village of Comfort"</note>. And in this same land of Gennesaret grew many pomegranates, palm trees, olive trees, vineyards, and many other beautiful fruits. The Romans had a custom house <note>original: "Tolhuys," a place for collecting taxes or tolls</note> here: for it was in the time of Christ a beautiful merchant city, and furthermore a ferry crossing to travel from one territory to another, so that it was a convenient and pleasant place, very suitable for Jesus and his disciples to live. This was not only for the sweetness of the land, but also because the sea washed up against it, and they had a good opportunity to support themselves sometimes with fishing. Furthermore, it was very well situated to serve the surrounding tribes of Israel with preaching. It was also not subject to the tyrannical house of Herod, but was governed by Roman military commanders, who were much more polite toward Christ than the envious Jewish nation, which, being corrupted by the sects of the Pharisees and Sadducees, persecuted Jesus. In this city the Lord Jesus performed many wonders and miracles, as will be described in due time: He healed Peter's <note>original: "Petri"</note> mother-in-law of a fever; he delivered a possessed man from the power of the Devil <note>original: "in de schoole van den Duyvel verlost," perhaps suggesting he was freed while in the synagogue or from the "school" (thrall) of Satan</note>. He also healed the Centurion's <note>original: "Centuri"</note> servant there, and the woman with the issue of blood: he raised the daughter of the ruler Jairus <note>original: "Jairi"</note> from death; also a paralytic <note>original: "Gichtigen," literally one suffering from gout or palsy</note> who was let down through the roof was healed there, and after that two blind men and one mute. And at various times many sick, possessed, blind, mute, deaf, and those with other ailments were cured: for since he lived there, they were brought to him from all sides, so that sometimes

### Observation.

Among other Passover Feasts that the Evangelists indicate during the journeying of Christ, this is the first—being in the thirty-first year of his age—occurring while John <note>John the Baptist</note> was still preaching, and while Jesus was traveling with his relatives and some Disciples. But before we come to the explanation of this text, we shall first take into consideration the form of the Temple: for it would otherwise seem absurd <note>original: "ongerijmt"</note> that oxen, sheep, and doves would come into that holy place; much less stand there for sale.

<margin>
1 Kings 6:1.
Ezra 3:10.
Josephus, *Antiquities of the Jews*, Book 15, Chapter 14.
</margin>
This Temple was first built by King Solomon, thereafter by Zerubbabel <note>The leader of the Jewish people who oversaw the rebuilding of the Temple after the Babylonian exile.</note>; and finally by King Herod in the eighteenth year of his reign. Its location was upon Mount Moriah, surrounded with strong and no less costly walls of marble stones, in so beautiful an appearance that it was a wonder of the world: and it was at once a fortress, or castle, to protect the city and the Sanctuary in times of need.

<margin>
Bünting in *Travel-book*, description of the Temple, and also another Jewish description. <note>Refers to Heinrich Bünting, a 16th-century cartographer and theologian known for his "Itinerarium Sacrae Scripturae."</note>
</margin>
It had various circuits or courtyards, of which the first was called the Court of the Gentiles <note>original: "voor-hof der Heydenen"</note>, where everyone was free and permitted to enter. The second was six cubits <note>A cubit (elle) is an ancient measurement of roughly 18 inches.</note> higher: the floor paved with costly marble stones; this was called the Court of the Women, because they were permitted to enter there. The third was the Court of the Temple, or the High Court, where the weapons, banners, and other signs of triumph hung, taken from defeated enemies. The fourth was the Court of the Israelites in general, one and a half cubits higher than the previous one: here was the Offering-chest <note>The treasury where people placed their donations.</note>, and also the place where the Lord Jesus and later his Apostles often preached to great crowds. The fifth was the Court of the Priests, being yet two and a half cubits higher than the aforementioned court: here was the Altar of Burnt Offering, and the molten Sea <note>original: "ghegoten Zee," a large bronze basin for ritual washing.</note>, standing upon twelve oxen, in which place the daily offerings [were made]...

### Observation.

Among other Passover feasts that the Evangelists indicate during the life of Christ, this is the first, occurring in the thirty-first year of his age / while the preaching of John <note>John the Baptist</note> was still ongoing / and Jesus was traveling with his kinsmen and some disciples. But before we come to the explanation of this text / we shall first take into consideration / the appearance of the Temple: for otherwise it would seem absurd that oxen, sheep, and doves would come into that holy place; much less be offered for sale.

<margin>
1 Kings 6:1.
Ezra 3:10.
Josephus, Antiquities, Book 15, Chapter 14.
</margin>
This Temple was built first by King Solomon, thereafter by Zerubbabel; and finally by King Herod in the eighteenth year of his reign: its location was on Mount Moriah / surrounded by strong and no less costly walls of marble stones / in such a beautiful appearance that it was a wonder of the world: and it was at once a fortress / or castle / to protect the city and the Sanctuary in times of need.

<margin>
Bunting in *Itinerarium* <note>original: "Reysb."</note>, description of the Temple, and another Jewish description.
</margin>
It had several passages or courtyards / of which the first was called the Court of the Gentiles / where everyone was free and permitted to enter. The second was six cubits <note>original: "ellen"</note> higher: the floor paved with costly marble stones / this was called the Court of the Women, because it was permitted for them to enter therein. The third was the Court of the Temple, or the High Court / where the weapons / banners / and other signs of triumph hung / taken from defeated enemies. The fourth was the Court of the Israelites in general / one and a half cubits higher than the preceding: here was the offering chest / and also the place where the Lord Jesus and later his Apostles often preached to great crowds. The fifth was the Court of the Priests, being yet another two and a half cubits higher than the aforementioned court: here was the Altar of Burnt Offering / and the Molten Sea <note>A large bronze basin used by priests for ritual washing</note> / standing upon twelve oxen / in which place the daily offerings were...
