## The Second Part / John 2. Matthew 4. Mark 1. Luke 4.

<margin>1 Kings 6:38.</margin>
<margin>Josephus, Antiquities, Book 15, Chapter 14.</margin>
[He] answers / with a reply just as obscure to their eyes / as the event itself: *Destroy this temple, and I will raise it up again in three days.* This clearly indicated that his entire action had a hidden meaning / and that this expulsion needed interpretation just as much as the Temple itself / and thus the glory of Christ was as if shrouded in a cloud / both in words and deeds / a stumbling block and confusion to the Pharisees. 4. Now it is to be noted how the Jews understood this: *This temple was made in forty-six years.* They spoke according to the outward sense / yet not of the Temple of Solomon which was built in the space of seven years <note>Solomon’s Temple took seven years to build, while the Jews here refer to the ongoing reconstruction started by Herod the Great</note>. It could hardly be the Temple of Zerubbabel <note>The leader of the Jews who returned from the Babylonian exile and rebuilt the temple</note>; for that had been torn down; and this present one was newly founded by King Herod: Josephus says in the space of eight years / but because he adds that a part of the wall was made a long time thereafter / the time is calculated from the first foundation to the time the Jews spoke this / which amounts to forty-six years / as if they meant to say: "It is forty-six years ago that this Temple was begun, and you see that it is not yet completely finished; and would you raise it up in three days?" This is very likely the meaning. The Jews interpreted this answer of Christ so bitterly and perversely / that they later brought it up against him as a capital offense / mixed with a false distortion / when he stood before Caiaphas <note>The Jewish High Priest during the trial of Jesus</note> to be judged / from which we can see into what wandering paths envy travels / because it is blinded by its own self: the Disciples did better / who, although they did not understand it now either / waited out the time / until they understood the truth of it through the deed, namely in the resurrection: Thus one ought not to judge hastily in everything that is hidden and obscure / but to wait patiently until God is pleased to reveal such / which happened in the resurrection of Christ / when the time of his burial was completed.

It is not improper to give some description here of the situation of the city of Jerusalem. It was first built (according to common opinion) by Melchizedek <note>The priest-king of Salem mentioned in Genesis</note> / and named Salem / though not very large / being inhabited later by the Jebusites / it was called Jebus after the same name. King David took this city from the Jebusites / and established his Royal throne there / greatly increasing and enriching it. After that, Solomon glorified it with the construction of the Temple and other Royal Palaces <note>original: *Palepsen*, an archaic Dutch form of palaces</note> / and thus it increased more and more in wealth, power, and majesty: consisting of four hills within it. <margin>1 Kings 6. Second, the mountain of Moriah, upon which the Temple was built. Third, the mountain of Akra, called the lower city / in which were the principal buildings of the Royal Palaces / the houses of great Lords / and the dwellings of prominent and wealthy citizens. Fourth, the mountain of Besetha, upon which the suburbs were situated, which were not included within the ring-wall / and where one might enter at all times. Otherwise, it was situated in a square / having in its circumference (according to the description in the Travel-book) one great German mile / which is about a two-hour walk : although others describe the circuit of this city as being three times larger / namely / a six-hour walk. It had a steep depth all around it / especially at the mountains of Sion and Moriah, in whose deep valleys the sight grew dizzy when looking down. From which it follows that the city of Jerusalem was situated very high / and for that reason it was said / when Jesus or his Apostles traveled there, that they "went up" or climbed to Jerusalem. It was surrounded by twelve Gates, among which were these: <margin>Nehemiah 3:1, 13, 15.</margin> The Sheep-gate, through which one went to the Mount of Olives / and the village of Gethsemane / through which Jesus was brought as a prisoner by Judas and his followers. The Fountain-gate, where he made his entry riding upon the Ass / and where the way to Emmaus was also located. The Valley-gate, through which one went out to the road of the Jordans. The Horse-gate, standing on the way to Jericho. Such that it was by nature an exceedingly strong city / which could withstand long sieges and great force / as very mighty Kings have tested. <margin>2 Kings 8:25, 9. Josephus, The Jewish War, Book 6, Chapter 27.</margin> It was twice utterly destroyed and burned / once by Nebuchadnezzar, the King of Assyria <note>The text identifies Nebuchadnezzar as King of Assyria, though he was historically the King of the Neo-Babylonian Empire</note> / and thereafter by Vespasian and Titus, Roman Emperors / and that through a punishment ordained by God for the sake of her sins; since which time it has remained desolate / along with the glory of the Jews and their temporal Dominion.

This city of Jerusalem was chosen by God to place his Sanctuary there / and was the only city in which it was permitted to offer outward sacrifices: for whenever the people, through unbelief, wished to perform their Divine service elsewhere on any other heights / or under green trees, it was held to be a shameful Idolatry / and even more so / when they set any image or likeness before them / as Jeroboam with the golden Calves / and others with Baalim, Astaroth, or similar Heathen abominations: <margin>1 Kings 12:28.</margin> For God wanted them to...

### Observation

Three things are made known here. 1. That Jesus performed various other signs at this Passover Feast, which nevertheless are not recorded / neither by this / nor by the other Evangelists / and are among the first signs / that followed the Wedding at Cana in Galilee. 2. That many were moved by the same to believe in him / more through outward conviction <note>original: *overtuppingh*, meaning to be intellectually overwhelmed or superficially convinced by evidence</note> than through heartfelt agreement / 
<margin>Exod. 8:8 and 9:27</margin>
just as Pharaoh, who was indeed perplexed and astonished by the signs of Moses / but nevertheless remained unchanged in his heart / and such a faith that is not mixed with love / and comes only from head-knowledge / is called a dead faith. 3. That Jesus did not trust the same, and that was no wonder: For it has 
<margin>John 8:59</margin>
appeared more often that many seemed to agree with him / to cling to him / and to hold him for the Messiah / who soon after stood with stones in their hands / threatening him with great bitterness. Jesus then, searching hearts and kidneys <note>original: *herten en nieren*, a common biblical idiom referring to the innermost thoughts and emotions</note> through his Divine power / saw all that hidden unfaithfulness / and therefore he did not hold them as his true Disciples / upon whom he might rely. I rejoice (says 
<margin>2 Cor. 7:16</margin>
the Apostle) that I can trust you in all things: For that is a sign of an upright and true foundation.

**JOHN 3.** ->Matthew 4. Mark 1. Luke 4.<-

and you do not receive our testimony. If you do not believe when I speak to you of earthly things, how would you believe if I told you of Heavenly things?

### Commentary.

Among those who took the signs of Jesus to heart (of which was spoken previously) was also this Nicodemus, who is described by the Evangelist as being a Pharisee—a people who were very hard and immovable in their opinions, and also possessed by a great bitterness against Jesus. Secondly, he was also a ruler of the Jews, as the Pharisees held the most power and influence among the people. These two things were a great obstacle for Nicodemus in coming to Jesus, and an even greater hindrance to believing in him; therefore he came by night, not wishing to be seen or noticed by anyone. Unhappy are they often before God who seem happy <note>In this context, "happy" or "fortunate" refers to worldly success and high social status.</note> before men. Nicodemus speaks here of such wonders, which no one could imitate, and which were a certain proof of an extraordinary Divine power. ->### Reflection.<-

It would be against nature if the earthly were to inherit the Heavenly; therefore Christ here sets forth his own example, that he who came down from Heaven shall ascend again to his first origin. In which Heaven he already walked and was according to his Divine essence. The common proverb says: *man is more where he loves than where he lives.* <note>original: "den mensch is meer daer hy lieft als daer hy leeft"</note> While sitting with Nicodemus, Jesus was in a certain way <margin>Phil. 3:20</margin> in Heaven. The Apostle Paul also walked in Heaven with that essence he had received from Heaven, also expecting that his body would ascend to Heaven after it became glorified and Heavenly. But in vain does a man hope for such a thing if he is earthly by nature and partakes of no Heavenly qualities.

<margin>Num. 21:9</margin>
The Lord here presents another parable of the **copper Serpent** <note>Commonly known in English as the Nehushtan or the "brazen serpent" from Numbers 21.</note> which was erected in the Desert for the healing of those who were bitten by the venomous Serpents. This was a contemptible and simple thing in the sight of men, yet it possessed great power, so that it was glorified and exalted, even physically on a pole—just as Jesus was on the wood of the cross—as a refuge for those who are mortally wounded by the hellish Serpent. The parable corresponds well with the truth: for a dead Serpent gave health through faith; likewise the death of Christ, although it seemed lowly and without power, healed our wounds and gave life to those who otherwise would have died, and that through faith.

The third part points out that damnation does not come from God (who sends His light into the world to enlighten everyone and help them onto the right path), but from man’s perverse will: those who hate and flee the light that is kindled for their improvement, loving the darkness more than the light. They were too proud, too self-wise, and too much inclined by love toward the wickedness in which they lay ensnared. If they had loved the Truth and hated the lie, they would have come willingly to the light; indeed, they would have thanked God for such great loving-kindness: for the light is sweet to the eyes where the sight is healthy. The pious who know this have nothing dearer, and do not flee from God, but seek to approach Him always more and more, saying with a thankful heart: <margin>Psalm 36:9</margin> With You is the living Fountain, and in Your light we see that light. The deeper they come into it, the sweeter it tastes to them; God is in them and they in Him, so that whatever they do in this light happens entirely through God, and they know nothing in the world on which they could spend their love more preciously or better.

### Historical continuation.

After Jesus had given many beautiful and excellent instructions to Nicodemus, and seeing that there was little fruit to be borne within Jerusalem—where the Pharisees were not only self-wise and proud-hearted, but also hateful toward him—he departed from that city. However, he did not leave the entire land, but rather ignited the light of the <term>Gospel<note>Original: "Evangelium." The "Good News" of Christ's teaching.</note></term> there, alongside John, who still blew the trumpet of his teaching just as strongly. These two might well be compared to those two silver trumpets that Moses <margin>Numbers 10</margin> had made to be used in the army-camp of Israel, to call them together and to make them march forth, according to the variation of the sound.

### John Chapter III.

<margin>verse 22</margin> After this, Jesus and his disciples came into the land of Judea, and he lived there with them, and baptized.
<margin>23</margin> And John was also baptizing in <term>Aenon<note>Aenon means "springs," explaining why the text mentions there was "much water" there.</note></term> near Salim, because there was much water there: and they came there, and were baptized.
<margin>24</margin> For John had not yet been cast into prison.

### Observation.

The place where Jesus stayed is not specifically recorded, other than that it was in the Judean land; not across the Jordan, nor in the land of the Samaritans, who are not included under this name. It is not written in vain that Jesus also received his disciples through water-baptism, just as John did. This practice remained with the Apostles afterward, and still exists among those who hold the Apostolic custom in high regard. The time that Jesus tarried here was reasonably long, for he "lived" here with his own, which requires some time. John also baptized alongside him, namely in Aenon, and this seems to have been in the summer, when the rivers commonly dry up and become very small in those hot countries. The sun goes very high there, such that when he is in the beginning of the <term>Crab<note>Original: "Kreeft." This refers to the sign of Cancer, or the Summer Solstice, indicating the hottest part of the year.</note></term>, a

It is very probable that the Pharisees and Sadducees and similar sects of the Jews despised John and his baptism, holding that Cleansing could better be achieved through the ritual washings of the Law and the traditions of the Elders <note>The "traditions of the Elders" refer to the *halakha*, the collective body of Jewish religious laws derived from the Written and Oral Torah.</note>. These disciples, taking this to heart, became troubled and came to their Master to present this matter to him, complaining that through his own testimony so many people had already begun to turn to Jesus that it might well lead to the downfall of him and his teaching. 19 But when Herod, one of the tetrarchs <note>Original: "vier-Vorsten," literally "four-princes," a title for a ruler of a fourth part of a province.</note>, was rebuked by him regarding Herodias, his brother Philip’s wife, and for all the evil that Herod did;

->Observation.<-

<margin>Matt. 14:3, Mark 6:18.</margin>
What Luke describes here briefly is described more extensively by the other Evangelists in other places; from which, with the addition of Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus, the famous 1st-century Jewish historian whose works provide outside context for biblical events.</note>, the history can be understood thus: This Herod, surnamed Antipas, had as a lawful wife the daughter of the Arabian King Aretas. Meanwhile, having cast his eye upon Herodias, the wife of his brother Philip, who was also a tetrarch (although Josephus attributes her to another brother, also named Herod), he made an agreement with the same Herodias that she would leave her husband and come to him; in exchange, he would also cast out the daughter of the aforementioned Arabian King, which took place.
<margin>Josephus, Antiquities, Book 18, Chapter 6.</margin>
Having thus laid the foundation for this incestuous adultery, several other wicked deeds followed, as one evil usually sprouts from another. John, as a pious Prophet of the Lord, rebuked these evil acts of his, just as Elijah did to Ahab and Jezebel. But although this was an act of God’s kindness, intended to move him to repentance and a turning away from sin, Herod was not improved by it, but became even worse, turning against this pious man just as King Amaziah once did toward his instructor.
<margin>2 Chronicles 25:16.</margin>
And because he could not decently arrest such a highly esteemed man as John was, he pretended that he was concerned—due to the great following <note>Original: "toeloop," referring to the massive crowds John attracted.</note> this teacher had—about some potential uprising to the detriment of the country and the displeasure of the Roman Emperor.
<margin>Josephus, Antiquities, Book 18, Chapter 6.</margin>
Under this pretext, he had him arrested and brought to his castle at Machaerus <note>Original: "Macherunt," a mountaintop fortress on the eastern side of the Dead Sea.</note>, situated across the Jordan, where this Herod held his court at that time. Even there, John did not cease to constantly instruct him and give him good advice. But the adulteress, inciting Herod against this "Elijah" like a second Jezebel, used every trick to bring him to his death, which occurred about a year after this, as will be related in due time. Now that John was imprisoned, the following for Jesus increased, which...

# Part Two.

<margin>JOHN 4.</margin>
<margin>MATT. 4. MARK 1. LUKE 4.</margin>
Jesus answered and said to her: Whoever drinks of this water will thirst again. But whoever drinks of the water that I shall give him will never thirst for all eternity. Instead, the water that I shall give him will become in him a fountain of water, springing up into eternal life. The Woman said to him: Lord, give me this water, so that I may no longer thirst, and that I no longer need to come here to draw. Jesus said to her: Go, call your husband, and come back here. The Woman answered, saying: I have no husband. Jesus said to her: You have said well, "I have no husband." For you have had five husbands, and the one you have now is not your husband: in this you have spoken truly.

### Observation.

<margin>SONG OF SOLOMON 4:12</margin>
Here you now have the true Fountain of Jacob <note>A reference to Jesus as the spiritual source of life, contrasted with the physical well of the patriarch Jacob.</note> alongside the symbolic one. Yet he was unknown to this woman, as he is to all whose understanding is clouded; to them, he is nothing other than a sealed well <note>original: "toe-gezeghelden put." This draws on the imagery of Song of Solomon 4:12, "a spring shut up, a fountain sealed," often used in this period to describe divine mysteries hidden from the world.</note>. However, to those to whom he is opened and known, he is worshipped, sought, and found: For he generously pours out from the eternal spring-vein to all who are thirsty. Now, while this woman was drawing water, she also "drew" from the Fountain of Life through her questioning reasons, and occasionally received a sweet draft. At first, she refused a drink to the one who would give to her so generously. In brief, we shall further observe these things: 

1. How kindly Jesus bows himself to the weakness of human understanding: he draws spiritual nourishment out of natural things and instructs the lowly like a Father. 

2. He was, as it were, clothed with a cloud <note>A metaphor for his humanity veiling his divinity.</note>; having nothing with which to draw water, he nonetheless gives living and overflowing streams. Appearing less significant than Jacob, he was actually greater than all Patriarchs and Prophets. Deep was the well of his Divine mysteries. 

3. He recounts the nature of the living water: that it not only takes away thirst by filling the soul with all fullness—which is impossible for natural things, as they cause even greater burning and unhealthy heat <note>likely referring to worldly passions or temporary pleasures that leave one craving more.</note>—but also this water becomes a spring-vein of life within the person. It is always welling up and pouring out, leaping through all things into eternity, from whence it originally came; just as all things long for and flee toward their own nature, in which alone they can find rest. 

4. Jesus, sensing that this woman had not yet been truly helped, introduces another subject by asking after her husband:

The Second Part / John 4. Matt. 4. Mark 1. Luke 4.

### Observation.

1. At first she had seen him as an ordinary Jew, now as a Prophet, and after further instruction as the true Messiah. In this way, people ascend by degrees / until they reach the perfect knowledge of Christ / with such eyes he is still seen today / according to the status of people / although with the mouth he is acknowledged more highly.

2. She begins to speak of matters of Religion / pointing to Mount Gerizim, an ancient sanctuary of the Samaritans.

3. Jesus gives a clear distinction <note>The OCR "onderschepot" is likely "onderscheyt," meaning distinction.</note> where / and in what manner God can best be served: He who is a Spirit, also requires such service as is like him. The greatest error usually occurs here / in that people seek God in a divided essence / and imagine something for themselves through a narrow opinion / as if it were God / and it is but a human invention / for God (as appears here) is an image-less being <note>original: "onbeeldelick wesen" - a being that cannot be represented by physical images or idols.</note>. From this misunderstanding arises much strife and calamity. The wisest among the Pagans have noticed something of this /

<margin>
S. Franck in Ark and Chronicle
Pymander Sermons
Tacitus, Annals, Book 4. <note>original: "Num. 43" likely referring to a specific passage or fragment.</note>
Acts 17:23.
</margin>

such as Socrates, who recognized only one single God / likewise Plato, Aristotle, Pythagoras, and most exceptionally among them all, Hermes Trismegistus, as appears in his *Pymander* and other works. But the other sort had their local religious services / times / rituals / and divided idol-gods / also quarreling over the service of the same / and who was most closely associated with them / just as, in their own way, the Jews and Samaritans. Therefore the Lord rightly says: You worship what you do not know. There is a great difference / however well-meaning people may be / between worshipping, serving, and honoring God with knowledge / or with ignorance / just as those in Athens served the "unknown God," and received little benefit from it / except through Paul's instruction / who / and what that same God was.

4. When the Disciples came, they wondered that he spoke with the Woman / a sign that they were unaccustomed to seeing this from him; Yet some circumstances cause one to go beyond custom / therefore they left it entrusted to his wisdom.

5. The Woman does not tarry: She leaves her jug behind, the zeal for Gospel matters makes one forget all things / she proclaims this Christ in the City, rebuking herein the careless people who let such weighty matters pass by with mere small talk. Neighborly love requires saving not only oneself / but also others. The Samaritans come at the woman's word, showing that they gladly wish to be instructed / and that their error came from a lack of knowledge.

In this it should be noted: 1. ### JOHN CHAPTER IV.

<margin>verse 44 45</margin>
Jesus Himself testified that a prophet has no honor in his own country. When He arrived in Galilee, the Galileans received Him, having seen what He had done at Jerusalem during the feast, for they had also attended the feast.

### Observation.

There is no doubt that John refers here to what happened to Jesus in Nazareth, as will shortly follow from the account of the Evangelist Luke. Thus, being despised in His own homeland, He was well received in other places. The cause, John says, was this: they had seen the signs in Jerusalem during the feast. Concerning what kind of feast this was, there are various opinions; however, the most probable is this: since a considerable time had passed since the previous <term>Passover</term> <note>original: "Paesschen"</note>, and the year was now mostly spent, this was the <term>Feast of Tabernacles</term> <note>original: "Lover-hutten"; an autumn harvest festival where participants dwelt in temporary booths to remember the Exodus</note>, which occurred at the beginning of October. It is believable that this occurred while Jesus was still in the land of Judea, as mentioned in John 3:22. That some make this a Passover feast, as if a full year after the first Passover mentioned in John 2:13, seems somewhat inconsistent, because the descriptions of the Evangelists express a shorter period of time. Thus, Jesus was generally very welcome among the Galileans, as will be shown in the following chapter. Yet first, it is appropriate to provide a description of the city of Sychar, where Jesus was so well received.

### Observation.

Even though the people of Nazareth had repaid the Lord Jesus so poorly for his soul-saving teaching, he nevertheless did not stop continuously pouring out his benefits over all distressed and miserable people who had need of him. It then occurred that Jesus, being here at Cana, was petitioned by a person of great standing, called here a Royal Official <term>Royal Official</term> <note>original: "Konincxken," literally "little king." This refers to a high-ranking courtier or nobleman serving under a monarch, in this case, Herod Antipas.</note>: some understand that he was a King’s courtier, serving in some office in the court of King Herod, and that he was named Chuza <note>Chuza was the manager of Herod’s household, mentioned in Luke 8:3.</note>. But whatever the case may be, we shall only observe what is necessary for our instruction. 

Firstly: how useful the cross <note>referring to the "cross" of suffering or hardship</note> and the adversity of this world are; for this humbles man and forces him to come to God to request his help and assistance. This Courtier, seeing his Son in a miserable state, left all joys and vain pleasures of this world and comes a long way of about five miles to seek the face of Jesus, whom he perhaps would have esteemed little if the concern over his Son’s deadly sickness had not driven him. He had heard that Jesus was there; some past miracles made him believe that he would be helped. 

Secondly: How little man understands his own affairs. He believes, indeed, but wants to prescribe a rule for Wisdom itself: *That he should come down, and heal his Son*, as if there were no other means. In him was also this defect:

<margin>1 Cor. 1:22.</margin>
that he only believed for the sake of the signs, just like the Jews in general. But the Lord seeks a faith that looks upon things that are not seen; that one believes God for his own sake, because he is so noble and perfect of being, even if it did not please him to fulfill our desires. 

Thirdly: the goodness and the fatherly compassion of Jesus toward his weak creatures. He does not reject him, even though his request is flawed; but seeing the earnestness of this Father over his son, saying: *Lord, come down before my Son dies*, he answers him immediately: *Go your way, your Son lives*. This was a comforting word for such a sorrowful Father, yet at the same time a trial to see how far his faith reached. 

Fourthly: the utility of faith. This Courtier did better than Naaman of Syria, for he

<margin>2 Kings 5:11.</margin>
was unwilling, seeing that his intention—that which he had imagined for himself—was not followed. But the Courtier believes the word of Jesus; he saw nothing and knew no assurance other than the power of Jesus, trust-

He, discovering the truth of everything, gave himself to God with a thankful heart; not only he, but also his entire household, believed from then on—contrary to the opinion of the scribes <note>Scribes: Scholars and teachers of Jewish law, often portrayed in the Gospels as being skeptical of Jesus' divinity.</note>—that this was the true Messiah and promised Savior: for they easily concluded this, that he who gives life also has life in himself, which is God alone. Thus the Sun proves itself through the clarity of its light, so that no one can deny it, even if they wished to speak against it. John calls this the second sign, because it was so great and excellent in proving the Divinity of Christ, whereas the first occurred at the wedding in Cana in Galilee. But otherwise, there have been several other miracles, just as there were those that caused this Courtier to come to Christ. Yet if one wishes to take this as the second since the last arrival of Jesus from the Judean land into Galilee, then it does not look back to the sign in the aforementioned wedding, but to yet another that is not described.

### MATTHEW 4. MARK 1.

So much so that even <margin>Deut. 33: 18, 23.</margin> Moses in his blessing might well say: *Zebulun, rejoice in your going out, and Naphtali shall have enough of what he desires, he shall be full of the blessing of the Lord*; for this blessing of the Gospel surpassed all earthly blessings. They had also become unworthy to keep such a light as John was any longer—he who with his calling voice had accomplished so little that they were always seeking Jesus's life; so far were they from being able to receive him. Being cleansed from the works of wickedness, they also had to believe the Gospel: that the kingdom of God was near. And that God would now, through his great love and heartfelt affection, fulfill his promises which he had pledged to the Fathers; for which they had to prepare themselves as much as was in them. And so that this preaching might occur with greater power throughout all the land, Jesus intended to call his most faithful disciples to the office of preaching alongside himself, gradually preparing them for it and calling them away from their outward manual labor.

Andrew and Peter had previously been disciples of John the Baptist, and then, through the pointing of their master <note>John the Baptist pointed his followers toward Jesus as the "Lamb of God."</note>, they followed Jesus, as has been said in its place. ### Observation.

In Jesus, both the active and the contemplative or meditative life were manifest <note>The "active life" (vita activa) and "contemplative life" (vita contemplativa) are traditional Christian categories for the balance between serving others and focusing on God in solitude.</note>: In the active life, he devoted himself to the service of people who needed his help / whether by setting the Divine teachings before their eyes through sermons / or by healing the sicknesses and infirmities among the people / or providing other help for the body's needs. In the contemplative life, he withdrew at certain times / to gather his senses / and pull back from all the earthly turmoil of the people / who overwhelmed him with their great numbers / so that he might pour out his prayers before his Father unhindered / and ascend into the high Divinity / to his great delight / strength / and union in the spiritual being. We find that he often withdrew to the mountains or the deserts / or to the seashore / or in enclosed places / just as he also advised us / to pray to the Father in secret / and to withdraw our senses.

And they brought the ships to land, and left all, and followed him.

### Observation.

Luke's intention is to describe a great Miracle, which Jesus performed to bring his previously called Apostles to a complete abandonment and renunciation of everything, to which they still seemed to be attached. Thus, in this description of his, we shall observe seven points. 1. The great influx of people from all corners of the land, leaving their trades, crafts, and household affairs to follow Jesus. What Cicero, what Demosthenes, what Plato or Aristotle <note>The author compares Jesus to the greatest orators and philosophers of Classical Antiquity to emphasize the power of his divinity.</note> has there ever been, who by his wisdom or learned speeches drew such a crowd of people to himself as Jesus did through his word—a certain sign that in taste and penetrating power it surpassed all Philosophical wisdom. 2. What Jesus did: Finding himself at the edge of the water, he saw two ships lying there, one belonging to Simon, with whom he had something to deal with in particular, seeing the Fishermen washing their nets, as those who had given up hope of putting any more futile labor into fishing. Stepping into the same, he prayed or requested of him that he would push out a little from the land: whereby he sought not only the convenience of teaching the densely crowded people on the shore, but also gave an indication how a Preacher <term>Prediker: a minister or one who proclaims the Gospel</term> who is to teach the people must push out from the land, and not make himself so common with the doings of men that there is no distinction between him and them, but that one may visibly see, in all his dealings and deeds, that he has said adieu <note>original: "adieu" — used here to mean a formal or final renunciation of worldly life.</note> to the world more than his listeners. And yet not so far and strange that one can neither hear nor understand him, but *a little*, that is, in such a form as Jesus did, so that one knows what he says or desires; but if he then wishes to sail into the deep, high into the Godhead and other

This signifies how, hereafter, the **Gospel Fish** <note>Meaning the converts or souls won over by the preaching of the Gospel.</note> from all corners of the world would join themselves with great willingness to the little ship where **Jesus** is present, <margin>Acts 2:47.</margin> as if to a powerful Magnet, as it is testified: *The Lord added daily to the congregation those who should be saved.* And that with such a multitude that a tearing would follow, some fish splashing out again, while the rest were brought aboard and saved through Apostolic assistance. 5. ### Description of the Waters of Gennesaret, or the Sea of Galilee.

The waters of Gennesaret are a part of the Sea of Galilee and are so named because at that same end lies the land of Gennesaret, being a beautiful, fertile, and well-inhabited land (in which Capernaum is situated). There is no lack of olive trees, fig trees, vineyards, and all kinds of green plants, as it is a beautiful, green, and pleasant countryside situated around Capernaum, Bethsaida, Magdala, and their surrounding hamlets. Now concerning the Galilean lake, which is often mentioned by the Evangelists; the same is about one hundred stadia <note>A stadium was an ancient unit of length; 100 stadia is roughly 11.5 miles or 18.5 kilometers.</note> long and forty wide, approximately as large as the Haarlem Lake in Holland <note>The Haarlemmer Meer was a large inland lake in the Netherlands, famously drained in the mid-19th century; to a 17th-century Dutch reader, this was a familiar point of scale.</note>. Its shape is in the form of a harp; for which reason it is also called by Moses <margin>Num. 34:12.</margin> Lake Chinnereth (that is, the Harp-lake). The Jordan, which has its origin near Mount Lebanon, runs through the middle of it and finally empties itself into the Dead Sea, called Asphaltites <note>original: "Asphaltidis"; a Greek-derived name for the Dead Sea, referring to the natural asphalt or bitumen that surfaces there.</note>. The Galilean Lake is a sweet, clear water, very pleasant to drink, and so tempered that it is as cool in the summer as in the winter; furthermore, it is provided with a multitude of fish, which are also of a particular kind, the like of which one finds nowhere else. Consequently, <margin>Josephus, *The Jewish War*, Book 3, Chapter 35.</margin> it was very suitable for sustaining oneself there through fishing. Around this water various cities were situated; first, Capernaum, where the Lord Jesus lived, the description of which is to be found above; then Chorazin, which lay on the other side of the river Jordan, where the river empties into the sea between the two aforementioned cities. Gadara, toward the rising of the sun, situated in the land formerly called <unclear>Gilead</unclear> but now Trachonitis, or the land of the Gergesenes.

### Historical Continuation.

Luke, continuing his history, tells of the leper who was cleansed by the power of Jesus, as does Mark. But while they briefly touch upon the preaching of Jesus in the synagogues of Galilee, this is described more extensively by Matthew, who mentions not only how great a multitude followed Jesus, but also what teaching he delivered to them on Mount Tabor <note>original: "bergh Thabor"; while traditionally the site of the Transfiguration, the author here associates it with the location of the Sermon on the Mount.</note>; so that his order must be followed in this, and first concerning the travels of Jesus through the land of Galilee, and the spreading of his fame in all the surrounding places.

->### Observation.<-

Let us first observe this journey through the surrounding lands that Jesus made in the springtime, around the months of February and March, when the sun in those lands begins to rise most gloriously, and when <margin>Song of Sol. 7:12</margin> the vines begin to bud, the pomegranate trees to sprout, and the fig trees begin to bloom; not only outwardly in the green fields of the Galilean land, but also inwardly in the "Galilee of the heart," for the sake of which he had come to behold its fruitfulness. Thus, walking through all Galilee, he visited many cities and places: for in that same land were situated Capernaum, Chorazin, Bethsaida, Tiberias, Magdala, Jotapata, Taricheas, Gamala, Gaulanites, Giscala, Sepphoris, Nazareth, both Little and Great Cana, and furthermore the small towns situated near the Kishon River: Cemeron, Kitron, Hannathon, Neah, Arbela, Saffa, and Buria, near which was situated Mount Tabor, a beautiful and pleasant mountain.

Secondly, let us observe how his fame spread round about into all the surrounding lands, not only in Galilee, but also in all Syria, in which were situated the famous cities of Antioch, Apamea, Seleucia, Tripoli, Damascus, Palmyra, Chalcis, Abilene, Tyre, and Sidon. From this it followed that a great multitude of people prepared themselves to follow him; first those who were forced by necessity to come because of their ailments—such as the possessed, the moon-sick, the paralytic, the sick, and the wretched, who were seized by many kinds of diseases and pains—having in their company their friends, kinsmen, neighbors, and good acquaintances, who reached out a hand to them, carried them, bore them, and helped <note>The text ends mid-word "gehol-", completed as "geholpen" (helped) on the following page.</note> them to Jesus.

The last part proves / that through the shining of these rays not only are others enlightened who walk in dark ways / but they also awaken the praise of God who is the source thereof. The Pharisees also displayed their works publicly / but sought themselves therein / aiming not for God’s but their own praise / but true Christians seek their Father’s praise through the evidence of good works; they know their nothingness and are so much more humble / the more God's grace shines through them.

### Reflection.

Since the teaching of Christ brought about a great change among the people / and as some hoped now to be released from the Law of Moses / and to lead a freer life / others openly said how Jesus sought in many ways to break the Law and to nullify it / just as the accusations of the Pharisees and the Scribes were mostly directed toward that. Therefore Jesus wishes to impress upon them and make known above all things: That his coming was not for the purpose of diminishing the Law in any part, indeed, not even in the smallest tittle <note>original: "tittel," referring to the smallest stroke or dot in Hebrew writing, emphasizing total adherence to the Law.</note>, nor to deprive it of its right, but much more to teach / to live / and to fulfill the same more perfectly according to the mind of the eternal God from whom he came / just as also his entire life / suffering / passion, and burial was nothing other than a fulfillment of all shadows / figures, and sayings that were prophesied concerning him. Besides this, he also fulfilled the same Law in its power / when he improved the weak / hypocritical, and outward keeping of the same with a power of the Spirit which he pours into his own for the renewal of the inner man / in order to live in the righteousness of God
<margin>Romans 8:4.</margin>
/ as it is also testified in another place: In order that the righteousness demanded by the Law might be fulfilled in us, we who now no longer walk according to the flesh, but according to the Spirit. Such that Christ, both through himself / and through the working of his Spirit / has become the righteousness of God, which is valid before God: Therefore he attaches this like a lock to his reasoning. Unless your righteousness be greater than that of the Scribes and Pharisees, you cannot enter into the kingdom of God. Now, what manner of righteousness that of the Scribes and Pharisees was / and what manner of righteousness it is that he demands according to the mind of the eternal God / for the planting of true virtue / and for the renewal of the heart, he makes known in the following.

### MATTHEW CHAPTER V.

<margin>verse 33</margin> You have also heard that it was said to the ancestors: You shall not make a false oath, but you shall <margin>34</margin> keep your oath to God. But I say to you, that you shall not swear in any manner: Neither by Heaven, <margin>35</margin> for it is God's throne. Nor by the earth, for it is His footstool, nor by Jerusalem, for it is the city of a <margin>36</margin> great King. Nor shall you swear by your head, <margin>37</margin> for you cannot make a single hair white or black. But let your words be: Yes, yes; No, no. Whatever is added beyond this comes from the evil one.

### Reflection.

It is a marvel what man will not devise to make his evil appear good. Perjury <note>original: "eedt-breuck," literally "oath-breaking."</note> was forbidden / but not the oath itself. Immediately, every liberty was taken to curse / swear / and make oaths / and then to pursue them / as was evident in the cunning plots against Paul: <margin>Acts 23:18. <note>Referring to the group of men who swore an oath not to eat until they had killed the Apostle Paul.</note></margin> And then the matter seemed justified / the person purified / and to have acquitted himself well / when he had kept his oath to God, even though this was a horrific perjury and a blasphemous sin against God and His holy being; Therefore Jesus, to prevent this evil / through the perfect wisdom that was in Him / forbade not only perjury, but also the oath itself, and this in order to lead man onto a good path / and to protect him from hypocrisy / and deceit / just as the Apostle James <note>original: "Jacobus"</note> renews this very thing, saying: Above all things, my brothers, do not swear, so <margin>James 5:12.</margin> that you do not fall into hypocrisy. Let your words be Yes, yes, and No, no / for that is enough to express the truth / and one finds various examples among men / that those who do not heed these words / and are not ashamed to lie / also do not hesitate to swear falsely and flippantly. The Essenes, a sect <margin>Josephus, *The Jewish War*, Book 2, Chapter 12. <note>original: "Ioseph. de Bello. Lib. 2. Cap. 12." The Essenes were a Jewish group known for their strict piety and communal living.</note></margin> among the Jews / whose piety and diligent practice of virtue are highly praised by Josephus / did not allow any oath among their own, knowing through experience what great evil had come from it. Jesus further advanced His teachings toward a perfect life in the Divine virtues with the following words.

And what is this reward? Namely, Himself, <margin>Genesis 15:1.</margin> just as He said to Abraham: "I am your shield and your very great reward": And there can be no greater or more glorious reward imagined than He who is all in all. Temporally He begins here in the heart and in the soul, but hereafter in all fullness.

### Observation.

The Our Father is the most perfect prayer / that could be gathered in few words / and therein is also an exceptional wisdom hidden. For in the first address **Our Father**, we are bound to the sonship of God <note>original: "kindtschap Godts," the state of being a child of God</note> / and if this cannot happen according to the truth / then all the following desires are vain. It also gives us a confidence / when we notice that God wants to be <margin>Ephesians 3:15.</margin> known / honored / and served by us as a Father. The word **Our** includes not only ourselves / but also our neighbor. **Who art in the Heavens**: makes a distinction between God who is the true Father / and men who by nature / or by virtue of their office are also called Fathers. **Hallowed be your name**: this rebukes all those who approach God with the mouth / and by their works profane his name. **Your will be done**: this teaches man to bow his own will under God’s will: For if he makes any choice / to demand this or that from God according to his own imagination / then he prays against himself / It also rebukes the disobedient / who with their works resist God’s will / since here such a pure fulfillment of God’s will is required as is done before him in Heaven by the Angels. **Give us this day our daily bread**: This is against greed which more...

### Observation.

Fasting is understood here as an abstaining from food / in which the Pharisees placed great holiness / pretending to observe such strictly / not only to be praised by men / but also to bargain for some right before God / just as their ancestors did in the time of Isaiah: *Why do we fast and you do not see it?* <margin>Isaiah 58:3</margin> *Why do we afflict our bodies, and you will not acknowledge it?* Yet this was not the true fasting / that God demanded / as the Prophet also declares; now Christ forbids maintaining such a hypocritical appearance. He desires that when such [fasting] occurs / whether out of true devotion / to tame the desires of the flesh / to lead a moderate / sober / and disciplined life; or whether it serves as a preparation for prayer / that all of this shall happen in secret before God. It is better to remain outwardly cheerful before men / than to give an appearance of great piety out of vain ambition; through which the fruit that should come from it is consumed. **They have their reward:** That is / they have already received everything they aimed for / and have nothing more to expect from God.

### Reflection

Fasting is understood here as an abstaining from food, in which the Pharisees placed great holiness. They pretended to observe such things strictly, not only to be praised by men but also to claim some right or merit before God—just as their ancestors did in the time of Isaiah: *Why do we fast and you do not see it?* <margin>Isaiah 58:3.</margin> *Why do we afflict our bodies, and you do not want to know?* However, this was not the true fasting that God required, as the Prophet also explains. Now, Christ forbids the adoption of such a hypocritical appearance. He desires that when fasting occurs—whether out of true devotion to subdue the lusts of the flesh and lead a moderate, sober, and disciplined life, or to serve as a preparation for prayer—all this shall be done in secret before God. He prefers that one should keep themselves outwardly cheerful before other people, rather than putting on a show out of vain ambition for great "religiosity," through which the fruit that should come from it is consumed. **They have their reward:** <note>original: "Sy hebben haeren loon wech"</note> That is, they have already received everything they aimed for in their actions and have nothing more to expect from God.

<margin>Genesis 12:4. Hebrews 11:26.</margin>

Thus the Lord wants the eye to be single, simple, and pure, directed toward the eternal Heavenly things. For if it happens that man lets this single light be darkened—so that he does not see the light of God in clear day, or looks dimly and cross-eyed—what shall he do at night when the darkness falls upon him? And if it is that the inward mind 

<margin>1 Corinthians 2:14.</margin>

For it cannot "taste" <note>In this context, "taste" means to spiritually perceive or understand.</note> what is of the Spirit of God, and of itself is as darkness itself. How then shall he be able to judge? How shall he be able to discern what is pleasing to God or not, when his eye is cast so full of dust, and is entirely darkened and blinded?

### Observation.

Two Masters are named here; God on one side, because He is the true Lord and ruler of all things. <term>Mammon</term><note>A Syriac word for wealth or profit, personified here as a false god.</note> or Wealth on the other side, because through the foolish delusion of men, it is set up as a Master over them, and they are also very willingly subject to it. Now, it is the case that when someone is to serve God sincerely according to what is required, he needs for that purpose all the powers of his understanding and all the ability he possesses, just as it stands written: *You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart,* <margin>Matthew 22:36.</margin> *with all your soul, and with all your mind.* Conversely, whoever shall serve wealth according to its demands—both in gathering it, in minding and using it, in keeping and protecting it, and also in satisfying the honor and all the attachments that are bound to it—likewise needs to expend all his understanding, strength, and ability upon it. And that such a thing is entirely impossible is what the Lord Jesus intends to say with these aforementioned words. Nevertheless, some people think that it can happen quite well; they hanker after wealth and spend their precious time on it, they greedily grasp and scrape without ceasing, and often through unjust means; and meanwhile, they still wish to appear very <term>godly</term><note>The original Dutch 'Godts-dienstigh' implies performing outward religious services or duties.</note> by hearing outward sermons, pouring out prayers, and displaying a similar <term>pretense</term><note>original: 'samblandt'</note>. But how faint and cold that heart is toward God, and with how little love He is loved by such people, is known by Him who speaks this <term>sentence</term><note>original: 'sententie'; here meaning a definitive moral judgment or maxim.</note>: that one cannot serve both these Masters at once. And just as faint as the mind is toward God in a lover of wealth, so also is the mind of one who loves God faint toward the riches of this world.

### Reflection

Two Masters are named here; God on the one side, because He is the true Lord and ruler of all things. <term>Mammon</term> <note>A biblical term, often personified, referring to riches, material wealth, or any greedy pursuit of gain.</note> or Wealth on the other side, because through the foolish delusions of men, it is set up as a master over them, and one to whom they are very willingly submissive. Now, it is the case that when someone is to serve God uprightly according to what is required, he needs for that purpose all the strength of his understanding and all the power he possesses, just as it stands written: <margin>Matthew 22:36.</margin> *You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind.* Conversely, whoever shall serve wealth as it demands—both in gathering it, in observing and using it, in keeping and protecting it, and also in fulfilling the honor and all the attachments that go with it—likewise needs to spend all his understanding, strength, and power upon it. And that such a thing is entirely impossible is what the Lord Jesus intends to say with these aforementioned words. Nevertheless, some people think that it can very well happen; they hanker after wealth and spend their precious time on it. And just as faint as the mind of the lover of wealth is toward God, so faint is the mind of the one who loves God toward the riches of this world.

### Reflection.

Two Masters are mentioned here; God on the one hand / because He is the true Lord and ruler of all things. <term>Mammon</term> <note>A biblical term used to describe wealth or profit, often personified as a false god or an evil influence.</note> or Riches on the other hand / because through the foolish delusion of men, these are set up as a Master over them / and to which they are also very willingly submissive. Now it is so, that when someone shall serve God uprightly according to what is required / he needs for that purpose all the powers of his understanding / and all the capacity he has / just as it is written in 
<margin>Math 22. 36.</margin>
it stands: *You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind;* Again / whoever shall serve riches according to their demand / whether in gathering them / in observing and using them / in keeping and protecting them / as well as satisfying the honor and all the trappings attached to them / likewise needs to spend all his understanding / strength / and capacity upon it. And that such a thing is entirely impossible / that is what the Lord Jesus intends to say with these aforementioned words. Nevertheless, some people think that it can happen very well / they hanker after riches / and spend their precious time therein: They greedily grasp and scrape together without ceasing / and often through unjust means / and meanwhile they still wish to appear very <term>devout</term> <note>The original Dutch 'Godts-dienstigh' implies someone who is diligent in their religious duties and outward worship.</note> / by listening to external <term>sermons</term> <note>The Dutch 'Predicatien' refers to formal religious discourses or preachings.</note> / pouring out prayers / and displaying such outward shows / but how faint and cold that heart is toward God / and with how little love He is loved by such people / that is known by Him who speaks this sentence; that one cannot serve both these Masters at the same time. And just as faint as the mind toward God is / in the lover of riches / so faint also is the mind of the one who loves God / toward the riches of this world.

### Reflection.

The anxiety of which the Lord Jesus speaks here must be considered in two aspects. 1. That which arises from the excessive management of things / which is characteristic of those who serve wealth / whether they possess it / or seek it with great effort. 2. Through idle minds of little understanding / and estranged from faith in God / wanting to provide for things over which they have no power / letting the senses wander now to this / then to that / which creates a great hindrance to the mind / and a constant imagining / such that those things which concern the kingdom of God can find no place.
<margin>John 2:14.</margin>
Now our <term>Savior</term> <note>original: 'Zalighmaker', literally 'the one who makes blessed' or 'brings salvation'.</note> wishes to keep man from this / to cleanse the inward Temple of oxen / sheep / and doves and of the money of the changers <note>A reference to Jesus cleansing the Temple in Jerusalem, here used as a metaphor for purifying the human soul from worldly greed.</note> / all of which is brought in through greed and earthly anxiety. And to instruct man / and to teach him how unnecessary such things are / which nevertheless seem necessary to him / he puts forward six reasons. The first is that he proves from creation itself / how He who created life—which is the greatest thing—well knowing by what it must be maintained / also takes care for the least / namely food and clothing, as necessary things for its maintenance / for what...

<margin>Matthew 7, Mark 1, Luke 5, John 4</margin>
...seeing that he had condemned himself with such a judgment, he changed his wrath into mercy: From which it is evident that man, driven by self-love and ignorance of his own crimes, is easily moved to judge, reject, and sentence others. ### Reflection.

He teaches prudence in all things. It is a "dog-like" nature <note>The author uses "honde wesen" (dog-being) to describe those who treat sacred things with contempt.</note> that someone, out of a good intention, would be ready to distribute the holy treasures of faith, and expecting to find people of good understanding, would instead encounter "dogs and swine" who, like the rooster in Aesop's Fables <note>Reference to the fable where a rooster finds a pearl in the dirt but declares he would rather have a single grain of barley, showing he cannot appreciate the pearl's true value.</note>, would prefer a grain of corn over a precious pearl.

In this, it should be noted that one must observe the proper time and opportunity to distribute heavenly treasures. Pearls can neither be received nor brought forth except in pure pearl-oysters <note>original: "Peerle-moeren." According to early modern natural history, it was believed that oysters created pearls by opening their shells to receive "heavenly dew" and sunlight.</note>, which await the heavenly dew and the beautiful, shining Sun with open mouths; otherwise, they remain closed so as not to violate their purity. Likewise, hearts that are not pure, nor hungering for the Sun of Righteousness <note>A title for Christ derived from Malachi 4:2.</note>, are not fit for the heavenly Pearl, to enjoy it in their soul. And in such cases, those people become worse; they show themselves, biting like dogs and snarling like wild pigs: of which there is no lack of examples.

<meta>This page continues the exposition of Jesus’s Sermon on the Mount from Matthew 7. Having warned against the "broad way," the text now explains how to identify the false prophets who lead people toward it, using the metaphor of the tree and its fruits.</meta>

<header>Of the Life of Jesus Christ.</header>
<sig>Bb 2</sig>
<meta>catchword: founded.</meta>

<margin>
Micah 3:5.
2 Cor. 11:13.
Phil. 2:21.
Ezek. 34:3.
</margin>
...to appear <note>This continues from the previous page's thought about how false prophets appear.</note>: Which here is expressed with these words: That they come in sheep's clothing, but are inwardly ravening wolves. They feign a love for and the preservation of the sheep, but meanwhile they look out for their own profit; let it go with the sheep as it will. Since these are so disguised, the question is: how shall one know them? The Lord answers: By their fruits; and what are those fruits? Is it their confession of faith? No: for they shall cry "Lord, Lord." Is it their prophecies? No: for they shall boast of having prophesied in Christ’s name. Is it their miracles? Also no: since they cast out Devils and do many powerful things. Which then are the fruits by which one shall surely know them? They are their deeds and works, which are evil and wicked; with which the Lord has no fellowship. For these deeds are witnesses of their inner nature, just as the fruits of a tree give testimony of the hidden power of the root from which they come forth.

<margin>
1 John 4:1.
</margin>
Therefore, whatever Spirit presents itself—whether within a person or outside of them—test it and see if it has sweet, well-tasting fruits that strengthen the soul and bring to it a medicinal, nourishing power. This power is that which accords with the Divine nature, implants upright righteousness and holiness, and creates a horror against all wickedness, cunning, hypocrisy, and similar evils; for these are the hallmarks of a true and good tree. In the time of Christ, there was a dispute as to who the true shepherds were: Caiaphas and his followers, or Christ and his dear Apostles. The High Priest, sitting in the governance of the church, boasted highly and held himself faithfully to the Law, or so it seemed. He slandered Christ as a deceiver of the people, and his words seemed well-grounded to everyone's ears. Yet, looking at the fruits, he lost his case; for Jesus, doing good to all people, let himself be slaughtered like a Lamb.

<margin>
1 Pet. 1:19.
Matt. 27:42.
Matt. 26:65.
John 15:1.
Isaiah 63:3.
</margin>
The other <note>referring to Caiaphas</note>, putting the flock in peril for his own honor, killed Jesus cruelly and showed the nature of a wolf. He could not do otherwise because he was such a man within; for from this hedge of thorns one could gather no figs. But from the true vine flowed the noble wine and all the sweetness of blessing when he lay under the winepress <note>original: "parffe." The "Christ in the Winepress" is a common historical image representing Jesus's suffering, where his blood is compared to the juice of trodden grapes.</note>. And thus he has instructed us to learn to know the tree from its own fruits.

<margin>26</margin>
...[foun]ded. <note>original: "deert" is the suffix of "gefondeert" (founded), concluding the previous page's sentence about the house built on the rock.</note> And everyone who hears these words of mine, and does not do them, shall be likened to a foolish man, who built his house upon sand. <margin>27</margin> And the rain descended, and the floods came, and the winds blew, and beat upon that house, and it fell: and great was the fall of it.

### Reflection

Therefore—namely, because so many shall find themselves deceived, imagining they can stand firm through miracles and words alone—only those shall be regarded as wise people who do not let themselves be satisfied merely with the hearing of the word, but act according to it. This parable is drawn from the conditions of those lands which, being rocky and mountainous, have many runoff rivers; these, swelling from torrential rains, create a strong current that carries away all soil and sandy ground. Those who had then built their houses only on these loose grounds found themselves cheated; but those who had founded the same upon a firm stone cliff did not tremble before any floods, downpours, nor hard winds, but remained steadfast. This **Stone** signifies for us **Christ**; the Sandy grounds, vain delusion; the downpours, the temptations of the world with its lusts; the winds and tempests, the persecutions, adversities, and hardships; the runoff floods, the deceptive enticements of **Satan**, who exerts his diligence to wash away the godly and bring them to ruin.

## MATTHEW CHAPTER VII.

### Reflection

The distinction between the teachings of Jesus and those of the Scribes <note>The Scribes (Schrift-geleerden) were the professional class of lawyers and copyists of the Mosaic Law.</note> was this: They read the Law according to the letter, and interpreted it according to their human understanding, which proceeded coldly and weakly without touching the bottom of the heart. But the words of Jesus went into the innermost parts and <margin>Heb. 4:12.</margin> pierced the hearts like a two-edged sword, separating the senses and thoughts—yes, even marrow and bone—from one another. It was such that the Scribes stood and looked as though they were oxen struck on the head <note>This Dutch idiom—*kijken als een os die voor de kop geslagen is*—describes someone who is utterly stunned, bewildered, or speechless.</note>, feeling [the power of his word].

### Description of Mount Tabor.

<margin>Heinrich Bünting in the *Travel Book*.</margin>
Tabor is a pleasant, beautiful mountain, situated in the middle of lower Galilee, fourteen miles from Jerusalem toward the north, within the borders of Zebulun and Issachar. It is very high and round, about one German mile <note>A "German mile" in this period was a unit of distance much longer than a modern mile, roughly 7.5 kilometers.</note> in ascent, having a plain at the top about a quarter-mile wide, singularly suited for many people to rest upon. There is a bright, clear, and healthy air, a fertile soil, tall and pleasant green trees adorned with birdsong, and a beautiful green field where olive trees, vineyards, and other fruits are found in abundance. The dew, which rises very thickly there, and the moderate rain with which this mountain is moistened, maintains everything there in a beautiful, green youthfulness. The Lord Jesus often climbed this mountain with his Disciples and spoke these aforementioned teachings before them and a great multitude of people; there he declared himself before his own, so that his face shone <margin>Matt. 17:1.</margin> like the sun, and his clothes were like snow in whiteness, as shall be said in the proper place.

In former times, Deborah and Barak also overcame and defeated Sisera, the captain of the Canaanites, upon this mountain. Even today, some large structures of old, decayed palaces are still found on this mountain, where in ancient times kings lived; <margin>Bünting in *Travel Book*.</margin> yet now, lions, bears, and other wild animals live there, from which one may observe the great changes of the world. The Saracens <note>A historical term for Muslims.</note> hold this mountain in great esteem; they call <margin>Josephus, *The Jewish War*, Book 4, Chapter 6.</margin> it a mountain of God, not permitting anyone to live upon it. Josephus, the Jewish historian, who also served in the Jewish war...

<note>The text likely refers here to the historian Flavius Josephus, who</note> had a great command in the war against the Romans, calls this mountain Itabyrius. <note>Itabyrius is the Hellenized name for Mount Tabor.</note> He had fortified it very strongly with a wall, offering great resistance to Vespasian <note>Vespasian was the Roman general who later became Emperor.</note> because it was nearly invincible; yet a Captain named Placidus came with six hundred cavalrymen and, through cunning, lured the Jews out from there. And thus was that clear mountain covered with the dark mists of wickedness, because they loved the darkness more than the light.

### Observation.

<margin>Luke 5:12. Judith 8:18. 1 Chronicles 6:77.</margin>
Matthew indicates that a great multitude of people came down from the mountain with Jesus. Mark and Luke add something more to this history: namely, that He came into a city which is not named. However, it appears from some passages of scripture that there was a city of the same name—which perhaps lay at the foot of this mountain—and was also called Tabor after it. We shall further observe in this history:

1. **The sickness of this man**, of whom Luke testifies that he was "full of leprosy," undoubtedly an incurable affliction <note>The Dutch "zeer" implies a painful, open sore or chronic condition.</note> which forced him, according to the law, to live apart from all human company.

2. **His humility**, of which 
<margin>Mark 1:40. Luke 5:12.</margin>
Mark and Luke testify that he fell on his face upon his knees, and thus worshipped Jesus with great reverence. He did all that he could; he had neither gifts nor presents to give, as Naaman of Syria once did <note>Referencing 2 Kings 5, where the commander Naaman brought gold and silver to the prophet Elisha to be healed of leprosy.</note>, so he offered up his heart and the devotion of his mind.

3. **His submission** <note>The original term "gelatentheydt" refers to a deep spiritual state of surrender or resignation to God's will.</note>: *Lord, if you will, you can make me clean.* He believed that Jesus was able to do it, but he did not know if it pleased Him to take that cross <note>In this context, "cross" refers to any heavy burden or suffering sent by God.</note> away from him at that time. This is an example that teaches us to present our desires in prayer with all submission, just as Christ did in the garden, Paul at Caesarea, and other saints have done.

4. **The mercy of Jesus**, who, being moved 
<margin>Matthew 26:38. Acts 21:13.</margin>
by the request of this miserable man, immediately granted what he desired. Let us also go with confidence to the throne of His grace, show our misery, and pray humbly; then He will help us and take the leprosy of our souls from us. *He stretched out His hand*: signifying grace, like the scepter of Ahasuerus <note>A reference to the Book of Esther, where King Ahasuerus (Xerxes) extends his golden scepter to spare Esther's life.</note> that descended upon Queen Esther when she came before him in great anxiety; this serves as a great comfort to us. *The leprosy departed*: there is nothing that can stand before His power; there is no sickness nor misery, neither bodily nor spiritual, that He cannot heal and take away entirely. There is no better refuge than Jesus. How? He Himself taught mercy upon the mountain, and shall He not then show it Himself? Assuredly yes, as was evidenced here.

5. **He forbids him to spread this miracle abroad**, the reason for which shall appear below. Furthermore, he was to show himself to the Priest according to the law and offer 
<margin>Leviticus 14:2.</margin>
what was required for it: namely, two living birds, of which one being killed, the one being cleansed had to be sprinkled seven times with its blood; the other was to be let fly away alive. <note>This refers to the purification ritual for lepers described in the Old Testament law.</note>

### Observation.

<margin>Matt. 9:1</margin>
Matthew calls the city of Capernaum "his city," for the reason that he lived there: It is thus that Jesus, having now returned home, was followed by a great multitude / as Luke expresses it / from all <margin>Luke 5:17.</margin> places of Galilee, Judea, and Jerusalem, so that the house was so crowded that some remained standing outside, listening to the Sermon that Jesus gave inside; a great zeal of the people described for our instruction. Furthermore, we have in this entire history several things to observe: 

1. The illness of this man / who was afflicted with a lameness or palsy <note>original: "beroertheydt", which can refer to a stroke or paralysis</note> / so that he could not go to Christ. 2. Let us <margin>2 Cor. 3:15.</margin> also thus break through the roof that separates us from Jesus. If the Veil <note>original: "Decksel", referring to the spiritual "veil" mentioned in 2 Corinthians 3:15 that covers the heart</note> were removed from our hearts, then we might behold Jesus face to face. 

3. ### Observation.

Their intention was to prove that Jesus and his followers did not live as strictly or holily as their own disciples and the disciples of John—even though they did not think much of John himself, they nevertheless used his example in this conflict. It is a wonder what partisan and narrow-minded people can achieve. The Lord Jesus answers them politely: That his disciples were wedding guests <note>original: "Bruylofts-kinderen," literally "children of the wedding," a term for the guests or attendants.</note>, and he the true Bridegroom (even according to John’s own testimony), and that accordingly it was not fitting that in the presence of the Bridegroom the wedding guests should mourn, or be burdened with anything that would diminish their spiritual joy. But after his departure, sufficient cause for sadness would arise, and they would fast then. This is a fasting that far exceeds the mere abstinence from outward food; when everyone else would be merry, they would sit in great sorrow because of the loss of their Bridegroom. Thus it was a small thing that they now still took some pleasure with their Bridegroom, without being burdened by any strict rules. 

By comparing the ceremonies of the Law and the institutions of the Pharisees to old wine, and the Gospel to new wine, he makes it known that he first wants to prepare his followers as new skins <note>original: "flesschen," meaning bottles or wine-skins.</note>, so they are fit to receive the new wine and preserve it. Otherwise, if one wanted to pour the new wine into old skins (or leather sacks, as other translations have it) which were accustomed to the old wine of the Law, they would not be fit for it; the skins would burst, unable to bear the strength of the new. Therefore, it is best to join the old with the old, and the new with the new. He also wishes to teach the same through the metaphor of putting a new, unshrunk <note>original: "onghebolden," referring to raw or unfulled cloth.</note> patch of cloth on an old garment. Furthermore, it would be difficult to break old habits if they were raised in them, as people always lean toward the first things they knew; as Luke explains more fully.

### Historical Continuation.

Around this time, a Passover feast of the Jews occurred, as is evident from the following text, noting that the grain stood in its ripe ears: which in those hot countries happens at the beginning of April. This is also the opinion of <margin>Baronius, Annals, Year 32, Num. 2.</margin> Baronius <note>Cesare Baronius (1538–1607) was an influential Catholic cardinal and historian known for his multi-volume history of the church.</note> and several others. It is thus to be believed that Jesus went to Jerusalem for this feast, and returning again through the grain fields, was addressed by the Pharisees because his disciples rubbed the ears of grain in their hands and ate them on the Sabbath, as can be seen in the following description by the Evangelists.

### The Eighth Chapter.

**Jesus, having been at Jerusalem for the Passover, goes through the grain on the Sabbath. He thereafter heals a withered hand; the Pharisees persecuting him, he withdraws to the seaside, performing many miracles.**

### LUKE CHAPTER VI.

<margin>verse 1</margin>
<margin>Matt. 12 verse 1. Mark 2 verse 23.</margin>
And it came to pass on a second-first Sabbath <note>original: "nae-Sabbath," likely referring to the Greek "sabbaton deuteroproton," a technical term for a specific Sabbath in the Jewish liturgical calendar after the second day of Passover.</note>, that he went through the grain fields, and his disciples plucked ears of grain, and ate them, rubbing them out in their hands.

### Observation.

This word "second-first Sabbath" signifies, according to the opinion of some, the last Sabbath of the Feast days, which was as glorious as the first. Furthermore, <margin>Deut. 23:24, 25.</margin> it was permitted in the Law for anyone passing through the grain to eat as much as he desired for his necessity, just as it was also allowed with vineyards and other fruits, provided they did not take anything away with them <note>The Law of Moses allowed hungry travelers to glean directly from fields, but forbade using a sickle to harvest a neighbor's crop.</note>. On this point, the Pharisees had nothing to say, but only because such [was done on the Sabbath].

# The Third Part /

<margin>John 4.</margin>
MATTHEW 9. MARK 2. LUKE 5.
...[new wine breaks] the bottles, and the wine is spilled, and the bottles are ruined: but new wine must be put into new bottles.

### Observation

Their intent was to prove that Jesus and his followers did not live as strictly or holily as their own disciples and the disciples of John—even though they did not care much for John himself, they still used him as an example in this conflict. It is a wonder what partisan and narrow-minded people can achieve. The Lord Jesus answered them politely: That his disciples were the children of the wedding chamber <note>original: "Bruylofts-kinderen," referring to the wedding guests or companions of the groom</note>, and he was the true Bridegroom (even according to John the Baptist’s own testimony). Accordingly, it was not fitting for the wedding guests to mourn in the presence of the Bridegroom, or be burdened with things that would diminish their spiritual joy. But after his departure, there would be enough cause for sorrow, and they would fast then. This is a fasting that far exceeds the mere withholding of physical food; when everyone else would be merry, they would sit in great sorrow because of the loss of their Bridegroom. 

Thus, it was a small thing that they now shared some delight with their Bridegroom without being burdened by strict rules. Furthermore, by comparing the <term>Ceremonies of the Law</term> <note>The religious rituals and traditional requirements of the Old Testament and Jewish tradition</note> and the institutions of the Pharisees to "old wine," and the Gospel to "new wine," he indicates that he first wants to prepare his followers as new bottles <note>original: "flesschen," referring to leather wineskins</note>, making them capable of receiving the new wine and preserving it. Otherwise, if one wanted to pour the new wine into old bottles (or leather-sacks, as other translations have it) that were accustomed to the old wine of the law, they would not be fit for it; the bottles would burst, unable to endure the strength of the new wine. Therefore, it is best to join the old with the old, and the new with the new. He wishes to teach the same lesson through the illustration of placing a new, unshrunken patch of cloth upon an old garment. Also, the old habit would be difficult to break if they were raised in it, always leaning back toward the first state from which they had emerged; as Luke explains more broadly.

The Pharisees, being a strict sect of the Jews who held the greatest authority over the Jewish Church (as we have spoken of more extensively in its proper place), constantly looked for ways to accuse Jesus and his followers of wrongdoing against the <term>Law of Moses</term> <note>The religious and social codes found in the Torah, which the Pharisees interpreted with great legalistic rigor</note>. Jesus refutes their cunning scheme through these following reasons. 1. He proves that the letter of the Law (even at the time when it was most strictly observed) was not so rigid that it did not have to yield to necessity; <margin>1 Samuel 21:4.</margin> which the example of David sufficiently confirms—he who was a God-fearing King, an exceptional Prophet, and a man after God's own heart. 2. He shall walk with love and gentleness alongside the weak; the <note>original: "ghekroockte riet"</note> **bruised reed** that still stands tenderly on its stalk he shall not break / unlike the
<margin>Luke 11:56</margin>
<term>Pharisees</term><note>A Jewish sect known for strict adherence to traditional and written law, often depicted in the Gospels as legalistic and burdensome.</note> who overburden the people with heavy packs / judge lightly / reject / and drive a strict lordship over the sheep / which makes them fleeting and shy / but he shall help such bruised reeds up and heal them. The **smoking flax** <note>A metaphor for a flickering or weak faith.</note>, which has been nurtured with so much effort / and where the fire now begins to glow a little / he shall not extinguish, but gently blow upon / for what would he rather see than that his fire, which he comes to ignite / might burn in Divine love? It is so far from the case that he would destroy or cry out against the Gentiles / that they shall hope in him with great longing through knowledge of his sweet and helpful ways, finding that
<margin>1 Kings 19:12</margin>
God's presence is not in great sound / winds / or display / but in a **still and soft whispering**.

Of the Life of Jesus Christ.
MARK 3. LUKE 6. MATTH. 12. JOHN 4.
