### Observation.

<margin>Mat. 4. 19.</margin>That which Jesus had previously foretold to his Apostles—that they would become **fishers of men**—he now begins to put into action, setting them apart from the crowd of disciples and choosing them for this office. But before he does this, he gives himself earnestly to prayer to God, his dear Heavenly Father, and as the Text says here: **A whole night long**, for it was a matter of great weight that he was to undertake; and he did not wish to do anything here without the perfect will, order, and approval of his Heavenly Father. He withdraws himself not only from his Disciples but also from the whole earth, going up high onto a mountain, so that he might speak with his Father purely, alone, and without hindrance, and also to set an example for us: that if we wish to offer true prayers, we must cleanse our senses and thoughts of all <note>original: "lemmeringe"</note> **hindrances** or distractions and lift them up on high. When day had come: He calls to him (as Mark testifies) **those whom he would**, not out of any human favor or inclination of the flesh—far from it—for then he certainly would not have desired Judas Iscariot in that company, whom he well knew would bring him a daily cross and great sorrow, and finally deliver him to death. Truly, what pain and resistance of nature this must have been, we can only imagine.

<margin>Marc. 3. 13</margin><term>Absalom</term><note>The son of King David who rebelled against him; he was banished from his father's presence for several years after murdering his half-brother.</note> was not allowed to come before his Father’s eyes for five years because of the murder committed against his brother <term>Amnon</term>. <term>Shimei</term><note>A man who famously cursed King David during his flight from Absalom; he was later executed under Solomon's reign.</note> was an abomination in the eyes of King Solomon because he had mocked his Father. <term>Haman</term><note>The antagonist of the Book of Esther who plotted to destroy the Jews; when his treachery was revealed, his face was covered as a sign of his doom.</note> had to have his face covered before the eyes of King Ahasuerus because of his treachery. And yet this one, who was full of all wickedness—a murderer, mocker, and betrayer of his Lord—would constantly hover before his eyes, and that even under the appearance of a holy Apostle! Oh! What a great trial in patience, serving as a lesson and example to us, so that in similar cases we might endure such ungodly and contrary persons with great long-suffering, bowing ourselves under the ordinance of God, just as Jesus did here, who gave himself over to this, choosing Judas as well as Peter, James, or John. Such is not the way of the choice of human wisdom, which always looks to persons with whom it finds comfort, rest, peace, and good agreement, fleeing from suffering as much as possible. Let us now hear what kind of men he chose.

### Observation.

<margin>Exod. 18. 19.</margin>
Just as Moses, through the counsel of Jethro, chose for himself Judges and helpers who would bear the burden of the people together with him: so also has Jesus chosen and ordained Apostles, that they should be with him as helpers, and whom he might send out at a convenient time to preach the Gospel, gifted and supported with such powers as were necessary for that purpose; namely, to take away the sicknesses among the people and to drive out the Devils. These powers must be present in all true Preachers: that they may be able, through the word of God, to heal the sicknesses of the souls, to help up those who have fallen, to bring the stumbling to a right gait in the race of the Gospel, and to drive out the Devils who, with heavy temptations and deceitful fantasies, consume that which is good and bring men to a <note>original: "vreemde rasernye"</note> **strange frenzy**; for if the good Spirit is to have a place in the soul, the evil one must first be cast out.

And since Jesus had come to establish the Spiritual kingdom of Israel, he also chose twelve Apostles according to the number of the twelve Patriarchs, who should be as the first Fathers of the future tribes of his church; he also renamed some, just as Jacob 
<margin>Gen. 49. 9</margin>
did his sons, with such names as agreed with their essence and condition. Simon he called Peter, just as had already happened 
<margin>John 1. 42.</margin>
previously, as soon as he came to him for the first time, thereby expressing his immovable steadfastness. James and John, the Sons of Zebedee, he called Boanerges, which is to say: Children of Thunder. Now, with Thunder there is commonly Lightning, a swift and bright light, through which 
<margin>Acts 12. 1. 21.</margin>
men are terrified and fear. As far as James is concerned, he thundered and lightened so much that men could no longer endure his light, and he was the first among the Apostles to be put 
<margin>Josephus, *Antiquities of the Jews*, Book 19, chapter 7.</margin>
to death. ### Observation.

<margin>Micah 6:8. Isa. 5:8, 6.</margin>
Mercy and love for one another has always been the only aim that God has intended from the beginning of the World, as the salvation of the human race is situated therein. Even many Heathens <note>original: "Heydenen"; referring here to the Greco-Roman world and other non-Jewish nations</note> understood this as well, and therefore made laws according to their own judgment regarding the best way this mutual love might take place and be promoted. The Prophets often presented this same thing to the people of Israel, and proved that this was the perfect will of God, toward which his other commandments looked. But since men withdrew more and more from the knowledge of God, they eventually fell away in this as well; wickedness increased, and the good will of God was rejected and neglected—first among the willful, who drank in wickedness like water, and thereafter others, who, in order to resist these, also at last became hateful.

Now Christ comes and teaches again the perfect will of his Father, and that his Disciples must not do as the Heathens, only showing good to those who are friendly to them, and being hostile toward their enemies. Instead, he wants them, through faith in him, to learn patience <note>original: "verduldicheydt"; meaning long-suffering or endurance</note>, to endure wrongs, and to give up their own possessions gladly, as they expect an eternal Heavenly good. In that place, all good deeds that are forgotten here and repaid with unthankfulness shall come abundantly to the profit of those who are included in the sonship of the Most High. Since God will most love those who are most like him in their nature of love, and will receive them as heirs of his kingdom.

The Apostles followed this teaching, taught it everywhere, and instructed their own to do good to their enemies, and to anticipate them with love and all benevolence, also proving the same with their own examples, just as...

it is written: <margin>1 Cor. 4:12.</margin> We are reviled, and we bless; we are persecuted, and we endure it; we are slandered, and we pray; and we have become as the curse <note>original: "vloeck"; meaning the offscouring or refuse</note> of this World, and the dregs of all things. <margin>Pelagius Book 16, Num. 13. <note>likely referring to the *Vitae Patrum* or "Lives of the Desert Fathers" translated by Pelagius the Deacon</note></margin>
One reads of a Desert Father <note>original: "out-Vader"</note> in the Thebaid <note>a region in Ancient Egypt famous for early Christian hermits</note>; when certain robbers had taken all his goods and were traveling away with what they had found, he discovered a little money still lying in a corner. He took it from his hut and ran after them, saying: "Children, you have forgotten something; come and take this with you." Another named Macarius helped load the donkey upon which the robbers were packing his goods, saying: "Blessed be the name of the Lord." Another stood by with great patience and watched the tearing down of his hut, and even gave them drink to refresh them in their labor. There are also various examples from our own time of people who received their slanderers and persecutors with great <margin>Pelagius Book 16, Num. 6.</margin> friendliness—even those who came to demand their death—saying: that they were very welcome. Others provided for the needs of those whom they knew were cursing and raging against them out of ignorance, by which they heaped fiery coals upon their heads <note>a biblical idiom from Romans 12:20 meaning to make someone feel the sting of shame through unexpected kindness</note> and brought them to conversion <margin>Rom. 12:21.</margin>, such that one sees how the nature of Christ has shone forth remarkably in times of need. There were also some among the Pagans who excelled in patience, such as Socrates, who endured the daily torments of his wife Xanthippe with great tolerance; and when the news of his death was brought to him, he accepted it willingly, drinking the prepared poison <note>original: "fenijn"; referring to the hemlock Socrates was forced to drink</note> with joy. Likewise, one reads of Phocion, who, when he was unjustly condemned and about to die, was asked what he had to command his children at the last? He gave as his answer: "That for this matter—even though I must die <margin>Plutarch in the Life of Phocion.</margin> an undeserved death—they should not bear a grudge against those of Athens, nor indeed ever remember it." Yet what more beautiful example do we have than Christ himself, who, while being cruelly stretched out upon the wood of the cross, said: "Father, forgive them, for they <margin>Luke 23:34.</margin> know not what they do."

### Remark

We have spoken extensively of judgment in its proper place; this text teaches us further that man is like a flowing river, having its source in an infinitely great body of water. Just as this river gives out more water, it is further filled from its source; for this is the meaning of these words: *Give, and it shall be given to you.* It is often found that blessing increases alongside generosity <note>original: "milddadigheydt"</note>, which is why the Apostle also adds this as an encouragement to works of mercy to the Corinthians when he says:
<margin>2 Cor. 9:8.</margin>
**God is able to make all grace abound toward you, that you, always having all sufficiency in all things, may abound to every good work.** With the words of a full, pressed down, and overflowing measure, he illustrates the generosity of God in rewarding that which
<margin>Esther 7:9, Judges 1:6.</margin>
is surrendered through faith. Also, receiving the same measure as one measures out is found as much in the retribution of evil as of good; just as Haman <note>A high official in the Persian Empire who plotted to destroy the Jews but was executed on the very gallows he built for Mordecai.</note>, who intended to hang Mordecai, was himself hanged; so too Adonibezek <note>A Canaanite king who had his thumbs and big toes cut off after he had done the same to seventy other kings.</note>, who gathered crumbs with cut-off thumbs just as he had done to others; and there are many such examples. However, the words of Christ refer mostly to the retribution in the hereafter, when he shall hold judgment in righteousness.

# On the life of Jesus Christ.
## Luke 6. Matt. 12. Mark 3. John 4.

<page-num>223</page-num>

### Remark

This parable applies to the preceding discourse; namely, that he who wishes to judge another, and is himself still blinded by his own faults, leads himself and his brother—whom he thinks he is helping—into the ditch. Also, he undertakes a work which his master does not do, who did not come to judge, but to <margin>John 12:47</margin> save; and thus he sets himself above his master, which is very absurd. And this fault is much greater than that which he wishes to remove, and is to be compared to a beam against a splinter <note>The "beam" and "splinter" refer to the "mote and the beam" from the Sermon on the Mount/Plain, symbolizing large versus small faults.</note>. So it is best then that he first removes that beam—namely, of judging and despising his brother—and then, out of a pure love inclined toward the healing of his brother, comes and sees in what manner he might remove that splinter from the eye of his brother. For the eye is a delicate member; he might handle it such that he would ruin it. Great caution must be employed in that labor; yet above all things, one must first clear his own eye, so that one may see perfectly how far to go in the matter of his brother. Let us not act like the Pharisees <note>A Jewish sect known for strict adherence to traditional and written law, often portrayed in the Gospels as legalistic or hypocritical.</note>, who, having the great wooden beam of the cross in their eye, <margin>John 19:6</margin> constantly cried "crucify him, crucify him," because it seemed to them that the splinter of their broken scepter <note>The "broken scepter" refers to the loss of Jewish political sovereignty under Roman rule, which the Pharisees blamed on Jesus's influence.</note> stuck in the eyes of Christ, which they wished to pull out by force.

### Remark.

<margin>Ovid in Metamorphoses Book 1, line 9 and in several other places.</margin>
The Poets <note>Refers to classical Greco-Roman authors, specifically Ovid</note> have not found it amiss when they compared man to a tree, and in consideration of his creation said: that he was an inverted tree, whose head, like the root, is fixed above toward Heaven, letting arms and legs hang downwards like branches, thus having the shape of a tree. Consequently, in consideration of the nature and change of man, they have very neatly stated how several persons are changed into trees, and into such a kind of trees as expressed the condition of those people. 1. This manner of speaking is common in the Holy Scripture, where pious people are described as good trees, and the impious as bad trees. 
<margin>Judges 9:8.</margin>
Abimelech <note>A figure from the Book of Judges who claimed kingship; he is the subject of the "Parable of the Trees" where he is represented by a useless bramble</note> was compared to a thorn-bush because of the bad fruits he bore; so also does the Lord Jesus, who compares wicked people to thorns and thistles, 
<margin>Luke 13:7. Rom. 11:24.</margin>
the Jewish church to an unfruitful fig tree, and Paul compares the Heathen <note>Non-Jewish nations or Gentiles</note> to a wild olive tree. 
<margin>Psalm 1:3. Jer. 17:7. Isaiah. Ezekiel 47:12.</margin>
So David compares the pious who walk in the law of the Lord to a beautiful fruit-bearing tree planted by the streams of water; so also do Jeremiah, Isaiah, and Ezekiel in various places. The Lord Jesus also retains this comparison here as a certain, infallible rule to distinguish good people from the wicked—as those who may indeed disguise <note>original: "bepysen", meaning to mask or deceive</note> themselves for a time, but nonetheless cannot completely hide themselves, any more than a tree can refrain from showing its natural character through its fruits. 2. He calls that which sits hidden in the heart a treasure, both for good and for evil; for both these things are increased in the depths of the heart, as if locked in chests and preserved until the time of revelation, which happens through words and deeds. Now it commonly happens that the mouth is overflowing and full of that which has the upper hand in the heart; yet sometimes the mouth can also hypocritically <note>original: "ghepijnsdelick", meaning feignedly or with calculated deceit</note> cry out loudly: "Lord, Lord," and mean nothing less—which falsehood appears here and there in the works that go against the words, such that one generally finds certain signs of a person's foundation. 3. Finally, Jesus makes known how wisely those act who take his words to heart and fulfill them with deeds; on the contrary, how miserably they deceive themselves [who only hear...]

### Commentary.

<margin>Ovid in *Metamorphoses* Book 1, 9 and in other places.</margin> The poets did not find it amiss when they compared man to a tree, and in consideration of his creation said: that he was an inverted tree, whose head, like the root, is fixed above toward Heaven, while the arms and legs, like branches, hang downwards, thus having the shape of a tree; subsequently, in consideration of man's nature and change, they have very aptly described how several persons were transformed into trees, and in such a nature of trees as expressed the condition of those men. 1. This manner of speaking is common in the Holy Scripture, where <margin>Judges 9:8.</margin> pious men are spoken of as good trees, and the unpious as evil trees. Abimelech, because of the bad fruits he bore, was compared to a thorn-bush; so does the Lord Jesus also, <margin>Luke 13:7. Romans 11:24.</margin> who compares evil men to thorns and thistles, the Jewish church to an unfruitful fig tree, and Paul compares Heathendom <note>original: *Heydendom*; referring to the non-Jewish or Gentile nations.</note> to a wild olive tree. <margin>Psalm 1:3. Jeremiah 17:7. Isaiah. Ezekiel 47:12.</margin> Thus David compares the pious who walk in the law of the Lord to a beautiful, fruit-bearing tree planted by the water brooks; so also do Jeremiah, Isaiah, and Ezekiel in various places, which comparison the Lord Jesus also maintains here, as a certain infallible rule to distinguish good men from the evil, as those who may well feign themselves <note>original: *beynsen*; to pretend or act hypocritically.</note> for a time, but nonetheless cannot entirely hide themselves, any more than a tree can omit its natural character by letting its fruits be seen. 2. He calls that which sits hidden in the heart a treasure, for both good and evil, because both these things are increased in the depth of the heart, as if locked in chests and preserved until the time of revelation, which happens through words and works. Now it generally happens that the mouth is overflowing and full of that which has the upper hand in the heart, though sometimes the mouth can also hypocritically cry out loudly: "Lord, Lord," and mean nothing less, which falsehood peeps out <note>original: *uythijckt*; literally "peeks out" or "looks out," suggesting the true nature is visible through gaps in the facade.</note> here and there in the works that go against the words, such that one generally finds certain signs of a person’s foundation <note>original: *grondt*; the underlying character or spiritual basis of a person.</note>. 3. This history teaches us first / how from Christ, as from an ever-flowing fountain / one benefit after another has flowed / he had truly fed a multitude of people with his Divine teachings for their souls. Now he comes to the city of Capernaum, his dwelling place / and does not cease to reveal his love / to the distressed and grieving people who had need of him. But who were they that sought his help? namely a Gentile <note>original: *Heydenschen*; someone not of the Jewish faith</note> Centurion <note>original: *Hooftman*</note>, a Roman <margin>Matthew 8:5.</margin> Commander / of a unit of soldiers / who is described here by Luke / just as also in another place by Matthew / that he surpassed so many learned and famous men among the Jews / who did not look toward Christ. In this Centurion, then, these virtues are to be observed. 1. His piety <note>original: *Godts-dienstigheydt*</note> according to his knowledge / for he had established a school <note>referring to the synagogue mentioned on the previous page</note> for the Jews within Capernaum / and this good zeal led him further to the knowledge of Christ. 2. ### Observation.

Matthew describes this history as if **Jesus** spoke to the Centurion himself. But **Luke**, expressing this more clearly / recounts that the response of Christ was given to his sent friends, while he himself <note>the Centurion</note> stayed at home. Thus Jesus, through this reasoning, takes away / the false boasting of the Jews / who thought that they alone were the chosen people of God / and that no one outside of their nation / custom / practice / or lawful worship would enter the kingdom of God / just as they boldly dared to say: *The people who know nothing of the law are damned.* <margin>John 7:49</margin> This is a fault that even today is only too much in vogue / everyone crying out: *Here is the Temple of the Lord* <margin>Jeremiah 7:4</margin>, outside of us there is no Salvation / but let us learn from this how God is a universal God / who shows no partiality to any person / but will judge with a righteous judgment. And if anyone shall be rejected / it will mostly happen because of this impolite boldness without understanding / just as he says: *That the children of the kingdom shall be cast out.* These are those who enroll themselves therein / and seek to exclude others. **Luke** further continues his account / regarding what the sent friends of the Centurion found / when they returned home.

### Description of the city of Nain.

<margin>Bünting in Travel-book <note>Referring to Heinrich Bünting's popular 16th-century work "Itinerarium Sacrae Scripturae" or Travel Book of Holy Scripture</note></margin>
The city of Nain is located twelve miles <note>The Dutch 'mijl' used here was roughly 5 to 6 kilometers, making this distance about 60-70 kilometers</note> from Jerusalem toward the North, formerly belonging to the tribe of Issachar, but now counted under the land of Samaria: It lies in a beautiful and pleasant place, which is why it is called Nain, which means "pleasant and lovely": half a mile to the East lies Mount Tabor, and a little to the South lies Mount Hermon, both of which are very beautiful and pleasant mountains. Mount Hermon is fully four miles long and excellent in fertility; David mentions in his Psalter the 
<margin>Psalm 133:3</margin>
dew of this mountain, as well as Mount Tabor, such that it is apparent to all that this is a beautiful region in which the city of Nain was situated. About half a mile East of this city lay the city of Shunem, where in former times the Prophet Elisha raised the 
<margin>2 Kings 4:32</margin>
Shunammite's son from the dead; so that the reports of Jesus spread only wider, because similar things had occurred in that same landscape before through the power of great and eminent Prophets.

### Description of the city of Nain.

<margin>Bünting in *Travel Book*.</margin>
The city of Nain is located twelve miles from Jerusalem towards the North / formerly having belonged to the tribe of Issachar / but now counted under the land of Samaria. It lies in a beautiful and delightful place / for which reason it is named Nain, that is, *pleasant and lovely*. Half a mile to the East lies Mount Tabor, and a little to the South lies Mount Hermon, both of which are very beautiful and delightful mountains. Mount Hermon is a full four miles long / and most excellent in fertility; David remembers in his Psalter the 
<margin>Psalm 133:3.</margin>
dew of this mountain / as also of Mount Tabor, such that it is evident to all that this is a beautiful meadow-land / in which the city of Nain was situated. About half a mile from this city to the East lay the city of Shunem, where in former times the Prophet Elisha raised the 
<margin>2 Kings 4:32.</margin>
Shunammite woman’s son from the dead / so that the rumors of Jesus spread only the wider / because similar things had happened in that very landscape in the past / through the power of great and eminent Prophets. <note>The author highlights the geographical connection to Elisha to show why the people immediately recognized Jesus as a "great prophet"—He was performing miracles in the same region where the ancient prophets once walked.</note>

### Historical continuation.

John the Baptist, still sitting imprisoned at this time / in the fortress of Machaerus, was still held in great honor by his disciples; they could only with great difficulty leave this, their faithful master / and go over to Jesus / although he had sufficiently instructed them / and given them to understand / that his end was near / and that the teaching of Jesus would steadily [take] the place of his own.

### Observation.

Matthew, who joins the election of the Apostles and their sending out together, did not pay such close attention to the chronological timing; therefore he differs in order in this history, as also in other things, from Luke and Mark. This history is therefore placed here in its proper location, according to the order of Luke, in which several things are to be noted. 1. The question of these <margin>Acts 26:6 Luke 24:20. John 4:25</margin> two disciples: *Are you He who is to come?* from which it appears that they, along with the Jews in general, were expecting a redeemer of Israel, but they did not know for certain who it was; their master lay in prison, and with that, enough courage was lost <note>The author suggests the disciples’ spirits were dampened by John’s imprisonment, leading them to doubt his previous testimony.</note> that he [Jesus] was not the one many took him for. And regarding Jesus, they also did not have full satisfaction that he was the one promised by the Prophets for the restoration of the kingdom of Israel. 2. Jesus’s answer; it had happened by God’s providence, exactly at that time, that he performed many more powers, miracles, and wonders than at ordinary times. So Jesus brings forward no other proof of his person than the deed itself; and this is the most powerful evidence that one can present. Generally, man wants to praise himself with words: the mighty of this world have themselves inaugurated and sworn in, forcing their subjects to confess their name and hold it in honor; others who have no power do all they can to make their <margin>2 Cor. 3:1.</margin> name great, praising and lauding themselves, yes, sometimes seeking fame through the completion of abominable evils, as did the one who set the Temple of Ephesus <note>A reference to Herostratus, who burned the Temple of Artemis in 356 BCE to ensure his name would be remembered.</note> on fire to make his name immortal. Jesus does not work in that manner; he does not cast before these disciples the testimony of their master, nor the opinion of the common people who held him for a great Prophet, but points them to their own experience, taking their eyes and ears as <margin>Isa. 35:5.</margin> witnesses: *Go and tell John what you see and hear, the blind see, the lame walk, the lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead rise up.* Judge for yourselves whether this is not what the Prophet Isaiah <note>original: "Esaias"</note> foretold. Besides this, the joyful message of the Gospel <term>Gospel: 'vrolicke bootschap' or 'glad tidings,' translating the Greek 'evangelion'</term> is proclaimed to the poor, forsaken, and inconsolable person, for whom the coming of the Messiah <note>original: "Messie"</note> is most relevant: *Blessed are those who believe God’s testimony, let themselves be taught by the truth, and do not take offense at my person* (which is plain and humble in the eyes of the world, and despised by the Pharisees and lawyers). 3. The lesson to be taken from this. Wherever the Spirit of Christ truly is, there his powers must be manifest; those who were previously blind, groping with their hand for the way, must now see clearly. *In your light* (said <margin>Psal. 36:9.</margin> David) *we see light.* The lame, whose limbs were sluggish and corrupted for all good works, must now leap and make a straight path with their feet. The lepers who were unfit to live alongside others because of their painful sickness, they must be...

### MATTHEW CHAPTER XI.

<margin>verse 12</margin>
But from the days of John the Baptist until now, the Kingdom of Heaven suffers violence, and the violent take it by
<margin>13</margin>
force. For all the Prophets and the Law prophesied
<margin>14</margin>
until John. And if you will accept it, he is Elijah, who was to come. He who has ears to hear, let him hear.

### Observation.

The Lord speaks here by a parable, as if he meant to say: There have been many of old, such as Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Moses, David, and others like them, who through faith gave up much, struggled, and suffered to reach the kingdom of God; but because the same then still consisted in a dark word <note>original: "doncker woordt." This refers to the obscure prophecies and "shadows" of the Old Testament compared to the "light" of the Gospel.</note>, and because the light of God has now broken through more clearly and gloriously, the forceful ones now come—those who are in earnest and apply all their strength to it—and they press through that opened door. Thus they take the Kingdom of Heaven by storm, just as a city is captured when those inside open the gates themselves, which were previously invincible; they do this so that the warriors, taking courage, might attack more fiercely to become citizens of that new Jerusalem. And therefore he is that Elijah who was promised to <margin>Mal. 4:5.</margin> come; for just as Elijah brought back the hearts of Israel—which were estranged and inclined toward <margin>1 Kings 18:18.</margin> Baal—to the true living God, so has John, as a great Prophet walking in the power of Elijah, converted the estranged, backslidden, and straying Jewish generation. He softened their hearts and brought them to a state of reflection, that they might come to God as children to their Father. This is received by those who have heavenly ears to understand the Divine voice; otherwise, no one needs to take John for an Elijah, for it would not serve them in an external way according to common human understanding.

->Observation.<-

<margin>Rev. 3. 20.</margin>
Five things are set before our eyes here. 1. The upright zeal of the common people, and also the tax collectors <note>original: "Tollenaren." These were Jewish officials who collected taxes for the Roman Empire, often despised as traitors and extortioners.</note>, who, feeling God’s conviction within, believed John’s words and gladly received his baptism. 2. The perverse hardness of the Pharisees and Scribes, who in their own minds were much wiser than John himself; they held his baptism as a joke and an unnecessary thing, not listening to the counsel of God, who knocked at their hearts both through John’s preaching and internally. 3. The parable which the Lord uses to depict the lightheadedness <note>In this context, meaning "frivolity" or "lack of seriousness."</note> of the Jewish generation—namely, the children in the market—which indicates that they were of those of whom Isaiah prophesied: namely, children of a hundred years. <note>original: "kinderen van hondert Jaren." A reference to Isaiah 65:20, suggesting people who are chronologically old but spiritually immature or cursed.</note> Herein one must consider how sad it is for a loving Father, who takes great pains for a long time to raise his children, and yet they become nothing but dwarfs, or poor simpletons who walk in long robes <note>original: "lange rock." This refers to the long tunics worn by toddlers or the "fools' garments" of the era, symbolizing those who refuse to grow up spiritually.</note>, playing with the children; and such heartfelt sorrow was in Christ, seeing this frivolous foolishness in men of such advanced age. 4. The various means God employs to draw man to Himself: now the austere life of John, then again the more sociable life of His Son, to meet the weak man where he is; and yet all is in vain, and interpreted in the worst possible way. 5. The conclusion of Christ: That wisdom is justified or mastered by those who declare themselves her children out-

...her own bonds in the contemplation of her own abominations. So also did this woman (whom some believe to have been Mary Magdalene); she felt the seven deadly sins burrowing, biting, and gnawing within her, as if she had been possessed by seven devils. She felt how terrifying it is to have seven "thickers" <note>likely "oppressors" or "burdens," referring to the seven deadly sins; the original Dutch *dickers* suggests something that thickens or weighs down</note> as executioners of the conscience, which put all her committed sins on display in the most gruesome manner, just as David said: <margin>Psalm 51:5.</margin> *My sin is always before me, oh Lord, how long.*

Observe secondly: How Jesus, through His great love, longs to deliver such distressed souls from their heavy burden, and like a true Master Physician <term>Medicijn-meester</term> letting His voice be heard: <margin>Matthew 11:28.</margin> *Come all unto me, you who are burdened and heavy laden, and I will give you rest.* This voice cried in the innermost soul of Magdalene, by which she was driven with an unceasing desire to seek Jesus as her only Redeemer and Savior. She learned where He was, and it mattered nothing to her what she might encounter—whether she would be mocked or ridiculed, scorned or looked at askance by that "great master" <note>Referring to Simon the Pharisee, the host</note> where Jesus sat at the table—she cared for none of it. Nor did she wish to come empty-handed; to show that she was in earnest, she took a precious alabaster jar of ointment, such as kings were accustomed to send to one another as a gift <margin>Baron. An 32. Num. 7. Esther 5:2.</margin> just as Cambyses <note>A King of Persia</note> did for the King of the Moors. This was a small thing for her to give to honor the King of her soul, if only she might obtain grace through the lowering of His scepter <note>An allusion to the story of Esther, where the King lowers his scepter to grant mercy</note>; meanwhile, her anxiety made her shake and tremble.

Observe thirdly: The time that she entered. There sat Jesus, who with His all-seeing eyes well knew the secrets of her heart and what kind of person approached Him. There sat that loveless Simon, who did not feel the sting of sin because of his imagined righteousness. He fixed sharp and fierce eyes upon this woman, whom he did not deem worthy to enter his house because of her sins; he feared that he might share in the ill repute that followed her. The salvation of this lost sheep was not worth enough to him that he would put even a shred of his honor in jeopardy for it. The disciples also sat at the table as witnesses of what occurred.

Observe fourthly what she did: First, she wept abundant tears behind Jesus at His feet, not daring to look Him in the face. She did not speak, but let her tears strengthen the witness of her heart. Thereafter, showing how little her head-ornaments <note>The elaborate hairstyles common for women of status</note> now mattered to her heart, she unraveled her hair from its braids and used it as a cloth to wipe the feet of Jesus, which were already drenched with her tears. Furthermore, to demonstrate how much she loved the one who could deliver her from the "agonizing worms" <note>A traditional metaphor for the gnawing of a guilty conscience</note> and unload her pack of sins, she kissed His feet unceasingly. Thereafter, bringing forth <margin>John 12:3. Song of Sol. 1:3.</margin> that precious jar of ointment, she caused a sweet and lovely fragrance to fill the entire house, hoping thus to obtain the oil of grace from Him who had the power to forgive sins.

She went in peace; previously she had unrest in her Conscience / was tempted by Devils / and feared the strict judgment of God / now the God of peace was her guide on all her paths. ### Observation.

<margin>States Bible <note>The "Statenvertaling," the standard Dutch authorized version of the Bible.</note> John 5:2.</margin>
The word **to go up** proves that Jerusalem lay higher than the surrounding land, as it is known that the city was built on four mountains: namely Zion, Moriah, Acra, and Bezetha. Thus, an ascent had to occur for anyone who wished to be in the city. This teaches us that when we wish to attain the "vision of peace" <note>A traditional etymology of the name "Jerusalem."</note> with Jesus, we must ascend from earthly contemplation to heavenly contemplation. This pool signifies the inner Spirit or the mind of man, around which are its five porches—these are places where the sick lie (according to other translations). These represent the five senses in which man lies sick; for through the indwelling of sensory things, the soul becomes unhealthy. This pool is sometimes stirred by the Angel, and whoever...

...whoever can descend from his sensuality <note>original: "sinnelickheydt"—referring to one's physical, carnal, or worldly nature</note> into this movement of the Spirit, is soon made healthy. And he who cannot do so is helped by a special power of Christ on the Sabbath, when man desists from dead works <note>original: "doode wercken"—religious or worldly acts performed without the life of the Spirit</note>. Let us now come to the History.

A certain man had lain ill for thirty-eight years—truly a long time—but that he did not give up courage through despair was his salvation; let us always wait patiently; perhaps (says David) the Lord will look upon my misery. Jesus comes to him unexpectedly and unknown; thus he could neither pray nor desire. See here a great compassion in the Divine nature. He knows what we need before we worship him; his prevenient grace <note>Grace that "comes before" human action or merit</note> supports us. *Do you wish to be made healthy?* It is sometimes necessary to ask this, for some take such pleasure in their sickness that they do not love or strive for health with enough earnestness; they seem to long for healing, but in truth, it is sometimes otherwise. *Lord, I have no man:* He declares his powerlessness and helplessness, by which he draws the mercy of Christ to himself: *Stand up and take your bed.* See how, following this powerful word, health immediately follows. In him was that life, and so he also gave life; what he commands, stands firm; these are the works of God and not of men. Jeremiah, knowing this powerful working of God, prays: *Heal me, and I shall be healed; help me, and I shall be helped,* showing that without God's accompanying power all things are vain and in vain; there is also little love or inclination among men to help the miserable. This man had found no one in all that time to let him into the pool, until Jesus himself let his mercy descend upon him. It was now the Sabbath; virtue has no law, just as the Sun takes no notice of the days that men calculate for it. Thus the beams of virtue also shine always, regardless of what boundaries are set for her.

### Reflection

The Evangelist relates a twofold cause for the bitterness of the Jews. The first: because, according to their understanding, he broke the Sabbath; to which Jesus gives them to know that the Sabbath is not such as they think, since God still performs his work daily, not being idle in those things which, without his providence and gracious help, cannot be accomplished. <note>The author argues that God's "rest" on the seventh day does not mean a cessation of sustaining the universe or performing acts of mercy.</note> The second: because he said God was his Father—not in the general way that they also acknowledged God as their Father, but in such a manner that he <margin>John 1:18</margin> called himself the own and only-begotten Son of God, whereby he made himself equal to God, as the Evangelist himself explains. For they well understood that the Son was as the Father, since every being brings forth its own like <note>original: "dewijl ygelick sijns ghelijck voortbrenght" — a reference to the philosophical principle that a child shares the same nature as the parent.</note>; and therefore they weighed this so exceedingly heavily that they forgot all else, considering this alone sufficient to be worthy of death, just as Caiaphas also in his legal sentence <margin>Matthew 26:64</margin> cited this as the most weighty matter. Jesus, in his defense, does not deny their accusation, but confirms openly that such is in truth the case: that the Father and the Son do equal works; only setting the Father as the source and first worker, and the Son as being from him...

### JOHN CHAPTER V.

<margin>verse 28</margin> And do not marvel at this, for the hour is coming, in which all who are in the graves shall hear his voice.

They sought life in those same scriptures, yet to him in whom life actually consisted, and to whom the scriptures were pointing them, they would not come, even though he had life in himself and was powerful enough to give it to them.

For he did not need the praise of men, any more than the Sun needs the praise of anyone to testify to its clarity; rather, their stubbornness was a certain proof that they did **not have the love of God in them**, however much they might imagine it. Thus did these people allow themselves to be enchanted by those who sought to make a name for themselves at the peril of others. ### MARK CHAPTER III.

<margin>Matthew 12, verse 32.</margin>
But whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit never has forgiveness in all eternity, but is guilty of eternal judgment. For they said: He has an unclean spirit.

#### Observation.

<margin>Jeremiah 13:23.</margin>
To blaspheme the Holy Spirit is something more / than sinning through weakness against the counsel of one’s conscience. It is an evil and harmful thing to persevere in sin / for through this habit a person eventually becomes like a leopard full of spots. <note>The author uses a biblical metaphor from Jeremiah 13:23 to suggest that habitual sin changes a person's nature, making it as difficult to change as for a leopard to lose its spots.</note> It is certainly true / that the less one sins against the known light the better / but to blaspheme the Holy Spirit is even worse; for that is to reject and trample underfoot the medicine / by which one must necessarily be helped. The Holy Spirit <margin>John 16:26.</margin> is an eternal being / and therefore he who blasphemes Him sins for eternity: He comes to offer lovely grace / invites man gently <note>original: "sottelick," here meaning in a soft or gentle manner</note> / and instructs him out of a burning love for his salvation; And <margin>Hebrews 6:6.</margin> whoever thrusts such a wholesome Heavenly messenger away / willfully rejects / mocks / and despises him / what else has he to expect but an eternal turning away and deprivation of the sweet face of God. All their speaking, singing, and poetry is of this treasure, by which one recognizes what is within them, just as the evil also make their malice known through words, countenance, and all kinds of evil works. Is it not a wonderfully sweet contemplation that <term>spiritual kinship</term> <note>original: "Geestelicke maeghschap"; refers to the bond between believers and Christ, which the author argues transcends blood relations.</note> so far overcomes natural kinship that it is neither recognized nor reckoned? MATTHEW 13. MARK 4. LUKE 8.
Wisdom is like the philosopher’s stone <note>The "philosopher’s stone" was a legendary substance in alchemy believed to turn base metals into gold; here, the author uses it as a metaphor for a hidden, transformative divine truth.</note>, which they say is hidden from all eyes, and yet can be easily found by the children of wisdom who know the way to it. Josephus, Antiquities: Book 8, Chapter 2.</margin> as far as the land of the Moors <note>original: "Mooren-landt." In the 17th century, this typically referred to Ethiopia or North Africa.</note>. And so also in the time of Christ, the creatures <note>In this context, "creatures" refers to all created things: plants, animals, and minerals.</note>, becoming aware that their Creator, the Eternal Word, began to rise over them like a beautiful Sun, broke out into wisdom: the trees, the herbs, the vegetables, the mustard seed, the plow, the seed, the field, the sower, the pearls, even the fish and the fishing net itself; each was ready to reveal the wisdom that lay within it. And these were the fruits of gratitude they delivered to their Lord: for they helped him as much as they could to confirm the truth of his Gospel, which he brought forth to the people who had fallen away from wisdom. Jesus then went out of the house to the shore of the sea; for he wished to be heard openly by everyone, just as a sower casts out his seed under the open sky. The multitude standing on the shore, made of as many different hearts as there were people, presented the field to receive this seed. He sat in a ship with his disciples, signifying that he was set apart from the common crowd, with whom some treasures still remained hidden—treasures too costly and precious to cast onto the land for everyone. Then he taught them what properly concerned them through a cloud of parables, telling of four kinds of sown seed, of which three types were infertile and came to nothing, and the fourth came to fruitfulness and to the sower's intended goal, though still varying in fruitfulness, as is mentioned in the text. He did not give an explanation of this at the time, only exhorting those who were observant, who had ears to hear, to pay attention to the meaning and to dig for what they did not know: for they could easily think that such an excellent man had not come before so great a multitude to tell simple proverbs unless they were mixed with deep mysteries. The disciples themselves, taking note of this and being amazed that the people were fed with parables, investigated the reason for it and learned it from him, as well as the explanations of the aforementioned parables.

### Observation.

1. The Disciples ask a question that is very useful: For to look at it from the outside, it seemed as if Jesus spoke in parables because he did not want to enlighten the listeners, and intentionally wanted them to remain in blindness; from which it would have appeared that he was not a lover, and much less a Savior <note>original: "Salighmaker," literally "one who makes blessed" or "Savior."</note> of all people, and that would not agree with the nature of the Father, <margin>1 Timothy 2:4.</margin> who desires that all people be saved and come to the knowledge of the truth.
2. Jesus responds to this: that it was given to them, namely his Disciples, to understand the mystery of the Kingdom of Heaven; but not to the others, such that they could be helped neither by declaration nor by explanation. He also gives the reason for this distinction of gifts: Whoever has, to him shall be given, so that he may have abundantly, but whoever does not have, from him shall also be taken what he has. By this he does not mean to say that these listeners had nothing at all, but that they did not have enough to comprehend his preaching. And he proves this to be their own fault, because they had not put the gifts they did have into practice. With these words: "From him shall be taken what he has," he applies this same sentence <margin>Matthew 25:18.</margin> to the lazy servant who had buried his pound <note>original: "pondt." In the context of the Parable of the Talents, a "pound" (or mina) represents a specific weight of silver or a significant sum of money, used here as a metaphor for divine grace or natural gifts.</note> in the earth, from whom that pound, for the sake of his negligence, was also at the last—

the side of man: **Their eyes have they closed, so that they should not even see once**: it follows that he who closes his eyes is willful, and that he proves he has not been deprived, having eyes; that is: the beginning of light through natural and general gifts, through which they—if they were faithful—could have come further. But being unfaithful and not wishing to see, that very light vanishes and comes to nothing; it is covered by a cloud, the place of understanding becomes dark, the heart hardened and stony, and entirely unfit for conversion and the healing of their souls. Meanwhile, it remains true of God that He distributes His gifts according to His pleasure, to one more than another, but to no one so little that he should therefore be lost. And the damnation of men is due to their own fault.

### MARK CHAPTER IV.

### Observation.

This parable is described by Mark alone. It is a beautiful image to set before one's eyes the stages of growth. Some people want to have full perfection immediately in those who are just beginning. But in this we are taught with what order the Kingdom of God grows within a person / that it does not reach maturity all at once / nor does it remain green and imperfect in its first youth / but steadily proceeds in a well-ordered mind. Thus we are presented here with: 1. A man who, sleeping and rising again, became aware of the growth of his sowing / by which is indicated the <term>long-suffering</term> <note>original: "lanckmoedigheydt"; meaning the patient endurance or forbearance of God.</note> of God / who in all things can wisely wait for the time of increase. 2. ### MATTHEW 13.

## Observation.

<margin>1 Cor. 5:6. Gal. 5:9.</margin> The word Leaven <note>original: "Suyrdeegh"</note> is sometimes taken in a negative sense, depicting the power of evil. But here it is used in a positive sense, proving the penetrating power of the Kingdom of God. Which, being mixed by wisdom into the three parts of the body—Spirit, Soul, and Body—is at first sour <margin>1 Thess. 5:23.</margin> through its chastening instruction: yet as it proceeds, the whole person is brought into submission to wisdom, such that nothing remains that is not overcome by it. <margin>Prov. 3:11.</margin> Furthermore, the preaching of the Gospel <note>original: "Evangelium"</note> has also been in the three parts of the world <note>Likely referring to the three continents known to the author: Europe, Asia, and Africa.</note> as a leaven that was difficult for them to digest: yet from small beginnings it has spread so far that there is no corner of the world where its power is not felt.

Thus Jesus drew teachings from all creatures and created things, such as had been hidden in them from the beginning of the world: for there is not a single thing so small that it does not contain a hidden lesson. For this reason, when the hermit Anthony <note>Saint Anthony the Great, a prominent Desert Father.</note> was asked about his books, he answered: "The whole world is my book, in which I exercise myself day and night." King Solomon had already given some opening to these things through the revelation of <margin>3 Kings 4:33.</margin> <note>In older Bible translations, the book of 1 Kings was often referred to as 3 Kings.</note> wisdom, but not as perfectly as has now happened through Jesus, who has now brought to light all mysteries—even those that were in God before the creation of the world—and displayed them through parables. Which David, seeing from afar, had prophesied and foretold.

Note first that this explanation was given to his disciples alone, after the people had departed: for in stillness Jesus teaches his own best. The children of the kingdom are those who, through the Divine seed from the beginning, have become children of the kingdom from natural men. The children of wickedness are those who, having received the evil seed of the Devil in their hearts, have become children of wickedness: each is named a "seed" according to what he has received, whether from the good or evil origin: for the Devil does not sow men, but his evil seed in men, through which they become his children. He sowed the seed of disobedience in Adam; the seed of envy in Cain; the seed of vengeance in Lamech; the seed of lust in the first world; the seed of mockery in Ham <note>original: "Cham"</note>; the seed of pride in Nimrod, and so on.

### MATTHEW CHAPTER 13.

<margin>verse 44</margin>
Again, the kingdom of Heaven is like a hidden treasure in a field, which a man found and hid; and for joy over it, he went and sold all that he had, and bought that field.

<margin>45</margin>
Again, the kingdom of Heaven is like a merchant seeking good pearls: who, when he had found one precious pearl, went away and sold all that he had, and bought it.

->### Observation.<-

These two parables are of the same nature: they indicate: 1. That both the Treasure and the Pearl were hidden, precious things, unknown to common men, just as the Kingdom of Heaven is. 2. That those who sought them through diligence and deep digging finally came to the knowledge of them; they were not the cause of the Pearl or the hidden treasure, but did nothing other than seek after them; the rest came through grace. 3. That the knowledge of these things gave rise to such great joy that they were willing to give up everything in order to obtain them; understanding by this that they had to sell not just a part of their goods, but everything, without which they would not have reached the desired end. 4. ### Reflection.

<margin>
Psalm 107:27.

<margin>
Jonah 1:5.
</margin>
<margin>
Luke 8:4.
Matthew 8:25.
</margin>
This is a very remarkable and instructive history, which is well to take to heart when anxiety and distress overcome us. Jesus made his disciples go into the ship in the evening: for a long time he had taught the people and his disciples with words; now he wanted to put them to the test in deed, to see what their knowledge and understanding, which they had received through his teaching, could do for them in their time of need. They put out from land. Jesus was with them, retiring for his night's rest; the other ships remained at shore and knew nothing of it. 2. It began to look bleak here; a sudden and unusual storm arose. It seemed as if the Gadarene Devils <note>The author suggests the storm was a spiritual attack by demons from the land of the Gadarenes—where Jesus was headed—intended to destroy him.</note> with puffed-out cheeks wanted to destroy this ship, or at least hold it back. The sky became covered with clouds; the winds gusted through ropes and sails; the foaming billows rose high and fell with such force upon the ship that it staggered like a drunken man <note>A reference to Psalm 107:27: "They reel to and fro, and stagger like a drunken man, and are at their wits' end."</note>. The dark night drew near, and the rearing waves sprayed over the ship so that it could not be recognized. There Jesus lay peacefully and slept as if he knew nothing of it, like a second Jonah <note>Unlike Jonah, who slept while fleeing from God's command, Jesus sleeps in perfect trust in God.</note>; the disciples were in great fear; they did not like to make their complaints: for they were experienced seamen, hoping to endure this distress without calling on Jesus. 3. When they saw that it became worse and worse, the ship at times filling with water and in danger of sinking, they lost heart and ran to Jesus, their last resort, who lay in the stern on a cushion without taking heed of their distress. They cried out very fearfully: Oh Master, Master, we perish! or as Matthew records: Lord, save us, we perish! thereby giving it to be understood that with him a means could still be found to deliver them. Others, as Mark testifies here: Do you not care that we perish?

### Observation.

The first thing we have to notice in this / is the variation among the Evangelists: Mark and Luke agree well with one another / yet Matthew differs from these two / in time / place / and person. Concerning the **time** / one must know that the aim of the Evangelist Matthew is not so much / to describe each thing at its own time / as it is to keep the subject matter grouped together: Having intended, then, to recount many things that happened within Capernaum / he places them after one another in his eighth and ninth chapters / among which this history <note>In this period, "history" often refers to a biblical narrative or account.</note> also occurs: The other Evangelists, paying more attention to the time / separate many things / which Matthew ties together / and likewise save this History until its proper time. Concerning the **place** / Matthew describes the region belonging to the Gergesenes <note>original: "Gergezenen"</note>: the other Evangelists describe the capital city situated therein / called Gadara. Concerning the **persons** / while Matthew speaks of two possessed men / Mark and Luke speak of only one / it should be known that there were two / yet one of these was the most prominent / and best known / also the one who acted as spokesman against Jesus / and had certain things happen concerning him / which the other did not have / and it is this one / whom both Mark and Luke remember; and for that reason their description from beginning to end is somewhat longer. Some consider it a great flaw in the Gospel History / and believe that its credibility is therefore lessened: but one must feel exactly the opposite: for when an excellent History sounds somewhat different in some small things / it is certain proof: 

1. That there are two witnesses to the same event / and that one was not taken from the other / or mimicked word for word. 
2. That no one has ever taken the liberty to remove those differences / such that the History has remained pure and unchanged for so many hundreds of years / until this our time. 

One could (if it were necessary) find many examples in the Old Testament / yes, also among other credible writers /

1 Chronicles 22:11.
2 Kings 4:8.
2 Chronicles 36:9.

who also differ here and there in the description of some circumstances / and yet for that reason are not esteemed less / but all the more / because there are many witnesses to the same matter / which thereby becomes firmer and more certain. 3. That it pleased God to let these things happen / so that faith in the truth of the Gospel would be more firmly grounded upon experience /

### Observation.

The first thing we have to notice in this is the diversity of the Evangelists <note>The "Evangelists" refers to the authors of the four Gospels: Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John.</note>: Mark and Luke agree well with each other, yet Matthew differs from these two in time, place, and person. Concerning the **time**, one must know that the aim of the Evangelist Matthew is not so much to describe each thing at its specific time, but rather to group the subject matter together: Having the intention to relate many things that happened within Capernaum, he adds them one after another in his eighth and ninth Chapters, among which this history also finds its place. The other Evangelists, paying more attention to the chronological time, separate many things from each other which Matthew binds together, and also reserve this History until its proper time. Concerning the **place**, Matthew describes the region which belonged to the Gergesenes: the other Evangelists describe the capital city situated therein, named Gadara <note>Gergesa and Gadara were both cities in the region of the Decapolis; Matthew refers to the broader region, while Mark and Luke refer to the specific district of the local capital.</note>. Concerning the **persons**, while Matthew says there were two possessed men, Mark and Luke mention only one; one should know that there were indeed two, yet one of these was the most prominent and best known, and also the one who acted as the spokesman against Jesus, having certain qualities about him that the other did not; and it is this man whom both Mark and Luke remember; and for that reason, their description from the beginning to the end is somewhat longer. Some consider this a great defect in the Gospel History, and believe its credibility is therefore diminished: but one must feel exactly the opposite: for when an excellent History sounds somewhat different in some small details, it is a certain proof: 1. That there are two witnesses to the same event, and that one was not merely copied from the other, nor mimicked word for word. 2. That no one has ever taken the liberty to remove those differences, so that the History has remained pure and unchanged for so many hundreds of years, up to this our own time. One could (if it were necessary) find many examples in the Old Testament, and indeed also among other credible writers,

Now we come to the observation of this History: Erasmus <note>Desiderius Erasmus (c. 1466–1536) was a famous Dutch humanist and scholar. His "Paraphrases" sought to make the New Testament more accessible by expanding on the text's meaning.</note> correctly perceives that the Lord allowed this frightful event to come before his Disciples in order to depict through it the cruelty and turbulence of certain nations who would at first resist the teachings of the Gospel, <margin>In the Paraphrase on Matthew 8:28.</margin> but which nonetheless, being finally tamed, would be brought to a quiet obedience. Furthermore, the following is to be noted: 1. The cruelty of this possessed man, who could not be restrained or tamed with any shackles, bands, or chains: teaching us the wild horror of sins, <margin>Jeremiah 2:24.</margin> which make the soul of man so wild that it can be tamed or brought to a proper reformation neither by the bonds of natural decency, nor by the shackles of the Government's power, nor by the chains of darkness which the Devil casts around it; but it gladly takes up its dwelling and residence among the dead, and around their graves, for which reason the soul itself is also counted as dead and passed away: <margin>Ephesians 2:3. Galatians 3:1. Proverbs 1:36.</margin> the wildness bewitches its senses, such that it strikes itself with gathered stones: For he who sins wounds his own soul. 2. His behavior before Jesus: Sins do not blind so much that there is not still a secret root in man through which the Majesty of God is somewhat recognized and feared; nonetheless, they do not wish to give way: man is so devoted to his foolish lusts (even though they tyrannize him like executioners) that he nevertheless prefers to keep them, and considers it a torment if the Divine power seeks to drive them out. 3. His name **Legion**, it is said that among the Romans this was a number of 6,666. <note>A Roman Legion was the largest unit of the army; while the number varied over history, the author cites a specific traditional figure to emphasize the overwhelming nature of the "army" of demons.</note> However, here it signifies an uncertain number of many. Teaching us that even if one principal sin rules over a man, nonetheless innumerable faults accompany it, such that they are like a Legion against which he has to fight. 4. The prayer of the Demons. It seems they were inclined to do even more damage, just as they had done to the holy Job, all to bring man to a contempt of God: but that they chose the pigs teaches us <margin>Job 1:6.</margin> that the Demons seek unclean dwelling places, and such degenerate people who through bad habits have become like the beasts. 5. The proclamation of the Herdsmen. This was the reason why Jesus permitted such a thing: namely, so that this Miracle would be all the more renowned and spread abroad; for that which costs a man the least is least esteemed. Therefore, the Gospel often brings a reduction of temporal goods with it, although it is rewarded a hundredfold in other circumstances. ### Observation.

### Description of the city of Gadara.

<margin>Reusb. in Travels of Christ. <note>original: "Peregrinat. Christi"; likely a reference to a contemporary travelogue or geographical study of the Holy Land.</note></margin>
The city of Gadara was also called Gerasa or Gergesa, which is why the Evangelist Matthew gives this region the name of the country of the Gergesenes; it is believed that it received this name from Girgashite, the son of Canaan, Genesis 10:16. Some maintain that this city of Gergesa was not the same as Gadara, but another city situated nearby, and that the surrounding region bore both names; this is not so strange, for we know that the land of Emden and East Frisia <note>The author uses a local Dutch/German geographic comparison to explain how one region can have two names.</note>, though having different names, are nonetheless one region, and there are more such examples. St. Jerome <note>original: "H. Hieronimus"</note> describes that the city of Gadara was still a magnificent city in his time, being situated across the Jordan, in the land of Gilead; a name which had mostly faded away by the time of Christ, as this land was also called Decapolis in addition to the aforementioned names. It was situated on a high mountain, on the shore of the Sea of Galilee, the land around it being grassy and fertile, suitable for keeping Swine, which were fed and fattened here by the Gentiles; although some believe that the Jews, for their temporal profit, kept these swine against the Law, and that for this reason the demons were given permission to destroy them. The city of Gadara was the strongest capital city in all the region on the other side of the Jordan. These messengers clearly show how little knowledge they had of the nature of faith / which looks upon things that seem impossible to men. Such trials as Jairus encounters here / still come daily like rising sea-waves to overwhelm faith. Note now. 1. How diligent Jesus is in this: Do not fear

### The Third Part / MATTHEW 9. MARK 5. LUKE 8. JOHN 5.

"Do not [fear], but only believe." These are comforting words for those who are faint-hearted <note>original: "flaumoedigh," meaning those whose spirit or courage is weak in the face of trial.</note>; for nothing is more necessary than faith in the mercy and omnipotence of God. When this faith is taken away, a person falls away from all trust and from the perseverance of virtue, like those who flee from a battle. Fear often prevents great and excellent victories, but keeping one's courage by considering the power of Him to whom the battle belongs is the cause of salvation. Thus Jesus instructs this grieving father that he should not allow himself to be turned away by those who do not know the nature and character of faith. 2. Coming into the house, he takes only his trusted friends, because the rest of the crowd was unworthy to see this great miracle, as they did not believe it could happen and were, therefore, full of vain gestures and mockery.

<margin>Matthew 9:23.</margin>
Some were wailing and crying, others were increasing the lamentations with pipes and flutes <note>This refers to the ancient custom of hiring professional musicians and mourners for a funeral.</note>, in every way as if this daughter were to be taken to the grave immediately. 3. The Lord Jesus, as one who saw all things with Divine eyes, regarded death as no more than a sleep; since he was not only powerful enough to awaken her instantly, but would also immediately put that power into action. He rebukes all this vain and staged behavior, which was more Heathen <note>original: "Heydensch," suggesting a lack of faith in the afterlife or God's power over death.</note> than becoming of people who believed in a future resurrection. "Why do you wail and cry? The girl is not dead, but she sleeps." This statement was laughable to them; they mocked and ridiculed him for it, for they well knew that she was naturally dead. This was, nonetheless, a sign of their fickleness <note>original: "lichtveerdigheydt," meaning a lack of seriousness or spiritual depth.</note>, since the powers of Jesus ought to have been partly known to them.

<margin>2 Kings 4:35.</margin>
4. He drives them all out. Elisha <note>original: "Eliseus"</note>, in the raising of the Shunammite's son, was alone in the chamber and allowed neither father nor mother to enter, as Jesus did here. He [Elisha] went around the child, stretched himself out over him seven times, warmed him, and showed great diligence with praying, pleading, and earnestly crying out to God. But this [Jesus' miracle] proceeded more easily. Jesus has the company of five people with him, having no hindrance from them; he takes the girl by the hand, as if she were still alive, and calls out just like one waking someone from sleep, thereby proving his Divine omnipotent power.

5. There a great wonder is revealed: the daughter opens her eyes, moves her limbs, stands up on her feet, and walks, giving a clear expression and proof-sign of how the dead can be raised by the voice of the Son of God—even those who are dead in their souls, and who are already lamented and wept over. As proof of her health, he commanded that she be given something to eat: for not only was death gone, but the sickness was also entirely removed. Just so, the works of Jesus are also perfect in the awakening of the Spiritually dead, so that with good health they may taste the Heavenly food.

### Reflection.

Let us observe in this: 1. What these blind men did on their part. They observe Jesus diligently / listen and inquire after him / and immediately upon perceiving him, they follow at his heels / crying out thereafter with great earnestness / as those who desire to be helped / calling him Son of David <note>original: "Davids Sone." This title identifies Jesus as the promised Messiah from the lineage of King David who was expected to bring healing and restoration to Israel.</note>, who appeared as a helper-in-need in Israel / to stand by those in distress: just as David appeared as a light to the great joy of all to take away the reproach of Israel. They do not come as those who have a right to demand anything / but only to seek mercy <note>original: "ontfermenisse," a term suggesting deep, bowel-felt compassion or grace given to the undeserving.</note> from him who could help them / and who was full of all kindness / saying: Have mercy on us. Behold our misery and grief. Behold how we are deprived of the light to behold the Heavens. Behold / Lord / behold with the eyes of your mercy our blindness / which is the cause that we cannot walk a right course with our feet / <margin>Hebrews 11. 12.</margin> <note>The text cites Hebrews 11:12, though the imagery of making paths straight for the feet more closely aligns with Hebrews 12:12-13.</note> being forced to beg / and to die among the most despised sort of people to be found in the world. Oh, how happy are those who may enjoy the clear and bright light of the Sun. 2. Observe what Jesus does: He waits until he is in the house / for in stillness he wishes to demonstrate his powers. <margin>Psalm 62:1.</margin> My soul is silent toward God who helps me. He let them follow him / and first examines what feelings they hold. Do you believe that I am able to do this? Many there are who call upon God for help / who pray and sigh to him so it seems / and yet they do not fully believe in the power of God / for then they would surely be helped. 3. The blind men make their confession. Yes Lord: we believe it, for that they had also

be with their earnest crying, praying, and pleading, yet they must likewise confess it with the mouth: *For with the heart one believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation.* At first, no more could be demanded of them. 4. Jesus touched their eyes; this touching was a powerful working for the restoration of sight. He touches our eyes when he shows us the works of his creation, when he lets us see his daily benefits and various wonders, through which we come to a keen observation to behold his Heavenly wisdom. He added to this: *According to your faith be it unto you*; immediately the power of her faith was revealed, for their eyes were opened. That many people now remain blind and are not helped comes through a lack of faith; for God cannot be accused of failing in his duty. Let us then go to Jesus according to the knowledge we have, earnestly calling upon him, showing our lack, believing in his power and Fatherly kindness, so we shall certainly be healed. 5. These blind men, being gladdened, spread this benefit everywhere; for how could they keep silent about such glorious things that had happened to themselves? Jesus had indeed forbidden them, yet not so that his wonders should remain in the dark, but so that they would not overwhelm him too much, as often happened. Thus he also showed that he did not display his powers for the glory or honor that would be brought to him through them, but for the salvation of men, so that they might come to God through them.

It seems that the afflicted people followed Jesus at his heels everywhere; one was no sooner gone than another came again. [pos]sessed, specifically by a devil who held his tongue in check: This still happens often in a spiritual sense, that the devil, through the bonds of evil habits, has certain tongues so much in his power that they are mute and speechless. <margin>Psalm 58:2</margin> David says: *Are you then mute, that you do not wish to speak what is right?* <margin>Plutarch, in the Life of Demosthenes</margin> The orator Demosthenes <note>A famous Greek statesman and orator known for his eloquence.</note> was made mute by money before the court: the greedy devil has great power among men. 2. How he was delivered: They brought him to Jesus; he would not have come of his own accord, for the devil closes the doors of understanding so that a person does not recognize his own defect, much less know the means for his healing. It is a work of mercy to lead such poor people—through prayers, exhortations, and conversation—to Jesus, the Physician of souls. 3. The crowd was amazed: for it is a great miracle <term>Mirakel</term> <note>From the Latin 'miraculum', a wonder or supernatural act.</note> that someone who used his tongue according to the devil’s will for ungodliness and all frivolity, and was as if mute in godly things, now speaks with new tongues, <margin>Matthew 16:17</margin> <note>The original text cites Matthew 16:17, though the reference to 'new tongues' is famously found in Mark 16:17.</note> understandably and clearly: it is a proving sign of faith. 4. The slander of the Pharisees: Envy is an evil beast; yet it consumes itself, for with this they revealed that they ascribed great power to the prince of devils. They would rather acknowledge him as a lord than God. Nor was it a wonder that they remained mute in the praise of God and in all polite conversation, since they were just as possessed as this man had figuratively expressed.

He traveled through all the cities so that they would have no excuse when his time passed, claiming they had not known; he placed the light on the lampstand <note>A reference to Matthew 5:15, meaning Jesus made his teachings public and visible to all.</note>, teaching in the public schools; he brought them the glad tidings of the Heavenly Kingdom, which was now approaching, and of which Daniel had prophesied that it would be established during the time of the fourth kingdom <note>In the Book of Daniel, the "Fourth Kingdom" was traditionally interpreted by scholars of this era as the Roman Empire, which was at its peak during the life of Christ.</note>, which was now at its height and near its decline. To confirm this, he healed all illnesses among the people, thereby giving the beginning of that same kingdom; for once illnesses and infirmities are driven away, everything flourishes in its prime. Death itself is nothing other than an illness of nature and a deprivation of life; therefore, when all illnesses of both body and soul are taken away, it is necessary that the Kingdom of God—the true health and lasting eternity, which had its beginning in Paradise—be established again. He looked upon the people with compassion, for they now wandered like lost sheep under the guidance of unfaithful and cruel shepherds, about whom Ezekiel had prophesied; therefore they were as if having no shepherd. They lacked the true shepherd, whom they did not know and therefore did not wish to shelter under his wings. He saw many hungry souls and willing hearts scattered here and there in the fields of Jacob, who were not yet bound into sheaves and had great need of a good Joseph <note>The author compares Jesus to the Old Testament Joseph, who gathered and distributed grain during the famine in Egypt.</note>, for which the help of his brothers, the eleven Patriarchs, was also needed. But because such a thing could not happen without the gracious sending forth by the Lord of the Harvest, he commands them to pray, so that such a calling might enter their hearts; so that even if, like Moses and Jeremiah, they were at first unwilling <note>Moses and Jeremiah both initially expressed doubt or unworthiness when called by God (Exodus 4:10, Jeremiah 1:6).</note>, they might afterwards, recognizing the Lord's will, be fiery and diligent in carrying out their office.

# Of the Life of Jesus Christ.

### MATTHEW 10. MARK 6. LUKE 9. JOHN 5.

2 First, Simon, who is called Peter, and Andrew
his brother; James the son of Zebedee, and John his
3 brother; Philip and Bartholomew; Thomas, and
4 Matthew the tax collector <note>original: "tollenaer"; in the Roman system, these were locals hired to collect taxes, often despised for corruption, making Matthew’s calling particularly significant.</note>; James the son of Alphaeus; Leb-
baeus, whose surname was Thaddaeus; Simon of Ca-
na, and Judas Iscariot, who also betrayed him.

---

## Observation.

<margin>Mark 3:13. Luke 6:13. Exodus 1:2. Numbers 1:44. Exodus 28:9. Revelation 21:14. Exodus 16:1. 1 Kings 4:7. 1 Kings 7:25. 1 Kings 19:19. 1 Kings 10:19.</margin>
How these twelve Disciples were first chosen as Apostles we have already pointed out from Mark and Luke, and we dealt with their naming there. Matthew, who does not describe this election, now comes and speaks of their sending out. Now, this number of twelve has its origin in the twelve tribes of Israel; and accordingly, several things have served as beautiful prefigurations of these twelve Apostles. Such as:

1. The twelve Patriarchs, and following them: 
2. The twelve tribes arising from them. 
3. The twelve Princes of those same tribes. 
4. The twelve stones in the breastplate of Aaron; just as the Apostles of Christ are compared in another place to twelve precious stones <note>A reference to Revelation 21:14, where the foundations of the heavenly city are inscribed with the names of the twelve apostles.</note>. 
5. The twelve fountains in Elim, which served to refresh thirsty Israel in the wilderness. 
6. The twelve officers of King Solomon, who were always about him and stood ready for his service, each fulfilling his office for one month. 
7. The twelve oxen upon which the cast-metal sea <term>The Brazen Sea: A massive bronze basin in Solomon's Temple used for ritual washing, supported by twelve bronze oxen.</term> stood, whose faces were turned toward the East, West, South, and North, as if the oxen wished to call out to the entire world. The ministry of these burden-bearing oxen—who would plow the wild fields in order to sow the Gospel grain therein and to sprinkle it with the Sea of God’s grace which they would bring to them—follows the prefiguration of these. 
8. The twelve golden lions at the throne of Solomon, which always kept watch there, attended His Majesty, and represented triumphant victors: those who would help execute the judgment of the wisest King over the twelve tribes of Israel. This number of twelve has always remained fulfilled: for when Judas Iscariot the traitor had departed, Matthias came in his place.
