Three kinds of comfort are set before the eyes of the Apostles here (and all others who endure distress and suffering for the sake of the Gospel): The first is the immortality of the soul, over which tyrants have no power. This is why the Apostles in other places refer to physical death as merely a "moving of house" <note>original: "verhuysinge"; a reference to the soul changing its residence from the body to heaven, as seen in 2 Corinthians 5:1.</note> for which they heartily longed. From this arose their joy when they met their end, just as the martyrs of the Old Testament did, as is evident in the seven sons of the Maccabees,

Furthermore, King Cyrus, when he was about to die, spoke to his children and the friends standing by: "I do not believe that you think I shall be entirely nothing, and that my soul shall perish, when I have departed from this mortal body: For you see my soul as little now as you shall after my death, but you know it only through its outward works."

<margin>Luke 12:8.</margin>
The second comfort is that they also cannot kill the body, except by the permission of their Father, whose Divine providence includes even the smallest of creatures. Among these, He names those that were always before their eyes, namely: the sparrows, which were sold for a small price—two for a penny, which is worth about half a stiver <note>original: "stuyver"; a small Dutch coin common in the 17th century</note> in our money. He further adds that even the hairs of their heads were numbered. This has been a firm support and comfort to all believers; it would take too long to recount all their examples here, but we shall only remember that the three youths in the book of Daniel, standing before the glowing furnace, trusted that God could deliver them from it—which indeed came to pass. The wild animals—lions, wolves, and bears—which were incited under the tyrannical Emperor Diocletian to devour a great crowd of martyrs, had their cruelty softened and tamed by the special guidance of God. This also happened to Blandina <note>Blandina was a famous Christian martyr in Gaul (modern France) in the 2nd century, known for her incredible endurance during torture.</note> and others, so that this reasoning of Christ is more than proven by experience. The third comfort is that, even if God allowed them to sigh pitifully under the power of tyrants—enduring persecution, the cross, torture, the seizure of goods, and even death itself—and even if such things lasted a long time, so that they seemed abandoned by God, like people sent to the slaughter-bench <note>original: "slacht-banck"; an old term for a butcher's block or a place of execution</note> as prey and plunder; nevertheless, they shall not despair or doubt the Divine mercy and Fatherly oversight of them. For all that remains unredeemed here, receiving no outcome or reward for suffering, shall hereafter be all the more glorious; provided that because of their faithful confession, He shall also confess them before His Heavenly Father. And there, everything shall be repaid double, indeed a thousandfold, for all that has been suffered and fought for here for the sake of His name.

### Remark.

Having exhorted his Apostles to patience in the coming cross <note>The "cross" here refers to the trials and persecutions the disciples would face for their faith.</note> and how they would be persecuted and oppressed like sheep in the midst of wolves, Jesus may have caused them to suspect that these words of his did not agree with certain Prophets who had prophesied of the coming Messiah: <margin>Isaiah 9:5</margin> That he would be a <margin>Micah 4:3</margin> Prince of Peace, and also that in his time people would not wage war, nor lift up one sword against another, but that people would make swords into plowshares and spears into sickles; in which time they would then sit in all peace, tranquility, and stillness. Thus the Lord Jesus first anticipates such suspicion with this teaching of his; for it is true that he is the only Prince of Peace, and loves nothing but love and peace, also wishing that all people accept his peace, and especially that his disciples shall love one another from the bottom of their hearts <margin>John 14:27</margin> with an inseparable love; <margin>John 15:12</margin> it is likewise true that through this, the prophecies of a peaceful time and the laying down of all discord and war are fulfilled in these same disciples and in all who obey him. But since this Heavenly <margin>1 Corinthians 2:14</margin> peace could not be accepted or understood—because the character and <margin>Luke 17:1</margin> nature of the evil world is in itself full of discord and entirely opposed to Christ, just as water and fire are opposed to each other, which are never at peace until one has completely overcome the other. And since the coming of Christ into this world is for the purpose of proclaiming the Gospel <term>Gospel: from the Dutch "Euangelium," meaning the "good news" of Christ</term> of peace to all people, and that this cannot happen except with their great disturbance and dismay because of the difference the world has with the nature of Christ. So he had certainly come to ignite this disturbance through his Gospel-fire, to stir up against each other those people who sat in a false and deceptive peace, just as Sodom and <margin>Ezekiel 16:49</margin> Gomorrah did in times past. The son, being instructed in the new teaching of the Gospel and wishing to instruct his father and deliver him from the old error, brings his father's hatred upon his own neck; the daughter, following the Christian way of Salvation <note>original: "Saligheydt"; refers to both a state of holiness and the ultimate rescue of the soul.</note>, is rejected by her mother and met with constant strife. Likewise also the son's wife by the husband's mother, and whatever more of the same might occur in the household, whereby not only strife but also the sword of persecution is sharpened and brought to light, of which examples are not lacking to prove this; Jesus then makes this known to his disciples, so that

## The First Chapter.

*The report of Jesus comes before Herod / who, having beheaded John / is terrified by it. The twelve Apostles returning / with the disciples of John / gather by Christ. Description of the Castle of Machaerus.*

### MARK CHAPTER VI.

<margin>verse 15</margin> AND that came before King *Herod*; for his name was now known, and <margin>*Matthew 14:1, Luke 9:7*</margin> he said: *John the Baptist* has risen from the dead, therefore <margin>16</margin> his deeds are so powerful. But some said: This is *Elijah*, others, this is a <margin>17</margin> Prophet, or one of the Prophets. But when *Herod* had heard that, he said: This is *John*, whom I beheaded; he has risen from the dead.

### Observation.

<margin>*Baronius, Year 33, number 1.*</margin> At the beginning of the thirty-third year of *Christ* / when the Consuls <note>original: "Borghermeesters." In a Roman context, this refers to the two annually elected chief magistrates.</note> in *Rome* were: Emperor *Tiberius* for the fifth time; <margin>*Ecclesiastes 10:3*</margin> and *Aelius Sejanus*, one saw fulfilled the proverb of *Solomon*: I saw servants sitting on riding-horses, and Princes walking on foot <note>This quote is found in Ecclesiastes 10:7 in modern Bibles. The author uses it to contrast the low-born Sejanus rising to power while the worthy are suppressed.</note>: For this happened in *Rome* / that the servant *Sejanus* was above his Master the emperor *Tiberius*: and in *Judea* an unworthy man sat in great honor / namely *Herod Antipas*. And *John the Baptist*, the holiest man born of women / sat locked in irons / being put to death as a criminal / and that for such a trivial cause <note>referring to the dance of Salome and Herod's rash oath.</note> / as if he had been worth nothing in the eyes of *God* / which the *Evangelists* have described at length as a memorable matter. So *Mark* then relates what is set down above as an introduction to what he will tell hereafter. Wherein two things are to be noted / 1. That the report of *Jesus* now came before King *Herod*. The *Evangelist Mark* calls him a King, since he was a Son of the great *Herod* / King of *Judea*. Yet *Matthew* gives him the name of Tetrarch <note>A "vier-Vorst" or Tetrarch was a ruler of a fourth part of a kingdom or province under the Roman Empire.</note>, as he also truly was / as possessing

### MATTHEW 14. MARK 6. LUKE 9. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; JOHN 5.

<margin>Eusebius Church History Book 1, Chapter 1.</margin> possessing a part of his Father's kingdom / by order of the Roman council / as previously mentioned by us. One might ask: why did this report tarry so long / before it came to the eyes of Herod / since it had already filled the land long before / and had even spread to foreign cities? Even to Abgar, the King of Edessa / on the River Euphrates, as Eusebius recounts / saying: that this King, being seized by a heavy sickness / through the report of the miraculous deeds of Jesus / sent to him in writing / that he should come there to heal him: whereupon he received a written answer in return / that such would happen afterward / by one of his Disciples / which was fulfilled after the Ascension of Christ / by Thaddeus: Eusebius writes that he found this in the records <note>original: "Libri."</note> of the city of Edessa in the Syriac language. <margin>2 Kings 5:1.</margin> Thus, this King Abgar, being driven by his infirmity / listened very sharply for a means to his health / as Naaman of Syria did in old times. Yet why this

<margin>Josephus Antiquities Book 18, Chapter 7.</margin> Herod lay hidden for so long as if under a bushel basket / can have various causes: Firstly, because he, as a wanton and arrogant man having no need for such a Physician / stopped his ears to all good reports / and allowed himself to be satisfied in his pleasures. Secondly, because while John lived / the report of Jesus was not spread by his disciples in that corner / as they were jealous of their master’s honor / which in their imagination would be diminished by it. Thirdly, because this Herod had been in Rome in the meantime (as can be noted from Josephus) to attend to certain matters there / and coming home: he had his head filled with the idle things of the Court. Yet it now broke out so much through the preaching / and miracles of the Apostles / that it could no longer be kept out of his bedchamber.

<margin>Genesis 4:14</margin> <margin>Baronius, Year 5, 6, Number 5.</margin> 2. The terror that Herod received through this: It is a characteristic of the ungodly / especially of tyrants. That a rustling leaf makes them tremble / as they have a restless and seared Conscience: as was evident in Cain. And in a certain Theodoric, King of Italy, who had tyrannically caused two excellent Roman Councilors, Boethius and Symmachus, to be put to death. And when at one time a fish with a gaping mouth was served before him on the table / he imagined that this was the head of Symmachus / which threatened him with its teeth / and came to demand vengeance for his crime. Which torment threw him into bed / and stayed with him so long: until with great lamentation he gave up his Spirit / and so departed the world.

<margin>Matthew 14:2.</margin> It was also thus with this Herod: Hearing of the powerful deeds of Jesus, he immediately imagined that this was John the Baptist whom he had caused to be beheaded, and that he now appeared much more powerful than he had ever been. And although some said he was Elijah, others: that he was Jeremiah or one of the old Prophets / who had now risen again from the dead / or was revealed in the person of Jesus through the migration of souls <note>original: "verhuysingh der zielen." This refers to the concept of metempsychosis or reincarnation, which the author suggests was one way the people explained Jesus' power.</note>

# Reflection

In what manner this Holy Man was thrown into prison / and why this happened / we have handled in its proper place / <margin>Luke 3:19.</margin> where the same is described by the Evangelist Luke: both Mark and Matthew relate the same now at this time / because they had previously been silent about it / and now include it together in one History. So we have first to note the cunning snares of Herodias, who constantly pressured this pious man to help him to his death. <margin>1 Kings 19:1.</margin> Playing here the part of Jezebel, who in like manner sought the life of Elijah <note>original: "Eliam"</note>: for godless people, having once given themselves over to all wickedness / find no rest / until they fill their measure. ...and strengthened him in his need. Up above in the Court, the people were merry, and here below comes the executioner with a naked sword: this was a sign that he was to be sacrificed, and that the time of his departure was near. He who had given testimony of the **Lamb of God** now bowed himself like a lamb under the will of his Heavenly Father, and was slaughtered like an innocent lamb to serve as a satisfaction for the bloodthirsty wolves. Observe now the conclusion. The Arabian King <note>Aretas IV, whose daughter Herod Antipas had divorced to marry Herodias.</note>, troubled by the insult to his daughter who was cast off for the sake of **Herodias**, prepares himself for war; he invades the land, robs, and plunders. **Herod** with his Commanders moves against him. The subjects of the Tetrarch **Philip**, troubled by their Lord’s shame, betray **Herod’s** army, which was defeated, and he was driven to flight. Oh, how dearly his Great Ones had to pay for the blood they had seen floating in the dish like water! For although **Herod**, ashamed of the death of this pious man, sought a fig-leaf <note>a metaphorical cover-up or excuse</note>, saying that he had him beheaded out of fear of rebellion, nevertheless, it lay in the minds of all people that it was an evil deed; and he was therefore punished by the Arabian. 

Later, the rod strikes him even harder: He goes to Rome (trying, like Aesop’s dog, for the shadow of the piece of meat <note>A reference to the fable where a dog drops his real meat to chase a reflection.</note>) and requests from Emperor **Caius** <note>Caligula</note> the portion that **Agrippa**, the brother of **Herodias**, possessed; but it turned out differently. He who falsely accused the Holy man of rebellion was himself punished as a rebel. And he had to surrender not just half his kingdom, as he had light-heartedly offered as a pledge, but the whole of it. Furthermore, he was sent with **Herodias** and her daughter into exile to Lyons in France, where they had to live meagerly; and the dancer <note>Salome</note> had her head roll upon the ice when, while dancing upon it, she fell through; so some write <note>This is a popular medieval legend rather than a biblical account.</note>. Thus, in this whole history, the riddle of **Zerubbabel** is fulfilled: First, the wine was powerful; then the women with their deceitful game; then the King in the command over **John**; at last, the truth overcame all, pricking the conscience of this **Herod** and bringing upon him a just and well-deserved vengeance.

MATTHEW 14. MARK 6. LUKE 9. JOHN 5.

<margin>Josephus, *The Jewish War*, Book 7, Chapter 10. <note>original: "Joseph de Bello. lib. 7. cap. 10."</note></margin>
...ruled shortly after the times of the **Maccabees** <note>A family of Jewish patriots who led a religious and political rebellion against the Seleucid Empire in the 2nd century BCE.</note> and was descended from their lineage. The situation of the place was naturally strong, being a high hill in the land of **Perea** <note>The portion of the kingdom of Herod the Great occupying the eastern side of the Jordan River valley.</note> on the Arabian borders; to the west was a valley two miles long, reaching to the Dead Sea called **Asphaltites** <note>original: "Asphaltides" — a classical name for the Dead Sea, referring to the bitumen (asphalt) that surfaces there.</note>. To the south and north, the trenches were so wide that one could not storm them; to the east was a deep valley about a hundred cubits wide, ending at a nearby mountain. Thus, the aforementioned **Alexander** <note>Alexander Jannaeus, the Hasmonean king.</note> first built a fortress here, which was later destroyed and cast down by **Gabinius**, the Roman commander, in the war against **Aristobulus**. But when **Herod the Idumean** <note>Herod the Great.</note> became king, and realizing this was a convenient location against the Arabs, he built there not only a fortress but also a city, surrounding the mountain with a special wall upon which were towers a hundred and sixty cubits high; and in the middle of this circle, a beautiful and magnificent palace, providing this place with water wells and all kinds of necessities. So it was that his son **Herod Antipas** held court there; **John**, having been mocked, was led there as a prisoner and finally beheaded.

<margin>Josephus, *Antiquities of the Jews*, Book 8, Chapter 7. <note>original: "Joseph. Antiq. Lib. 8. Cap. 7."</note></margin>
In this palace grew a beautiful, large **rue bush** <note>original: "Ruyten-struyck" — Rue was often associated with bitterness and regret.</note> as thick as a fig tree, which was cut down by the Jews—not poorly representing this **John**, who was a magnificent growth, yet bitter to the voluptuous **Antipas**. There was another representation through the **Baaras root**, having the appearance of fire, and in the evening a glimmer like lightning, which could not be pulled up except with the loss of the puller's life; therefore, they tied a dog to it, which, in running away, pulled it with him and thus uprooted it, and immediately died thereafter. This is to be compared to **Antipas**, who, like an unworthy dog, having uprooted this lightning-bright shining root through the urging of **Herodias** and for the increase of his dominion, ran from this palace to Rome, and thereby caused his own punishment and downfall. This root had the power to drive out demons, as **Josephus** describes, just as the sins and evil spirits of men were driven out through the teaching of **John**. The warm and cold waters that, when mixed together, were pleasant and healthy to drink, also had their significance to the same end.

<margin>Josephus, *The Jewish War*, Book 7, Chapter 25. <note>original: "Joseph de Bello lib. 7. Cap 25."</note></margin>
Furthermore, this city of **Macherunt** <note>Machaerus.</note> long defended itself against the Roman war under **Vespasian**, but was finally besieged and attacked with force by **Bassus**, a commander; for capturing a brave, strong youth named **Eleazar**, he threatened to crucify him, whereby those in the fortress, taking pity on him, surrendered; but those in the lower city were almost all slain, at least seventeen hundred remaining on the spot. # Of the Life of Jesus Christ.

->MATTHEW 14. MARK 6. LUKE 9. JOHN 5.<-

<margin>Josephus, *The Jewish War*, Book 7, Chapter 10. <note>original: "Ioseph de Bello. lib. 7. Cap. 10."</note></margin>
[The fortress of Machaerus] was ruled shortly after the time of the **Maccabees** <note>A Jewish dynasty that led a revolt against the Seleucid Empire in the 2nd century BCE</note>, having sprung from their lineage. The situation of the place was naturally strong, being a high hill in the land of **Perea** <note>The region of the northern Transjordan</note> on the Arabian borders. To the west was a valley two miles long, reaching as far as the **Dead Sea**, called **Asphaltides** <note>term: <term>Asphaltides</term> is the Greek name for the Dead Sea, referring to the bitumen or asphalt that occasionally floats on its surface</note>. To the South and North, the trenches were so wide that they could not be stormed; to the East was a deep valley about a hundred ells <note>An "ell" or cubit was a measurement of length based on the forearm; about 18-22 inches</note> wide, ending at a nearby mountain. Thus, the aforementioned **Alexander** <note>Alexander Jannaeus, the Hasmonean king</note> first built a castle here, which was later destroyed and thrown down by **Gabinius**, the Roman General, during the war against **Aristobulus**. But when **Herod the Idumean** <note>Herod the Great</note> became King, and noticing this to be a convenient location against the Arabians, he built there not only a castle but also a city, surrounding the mountain with a special wall upon which were towers one hundred and sixty ells high. In the middle of this circle was a beautiful and magnificent Palace, providing this place with water-wells and all kinds of necessities. So it was that this fine son, **Herod Antipas**, held court there, where, as has been said, he held **John** prisoner and finally beheaded him.

<margin>Josephus, *Antiquities of the Jews*, Book 8, Chapter 7. <note>original: "Ioseph. Antip. Lib. 8. Cap. 7."</note></margin>
In this palace grew a beautiful, large rue-shrub as thick as a fig tree, which was cut down by the Jews; this not poorly represents this John, who was a magnificent growth, yet bitter to the lustful Antipas. There was another representation through the **Baaras** root <note>A legendary root described by Josephus in *The Jewish War*, Book 7</note>, having the appearance of fire, and in the evening a glimmer like lightning, which could not be pulled out except with the loss of life of the one pulling it. Therefore, they tied a dog to it, which, in running away, pulled it along and thus uprooted it, and immediately died thereafter. This is to be compared to **Antipas**, who, like an unworthy dog, having pulled out this lightning-clear, shining root through the urging of **Herodias** and for the sake of increasing his own dominion, ran from this fine Palace to Rome, and thereby caused his own punishment and downfall. This root had the power to drive out demons, as **Josephus** describes, just as the sins and evil spirits of men were driven out through the teaching of John. The warm and cold waters that, when mixed together, were pleasant and healthy to drink, also had their significance to the same end.

<margin>Josephus, *The Jewish War*, Book 7, Chapter 25. <note>original: "Ioseph de Bello lib. 7. Cap 25."</note></margin>
Furthermore, this city of **Macherunt** <note>Machaerus</note> defended itself for a long time against the war of the Romans under **Vespasian**, but was finally besieged and attacked with force by **Bassus**, a Commander. For having captured a brave and strong youth named **Eleazar**, he threatened to crucify him, whereby those in the castle, taking pity on him, surrendered. Yet those in the lower city were almost all put to death, at least seventeen hundred remaining dead on the spot. And after that, a gathering of three thousand Jews in the forest of **Jardes**, together with their leader **Judas Giore**, were surrounded and miserably perished and were destroyed: such that the

</margin>
the shame of their Lord, betrayed Herod's army, which was defeated, and he was driven to flight. Oh, how dearly his Nobles had to pay for the blood they had seen floating in the dish like water! For although Herod, ashamed of the death of this pious man, sought a fig leaf <note>a symbolic cover-up or excuse</note>, saying that he had him beheaded for fear of rebellion, nevertheless, it lay in the minds of all people that it was an evil act; and he was therefore punished by the Arabian. Later, the rod struck him even harder: He traveled to Rome (striving like **Aesop's dog** for the shadow of the piece of meat <note>A reference to the fable where a dog loses his actual meat by snapping at its reflection in the water—Herod's greed led to his loss</note>), requesting from the **Emperor Caius** <note>Caligula</note> the portion that **Agrippa**, the brother of Herodias, possessed; but it turned out differently; he who falsely accused the holy man of rebellion was punished as

### Observation.

With great sorrow, they brought the body of their master to Sebaste, formerly called Samaria, so that it would not be further mistreated. Now they took their refuge in Jesus, whom they knew would have compassion for them and, like a Shepherd, would protect them under His wings in His hope. Shortly after this, the twelve Apostles also returned home from their journey, not a little troubled by what they had heard concerning the death of this holy man. The return of the Apostles is described in what follows as such:

And the Apostles gathered together with Jesus and announced all 31 things to Him; both what they had done and what they had taught. And He said to them: "Come aside 32 into a wilderness and rest a little." For there were many coming and going, and they had no time even to eat.

### Observation.

So then the twelve Apostles also returned from the journey upon which they had been sent, informing Him of what they had heard about the death of John the Baptist, and also relating their experiences in teaching and in the performance of miracles. And because they were weary from the journey and dismayed and saddened by the news of the killing of John, Jesus comforted their hearts somewhat. For their refreshment, He went alone with them into a wilderness, to lead these sheep of His onto a green <margin>Psalm 23:1.</margin> meadow there, away from all the noise and distraction of people, just as David says: *The Lord is my Shepherd, I shall not want; He leads me to a green pasture, and guides me to fresh water; He refreshes my soul and leads me on the right path for His name's sake.* <note>The author draws a parallel between Jesus providing rest for his weary disciples and the imagery of the "Good Shepherd" in the Psalms.</note> Meanwhile, Jesus was followed from all sides—

The most notable thing that the **Evangelist John** observes is the time when this occurred; namely, that it was near the upcoming **Passover** <note>original: "Paesschen"; though the word often means Easter in Dutch, the author clarifies it is the "high feast of the Jews," referring to the Passover.</note>, the great high feast of the **Jews**, when they traveled to **Jerusalem** from all lands, which fell on the fifth of April. So this history took place around the month of **March**; at which time those lands are in a beautiful, lovely bloom, being quite as warm, fertile, and summery as the month of **May** is here in **Holland**: the **Sun** being at about the same height in the south, standing more than 50 degrees elevated above the **Horizon**. How the people gathered there is subsequently described by **Mark**.

### Observation.

The **Evangelist** means to say that as soon as they saw **Jesus** sailing away, they made a guess as to where he might be; immediately the report spread everywhere along the coast of the **Galilean Sea**: in the cities situated nearby, such as **Tiberias**, **Bethsaida**, **Taricheas**, **Gamala**, and others like them, from which the people hurried in heaps and arrived bit by bit: for as the **Evangelist** says, there were many who knew him, who brought the news, and ran out so quickly on foot that some arrived before **Jesus** and his followers. Others followed somewhat more slowly on the road in entire troops, forming a great multitude, the loveliness of the season assisting therein. Although **Jesus** knew they came mostly out of curiosity, and others for their physical health, <margin>Ezekiel 34:11</margin> he nevertheless looked upon them with eyes of mercy, like lost and strayed sheep, pouring out not only his teachings for <margin>Luke 9:11</margin> the improvement of their souls, but also healing the sicknesses of the body, as **Luke** explicitly says. The people who were crowded there in the field, like a sizable army, and there was every kind of person: men, women, children, young and old, among whom no one seemed concerned about going home in time, or providing themselves with lodging and food—things that nature cannot do without, unless a special Divine power accompanies them. ## MARK CHAPTER VI.

<margin>Matt. 14 verse 15. Luke 9 verse 12.</margin>
36 And when the day was now nearly gone, his Disciples came to him, saying: It is desolate here, and the day is now gone, let them go from you, so that they may go into the nearby villages and hamlets <note>original: "kasteelen", which in 17th-century Dutch could refer to fortified towns or settlements</note>, and buy
37 food for themselves, for they have nothing to eat. But Jesus answering, said to them: You give them to eat. And they said to him: Shall we then go and buy two hundred pennies <note>The "penning" or denarius was a standard day's wage for a laborer</note> worth of bread, and give them to eat?

---

### Observation.

The day was nearly gone: not yet the twilight of the day, but the Sun has begun to descend low. In those lands <note>referring to the Holy Land</note>, the sunset and sunrise are faster because of the steepness <note>the sun's vertical path relative to the horizon near the equator</note> than in this country, so that people there are much more suddenly overtaken by the evening hour. The Disciples are not so much concerned about the lodging of these people as about the *food*, since, lacking food, they could hardly reach lodging; also it was in the pleasant season, and not unpleasant to remain outside at night, but distressing to suffer the need of hunger. Notice that Jesus, like an attentive Father of the house, hears the counsel of his Disciples in such a weighty matter. They contemplate the desolation of the places and the multitude of the needy people; it is a strange answer to them: *You give them to eat*; thus God sometimes commands impossible things, which are nevertheless doable, indeed very easy to do when He lends His hand to it. He has something special in mind when He lets His word go forth to things that are so improbable and seem unable to happen. They deliberate according to their human

### Observation.

The Evangelist John, leaving aside what the other Evangelists have described / namely the teachings and healings of Jesus / comes immediately to the Miracle / recounting briefly how Jesus, still sitting on the mountain / lifted up his eyes, and saw a great multitude coming to him, whom he (as has been said) / looked upon with great compassion / first feeding them with the food of life <note>referring to spiritual teaching</note> / whereupon follows now this description by John / which expresses the Miracle completely / setting it before our eyes.

Now we come to the second point: Jesus had drawn forth all their ability and heard all their counsel; after which, wishing to prove that his purpose was not to provide a multitude for the satisfaction of the eyes or to satisfy human reason, but that what was at hand could be sufficient to begin with, he said: **Have the people sit down**, for all things had to proceed with order; perhaps a clamor and crying of women and children had begun to rise, which was brought to silence by this sitting down. **In that place there was much grass**: Hereby is indicated the suitability of the location and the season of the year; for in the spring <note>the Dutch "voor-Jaer" literally means the "fore-year" or spring</note> much grass commonly grows, especially in those lands where the winter is short and the spring is warm and fruitful; although this sitting down also teaches us humble bowing under the commands of Christ and the suppression of the "green youth" <note>likely a metaphor for worldly vanities or the untamed impulses of the flesh</note> of the world. He broke the loaves; Jesus unlocks and opens all things, showing the hidden powers. His breaking of the bread was so uncommon that he could be recognized by it, as became clear to the two disciples walking to Emmaus. He gave to the disciples, for these were the distributors of the Divine mysteries; the Apostles also first received the bread of the Spirit in order to share it with all the world. The people ate and were satisfied, and that with great wonder from them all, for they saw more fragments lying fallen than the loaves themselves could have produced. It is believable that these loaves constantly multiplied, both in the hands of the Disciples and also in the people’s hands, mouths, and lips. In the fourth part: when they were all satisfied, Jesus said: **Gather the fragments, so that they do not perish.** This was partly to prove the greatness of the miracle, and partly to teach that one shall not recklessly waste, but use with moderation and hold in honor that which God gives out of such mild love. There were as many baskets of leftovers as there were Apostles, namely twelve, from whose leftover fragments we are still served today in a spiritual manner; and the more diligently one gathers them, the more power one finds in them, such that the whole world must wonder at it. Among these, one also finds fragments of deep-swimming fish, and through this one enters a sea without a bottom; to play in this sea is the delight of wisdom, though it does not serve everyone <note>This likely refers to the "deep" or esoteric spiritual interpretations of the miracle</note>. What greater impression this miracle worked in this crowd is described by John in the following.

### Christ comes to His Disciples, walking on the Sea.

#### *MATTHEW XIV. verse 25. etc.*

> Distrust <note>original: 'Wantrouw'; refers here to Peter’s doubt or loss of confidence.</note> full of terror had stirred Peter’s heart,
> There where Christ by His word had leveled <note>original: 'gevloert'; literally 'floored', suggesting Christ subdued the waves and made the water as firm as a floor to walk upon.</note> the water.

## Observation.

This glorious Miracle, which is described by three Evangelists—namely Matthew, Mark, and John—is not only an excellent proof of the divine power of Christ, but also contains several beautiful lessons within itself. And to observe it usefully, we shall divide it into four main parts, the first of which is: In what manner the disciples first entered the little ship. The second: What they encountered on the sea, and at what time. The third: How Peter behaved himself in this. The fourth: The good outcome, and what fruit this miracle brought about. # JOHN 6. The Fourth Part / Matt. 14. Mark 6. Luke 9.

...[the lake] has been named (which is as much as to say Harp-sea <note>original: "Harp-zee." This refers to the Hebrew name for the Sea of Galilee, *Chinnereth*, which is derived from the word *kinnor*, meaning a harp, due to the lake's shape.</note>). The aforementioned **Herod** <note>Herod Antipas, son of Herod the Great.</note> built this city very magnificently and granted it many privileges. Because there were many graves in that place, it was unlawful for the **Jews** to live there according to the Law <term>ritual uncleanness|According to Jewish Law (Numbers 19:11-16), coming into contact with a grave or a corpse made a person ritually "unclean" and unable to participate in religious life for seven days.</term> because of the uncleanness. Therefore, he lured the inhabitants with many gifts, presenting them with fields, vineyards, houses, and other goods. He even forced some of the nobility to live there, so that this city might be populated in honor of the **Emperor**. He also built a beautiful palace there, which—because the roof was gilded and it was further decorated with much sculpture of painted animals—was later burned in a riot at the start of the Jewish War. For a long time, it was one of the capital cities of the land of Galilee—namely, from the time of the aforementioned Herod until the time of **Felix**, the Governor of Judea. During that time, the Chancellery and the Royal Table were also located there.

But at that time, King **Agrippa** (the second of that name, who had received this city as a gift from the Emperor **Nero**) took all of this away and placed the city under **Sepphoris**, which was the largest city in all of Galilee. This served as a cause for a riot by one **Justus**, son of Pistus, to incite the city against the aforementioned Agrippa and the **Romans**; however, it was stilled by **Josephus**, who was at that time made the commander in Galilee. Many notable strongholds lay around and near Tiberias, such as **Tarichaeae**, **Gamala**, **Gischala**, **Jotapata**, and others. A certain **John**, a rebellious and cunning man who resided within Gischala, caused Josephus no small amount of trouble; for he made the citizens of Tiberias defect from him and brought Josephus’s person into great peril, such that Josephus barely escaped; but this was later stilled. 

After that, Josephus came into no less peril and danger to his life through one **Jesus**, son of Sapphias, who had stirred up the citizens of Tiberias against him; but he also escaped this with great cleverness. Later, when the city had again completely defected from him through a man named **Clitus** who acted as the master there, Josephus used a great ingenuity against them. He had the gates of Tarichaeae (where he was at that time) closed, and took from there, as well as from other places on the Galilean sea, two hundred and thirty ships—empty, without any people except for the sailors—save for his own ship, on which he took seven guards. When all the citizens suspected that those ships were full of people, and that their city would be overtaken in haste, they begged for mercy and delivered their leaders into the hands of Josephus. The Fourth Part / JOHN 6. Matt. 14. Mark 6. Luke 9.
<meta>catchword: JOHN:</meta>

# Observation.

<margin>Num. 11:4 <note>original: "Num. 11. 4." This refers to the Old Testament account of the Israelites craving meat in the desert.</note></margin>
They inquire—to satisfy their own wonder—at what time the Lord arrived there. Jesus, in His usual manner, aiming for an instruction toward the salvation of mankind, gives an answer that served to sharpen their attention and lead them to examine themselves: namely, that their zeal did not arise for the sake of the signs, which demonstrated His Divine power; but from the taste of the loaves to satisfy their earthly desire, just as their Fathers did in the past. He exhorted them that this was not the way to come to true knowledge; that they must indeed strive for food, as it is in itself a precious and glorious thing; but not for such food that perishes along with the body. Rather, they should seek that which feeds and sustains the soul; for the soul, being created for eternal life, remains, and thus such labor is repaid a thousand times over by the great treasure acquired through it. And where they shall find this food, He also tells them: namely, in Him, the Son of Man, who has been confirmed and sealed by God through miracles. Upon this, they present themselves as teachable, saying: *What shall we do, that we may work the works of God?* It is a good question: but at the pointing out of this path, they draw back. *God's work is, believing in him whom he has sent.*

<margin>John 6:14, Isaiah 55:8</margin>
There they stand: previously they cried out that He was the true Prophet and wanted to make Him King; now they ask what sign He performs to prove such things? Thus the human understanding wanders against itself without stability. Therefore, with great reason, faith may well be called a work of God and not of man: for it always looks upon things that do not seem true according to natural wit. If it were so easily grasped by man, how quickly would these Jews—who had already acknowledged Jesus as a Prophet—have joined Him? But there was something else to do: there was the forsaking and surrendering of one's own understanding, wisdom, and will, and the complete bowing of these under the wisdom of God; and that is difficult to do, unless God works alongside it through His almighty power. They boast of the signs shown by Moses, of the Heavenly bread: from this, Jesus took the opportunity to speak of the true and upright Heavenly bread, of which the first was a figure <note>A "figure" is a historical event or object—like the manna in the desert—that serves as a symbolic foreshadowing of a spiritual reality to come.</note>: saying that this alone came down from God, giving such nourishment through which the consumer obtains eternal life. Yet their senses, being full of earthly thoughts, understand Jesus's words as referring to the distributed bread recently enjoyed near Bethsaida in the Wilderness. Therefore, Isaiah may rightly say: *that the thoughts of men are as far removed from the thoughts of God as the Heaven is from the Earth.* <note>original: "Esai 55. 8"</note> Now Jesus begins to speak somewhat more clearly of this Heavenly bread, who and where it is, and how they should seek it in the right way.

# JOHN CHAPTER VI.

**35** Jesus said to them: I am that bread of life: whoever comes to me, shall not hunger, and whoever believes in me, shall never thirst.
**36** But I have told you, that you have also seen me, and you do not believe
**37** me. All that the Father gives me shall come to me, and whoever comes to me, I shall not reject.

**39** me. This is the will of the Father who sent me, that I should lose nothing of all that he has

## Observation

He does not only make it known that he is the bread of life, but also in what manner he can be enjoyed, namely: through faith. For through faith one draws the powers of God into oneself, just <margin>Mark 5:30.</margin> as one draws in the power of food through eating, chewing, and swallowing; and likewise the power of drink by distributing it through all the limbs. Now he makes known that he is a food of complete satisfaction, such that nothing more is wished for or desired where God is with all his perfect attributes, thus fulfilling the <margin>Matt. 5:6.</margin> hunger and thirst of the soul. Thus Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), a central figure in Western Christianity whose writings on grace and faith were highly valued by Dutch Reformed and Catholic scholars alike.</note> says quite rightly: he is <margin>Psalm 36:8.</margin> <margin>Song of Solomon 5:11.</margin> altogether greedy who does not let himself be satisfied with God. 2. He also gives to understand that such hungry souls, who cannot be satisfied with any other thing, are sent and given to him by God the Father. And that such shall undoubtedly come to him, without there being anything that would prevent it, or lead them onto a wrong path: for the matters of God stand firm and certain. 3. Declaring further such to be his Father’s will, and the cause of his mission: indeed, that he shall also not lose a single one of all that God has given him. And looking toward the end, and the final result, he says that he shall raise such in the last day <note>A reference to the Day of Judgment and the resurrection of the faithful at the end of time.</note>: through which everything shall then be made good, and concluded, which here seemed somewhat to waver, or to be unsteady or uncertain. limbs. So that one can recognize a true disciple of Christ <note>original: "Christi"</note> by this:

is also not given to everyone to eat, but it is a special 
grace that belongs only to the overcomers, as it is written:

than human ingenuity can comprehend. Over the meaning of these words 
have not only these Jews, but also the so-called Christians, 
conducted endless disputes; yet it is best (following the counsel of Christ) not 
to murmur about this, but humbly [wait] upon the teaching of God in the soul...

And all those who <margin>58</margin> touched him were made whole.

### Observation.

<margin>Mark 5:25</margin>
From this it appears that Jesus, departing from Capernaum, walked through many places, as he often did when traveling up to Jerusalem; furthermore, great miracles are described here, namely that they were made whole simply by touching the hem <note>original: "Zooms"; referring to the ritual fringes or tassels on the corners of a Jewish garment</note> of his garment. A remarkable example of this is described in another place, concerning the woman who had suffered from a flow of blood <note>original: "bloedtganck"; a chronic hemorrhage</note> for twelve years, who, approaching through her faith and touching his hem, drew the power of Jesus to herself, just as happened here with this multitude. These are instructive examples to stir us toward the grace of Christ through the Spirit, so that we may obtain through it the true healing of our souls; for it is certain that these medicinal powers during his bodily travels were prototypes of the spiritual healings <margin>Heb. 5:3</margin> that he would perform, having ascended in his power and glory, where he is established as a throne of grace <note>original: "stoel der genaden"; the Mercy Seat, referring to Christ's role as intercessor</note>, to comfort and provide help...

### The Fifth Chapter.

->Jesus, returning from the Passover feast, departs for Galilee; the Pharisees following him, rebuke him over the washing of hands, which he refutes.<-

verse
### JOHN, CHAPTER VII.

<margin>1</margin>
After these things Jesus walked in Galilee, for he would not walk in Judea, because the Jews sought to kill him.

### Observation.

After these things Jesus walked in Galilee; This proves that he had previously departed from Galilee, namely: At the Passover in Jerusalem, which was located in Judea. Now, he did not wish to remain or dwell in that land, and returned to Galilee; the Evangelist relates the reason, namely: Because the Jews sought to kill him, whereby they made themselves unworthy of his presence and the preaching of the Gospel. Jesus has not only proven by his example <margin>Matt. 7:6</margin> that one must not cast pearls before swine <note>A reference to the teaching that holy things should not be given to those who will only mistreat them</note>, but also that one ought to yield to angry men, as far as time and opportunity allow. Thus, Jesus currently withdraws from such places where they seek to kill him, and chooses rather to dwell in "heathen" Galilee with freedom, than in the blinded Judea where they lay snares for him. Now that Jesus has departed, the Pharisees and some of the Scribes from Jerusalem have meanwhile followed him, so that they might spy on him everywhere, and accuse him wherever they could find cause, as appears below from the other Evangelists.

### Explanation.

The healing of this deaf man seems to proceed with great difficulty, which we must not attribute to any lessening of Christ’s power, but to the unbelief of the people, who had already prescribed to Him the method of how He should do it. However, it is especially important to note what lessons this example gives us. There is no greater defect than deafness: for, 1. When a person is inwardly deaf, such that he cannot hear the voice of God, and additionally mute, so that he can speak no divine words for edification, then he is difficult to help. 2. He must first be led away from the people <note>original: "uyt den volcke," meaning out of the crowd or worldly society.</note> to unlearn all foreign noise: for through many idle rumors one becomes deaf, and the internal hearing is blocked, like a filled-in fountain. 3. The finger of Jesus' power <term>mogentheydt</term> <note>a term implying sovereign might or divine authority</note> must touch his ear and tongue, otherwise this leading away would not help. 4. The piercing voice that can even awaken the dead must open his ear, as it is written: *He opens my ear.* Hearing must come from Him who planted the ear; all other remedies are in vain without His help. 5. The sighing of Christ must be heard—

Then one awaits God’s praise rightly and brings forth fruit in patience; for as the ancients taught: <margin>James 1:19.</margin> the chatter <note>original: "gepleyt," referring here to excessive or contentious speech</note> of the tongue diminishes attention and breaks devotion; also James teaches us: that we shall be quick to hear, but slow to speak. ¶ Finally, note what a praiseworthy thing it is, that the deaf man—who previously could not be awakened <margin>Isaiah 42:19</margin> even by making much noise, and of whom the Lord complained: *Who is as deaf as my servant?*—now hears the most subtle voice of the Gospel, and that the stammering tongue now speaks learned and perfect words to spread the praise of God, without any further hesitation being noticed.

### Of the Decapolis, or the borders of the ten cities.

<margin>Bünting in his Itinerary. Josephus, The Jewish War, Book 4, Chapter 2. Joshua 12. Judges 11:39. 2 Kings 12:34. Numbers 22:27.</margin> These ten cities were situated (according to the opinion of Henricus Bunting <note>Heinrich Bünting (1545–1606) was a German pastor and cartographer famous for his "Itinerarium Sacrae Scripturae," which mapped the travels of biblical figures.</note>) in the land of Gilead across the Jordan: such as, firstly, Chorazin, which was described by us previously; Gamala, a strong city where Vespasianus <note>The Roman Emperor Vespasian, during the Siege of Gamala in 67 AD.</note> was wounded in his arm; Julia, built by King Herod in honor of the Empress <note>Livia, the wife of Augustus.</note>; Gadara, also previously described; Ashtaroth, where King Og of Bashan held his court; Jabesh <note>Jabesh-Gilead</note>, where Saul’s bones were buried; Mizpah, where the children of Israel often used to have their gathering and where Jephthah sacrificed his daughter; Ramoth, where King Ahab was shot through; Edrei, where Og the King of Bashan was defeated and perished; and Abel-Keramim <note>The "Plain of the Vineyards."</note> where Balaam’s donkey spoke. Others feel that these cities were very inconveniently located for passing from the borders of Tyre and Sidon toward the Sea of Galilee, and that they must therefore have been others; but because the Evangelists do not name them, nothing certain can be established. We only have this to learn from it: how Jesus, as a Savior <note>original: "Salighmaker," literally "One who makes holy/blessed."</note> of mankind, spared Himself no effort or labor to wander through these lands as a pilgrim, sharing with them the grace of the Gospel. Everywhere He did good deeds <margin>Zechariah 13:1</margin> where they came to approach Him through faith, like the aforementioned deaf man and many others who will be described hereafter; so that He was the true open fountain for the house of Israel, to heal all defects of the body and the soul.

### The Seventh Chapter.

Jesus, sitting on a mountain, is followed by a great multitude, whose infirmities he heals, preaches the Gospel, and feeds four thousand men. Description of the city of Magdala.

### MATTHEW CHAPTER XV.

<margin>verses 29, 30</margin> And Jesus, departing from there, came near the Sea of Galilee, and climbed up a mountain, and sat down there. And many people came to him, bringing with them the lame, blind, deaf, and mute, and many others, and they laid them at Jesus' feet; and he healed them.
<margin>31</margin> So that the multitudes marveled when they saw the mute speak, the lame walk, and the blind see: and they praised the God of Israel.

### Observation.

The most merciful Lord, whose eyes remain constantly open to help the miseries of mankind, coming out of Decapolis <note>A region of ten cities east of the Jordan River</note>, places himself by the sea upon a high mountain; there he might behold both sea and land, seeing his poor creatures wandering upon the earth. He saw the little fishermen busy with their nets, the merchant ships bringing their cargoes back and forth, and saw towers and buildings shining out on the opposite side, while high mountains covered with green trees appeared very blue in the distance. On the land side, he saw the countryman busy with the plow, wild and tame animals skipping and jumping in the field, and thus viewed the bustle of the world. He observed the fertile Galilean land with sighs, knowing through his Divine providence how that flourishing state would very soon, in a few short years, change into a sorrowful war <note>A reference to the First Jewish-Roman War (66–73 AD), which resulted in the destruction of many Galilean towns and eventually Jerusalem.</note>. But he had not sat here for long before a great multitude began to approach, bringing with them the lame, blind, deaf, mute, and similar sick folk, proving by all their manners that they had need of his help. What shall he do? Shall he leave them uncomforted? His mercy cannot allow that. If he is to help them, he must set aside his solitude and sweet silence; this is a heavy burden, yet love and compassion for the people overcame him. He then gave himself to these miserable ones; their crying and

works. **Jesus** had compassion for both soul and body, and He was a **Master** of helping: "I pity the people"—where there is power, nothing more is needed than compassion, and both were present in **Jesus**. There are many who are well able to feed the hungry, but they lack compassion. 1. He takes into consideration their great zeal to hear the word of **God**; He reflects on the impending danger of them fainting on the way; He considers how far they had to travel, thereby proving that the company of **Jesus** was dearer and more pleasant to them than their house, yard, wife, child, or anything they had left behind. 2. The **Disciples** are at a loss, having forgotten the glorious **Miracle** that occurred so recently. See how little man learns from previous examples! Thus was **Israel** in the Wilderness; doubting, they said: <margin>Psalm 78:19</margin> "Yes, **God** has indeed given water from the stone, but how can He give bread and provide meat for His people?" **Lord**, keep such unbelieving thoughts far from us. 3. **Jesus** is satisfied with the little they have; He is not anxious for more bread; He makes the people sit down; He trusts in the power of **God**. He **takes** the seven loaves that were at hand, as well as the few small fish, showing gratitude for them. **Many** there are who complain and groan out of fear of the future, instead of praising **God** for the present. Thanksgiving to the Creator earns a blessing; **God** helps where help is needed; where there is lack, His powers are made known. He broke them; through His breaking, He opens the taste of all things. <margin>Psalm 34:9</margin> **Taste** and see how friendly the **Lord** is, He who breaks and distributes His **Divine** word for us. 4. It was a humble sight when the **Disciples** arrived with that little broken bread, but the outcome taught that a wondrous power of several <margin>Wisdom 16:20; Numbers 11:8; Matthew 6:33</margin> loads was hidden within it. **Four thousand** ate and were satisfied—not only satisfied, but found an exceeding sweetness in it, like **Israel** with the **Manna**. It was cast to them without their labor; those who first seek the kingdom of **God** become aware of His miraculous hand. 5. **Here** there was no limited power; even if there had been many more thousands, all would have had enough, for the leftovers were greater than the beginning. Seven loaves cannot fill seven baskets, except through **God's** increasing power. **These** seven baskets are a representation of the seven writers of the New **Testament** <note>The "seven writers" likely refers to the traditional grouping of New Testament authors: Matthew, Mark, Luke, John, Paul, Peter, and the authors of the General Epistles (James/Jude).</note>, with a small fish running among them; these have left us so many fragments that we need no more. Indeed, when one begins to break even one of those, it expands so wide that entire armies can be fed by it. **O** wondrous blessing of **God**! Both in physical and spiritual things, how great is His fullness in everything.

When these people had been dismissed, **Jesus** departed across the sea to the regions of **Dalmanutha**, otherwise called **Magdala** by **Matthew**. What sweet conversations and **Divine** reflections the **Disciples** had among themselves regarding the miracles of their **Master** is more for us to imagine than to know for certain.

The Fourth Part /
MATTHEW 16. MARK 9. LUKE 9. JOHN 7.

### Description of the city of Magdala.

<margin>
Johann Alsted in *Chronology* 11 <note>Johann Heinrich Alsted (1588–1638) was a famous German Protestant theologian and encyclopedist.</note>
</margin>
Magdala is a small town situated on the Sea of Galilee, on this side of the Jordan, belonging to the tribe of Issachar, thirteen miles north of Jerusalem. The region surrounding this place was called Dalmanutha; from this arises the difference between Matthew and Mark, where one says Jesus came to the borders of Magdala and the other says He came to Dalmanutha—and yet it is both the same place. For this reason, it is sometimes necessary to have some knowledge of the geography of those lands and other matters of that time if one is to understand the Evangelists <note>Evangelists: the authors of the four Gospels (Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John).</note> correctly and recognize that they are not in disagreement regarding the history but are all of one mind; for conflicting-seeming phrases often arise from different names, as this example teaches. To the west and north of this place was a beautiful, fertile land and green meadows, as the land of Galilee generally is. Jesus often crossed the bay of the sea between this city and Capernaum, as also happened immediately after this. Some believe that Mary Magdalene was born in this city and received her name from it, and that one could still show the house where she lived today. Furthermore, there are some who believe that around this time when Jesus was in Magdala, a Pentecost feast <note>Pentecost: also known as the Feast of Weeks, one of the three major Jewish pilgrimage festivals.</note> occurred, after which feast the Pharisees and Sadducees <note>The Pharisees and Sadducees were the two primary, and often rival, religious and political parties in Jewish society at the time.</note> prepared themselves anew against Jesus, as follows below.

### Observation.

Although these two sects [the Pharisees and Sadducees] were very much at odds with one another, nonetheless they agreed here in opposing Jesus Christ. They were like two evil plants that commonly create a storm through their conjunction <note>The author uses the term "conjunction"—likely borrowed from astrology or physics—to describe how the alliance of two opposing forces creates a greater disturbance.</note>; the Pharisees had not been able to achieve anything in the previous investigation, so now they took the Sadducees to their aid. The Sadducees did not allow themselves to be bound by the same traditions, <margin>Acts 23:8</margin> since they believed in neither angel nor spirit, nor in any future life. Hearing more and more of the miracles of Christ and that he had recently fed so many thousand people, they thought to attack him on another footing—not that they wished to be taught, but to do battle. 1. So they came by common counsel, speaking in this manner: "We hear indeed of some wonders that you do, whether of healing the crippled, blind, lepers, mute, and deaf, and also that you have miraculously fed some thousand people, but these are all earthly things that could be explained otherwise, which could be done through some hidden powers of herbs or stones, or communion with spirits and the like. <note>The religious leaders are accusing Jesus of using natural magic (herbs and stones) or sorcery (spirits) rather than divine power.</note> But if you are the Son of God, then show us a sign from Heaven, whether you make the sun stand still or go backward, as happened in olden times, or something similar. Otherwise, if you do not show such a sign, we do not believe you."

2. This proposition seemed to have some reason, but was in fact nothing other than a way of tempting <note>original: "temteeren", from the Latin *tentare*, meaning to test or put God to the proof.</note>; just as the Israelites <margin>Psalm 78:41</margin> did to Moses in times past, requesting now this, now that, and never being <margin>Psalm 95:9</margin> satisfied with what God showed them, about which the Psalmist complains:

> Where your fathers tempted me, they proved me, and saw my works for forty years long.

In the same manner was also the voice of the Devil: <margin>Matthew 4:6</margin>

> If you are the Son of God, then cast yourself down?

For to tempt is to request something without necessity, to refuse to believe what has already been shown, and to constantly demand that the curious senses be satisfied. 3. <margin>Mark 8:12</margin> The Lord Jesus, knowing their willful nature, gave a deep sigh (as Mark testifies), saying:

> Why does this generation seek a sign?

As if he wanted to say that they do not lack for signs; yet nevertheless, to serve them somewhat in their request, he pointed them to a common sign of heaven, how they could judge from the red evening the following fair weather; and from the red mor-

### Observation.

On the other side, that is the side of Bethsaida, as appears from what follows. Furthermore, these things are to be noted here. 1. The teaching of Christ: this is in a figurative way of speaking / as he was often accustomed / to make great things known under hidden words: From this it follows that without his explanation / his teachings could not be well understood; which still holds true today. Many people think they can well understand the mind of Christ / yet they judge according to their own understanding: just as these Disciples also did. He calls the false teachings a <term>leaven</term> <note>original: "fuyrdeegh," referring to sourdough or fermenting dough</note>, thereby expressing their destructiveness / and puffed-up pride; just as leaven is rising / and drives out all sweetness. 

<margin>Mark 8:15.</margin> 
In Mark he also mentions / the leaven of Herod: for some flatterers and earthly-minded people wanted to present this Tyrant as the promised Messiah / because much external power had fallen to him: And they pushed this opinion strongly / which is why they were called Herodians among the people; being a specific sect alongside the Pharisees and Sadducees. 2. The wrong interpretation of the Disciples. 

<margin>Mark 8:14.</margin> 
Mark says: They had only one loaf in the ship: a small supply / the rest they had forgotten through distraction / through contemplation / their senses being full of the teachings of their master. It is said of Bernard <note>Saint Bernard of Clairvaux (1090–1153), a medieval mystic known for being so absorbed in prayer that he was oblivious to his physical surroundings.</note> that he once drank oil instead of water; being so absorbed in thought that he did not know it: concern came upon them / they took the words of Jesus as a rebuke in that regard. Thus are the thoughts of every man according to his understanding and grasp. From Mark it appears / that they tossed many thoughts around / regarding the meaning of these words: at last they thought: "that must be it, because we have no bread." Such concern easily befalls a man / when he sees a small supply. 3. The rebuke of their master: this had all the more foundation...

### Observation.

<margin>Rufinus, Book 11, Chapter 7. Tripartite History, Book 8, Chapter 8.</margin>
There were no places where this healer came / where they were not partakers of his kindness; he looked not upon the ungratefulness of this city / but upon the need of the infirm people. They came then and brought this blind man, yet not with a slow faith / and therefore the healing also proceeded slowly. This blind man was an image of the entire citizenry / who had no eyes to recognize the day of their Salvation. They forgot themselves and brought him forward to be helped: *Didymus* <note>Likely referring to Didymus the Blind, a 4th-century Alexandrian theologian who lost his sight at age four but became a renowned scholar.</note> valued the inner sight much higher and more precious than the outer sight / but these thought otherwise / yet had no knowledge of the true light of Heaven. 1. He led him out from among the people; the noise of the crowd is harmful for learning to know *Christ* / one must withdraw one's heart from all things / for the creatures <note>In this context, "creatures" refers to all created, worldly things as opposed to the Creator.</note> are like scales that cover the eyes.

<margin>Appian of Alexandria, Book 10, Chapter 6.</margin>
One can become blind through evil habit / just as *Geta* <note>Geta was a Roman who, during the proscriptions of the Triumvirate, disguised himself by wearing a patch over one eye; when he eventually removed it, the eye had lost its function from disuse.</note>, being one of the proscribed / and wishing to make himself unknown to escape the danger of his life / stuck a piece of parchment over one eye / and when it was later removed, that same eye had become entirely blind: so many cover their sight / not thinking that evil habit blinds the soul; he who is so disposed, let him come to *Jesus*. 2. He spat in his eyes, making him a partaker of his power: the spit of *Jesus* is better than any medicine.
<margin>Isaiah 41:19. Judges 9:8. Matthew 7:16.</margin>
Through this he saw men somewhat like trees; it is a great gift to distinguish trees well / whether they be exalted Cedars, sharp thorn-bushes, willows, and similar barren wood: or whether they be olives, figs, and fruit-bearing trees. As trees one sees people by their outer bark / when the sight is still dark / the branches cause a great shadow / and daze the vision.

<margin>Psalm 36:9</margin>
3. Afterward he laid his hands upon him: Oh blessed touch of *Christ*! without which no one comes to a right sight. After that, he saw all things clearly; even his healer himself. Thus one climbs by degrees and steps: for long the eyes of understanding remain clouded / for which one must pray / that God may please, through the helping hand of his Spirit, to so enlighten us / that we may say with Holy *David*: With you is the living fountain; and in your light we see the light.

<margin>John 9:42.</margin>
4. *Jesus* commanded him / to go into his house, and to keep still. It is good that a person enters into himself / and does not wander so far with his sight / that he receives a worse blindness through dust and filth than he had before. The seeing Pharisees were more incurable / than the man born blind / because they wandered outside themselves / and thereby imagined that they saw: for who is further from the light / than he who does not feel his blindness, which is beyond measure great?

# Of the life of Jesus Christ.

**MATTHEW 16. MARK 8. LUKE 9. JOHN 7.**

<margin>Mark 8:32. Gen. 3:4. 2 Sam. 16:9. Job 2:9. Acts 20:13. Psalm 62:10.</margin>
...various reasons: 1. So that they, being warned, would not be too greatly terrified when the time of Christ's suffering would begin to approach. 2. So that they would know that Jesus would not undergo this suffering through coercion or anyone’s deceit, but out of his own free will and the premeditated counsel of God. 3. So that they would know everything beforehand—not only his suffering and death, but also the good outcome through his resurrection—and that they might meanwhile comfort themselves with this. 4. But especially this served to test Peter, who had now climbed to a high degree <note>referring to his recent confession of Christ’s divinity</note>, and to see what was hidden in his heart: he conducted himself presumptuously <note>original: "meester-lick," meaning in a master-like or authoritative manner</note>: pulling his Lord aside, making it known that such propositions did not please him well. He rebuked him, as if he wanted to say: "What has come over you? Now that you know all this beforehand, will you then of your own accord walk into the teeth of the wolf? Will you be so hard on yourself as to give those willful people the means to do evil? Then you are the cause of your own death: for he who sees the murderer from afar, and yet will not shun the path where he is, he brings himself to destruction <note>original: "om den hals," literally "around the neck," an idiom for being killed or ruined</note>. It would also grieve my heart to see you so innocently put to death by so many cruel executioners; the love I bear for you forces me to warn you: You have mercifully helped so many people; be also merciful to yourself, and never allow such things to happen to you." 5. This was indeed a good intention in Peter, but it came through the deceit of the Devil, who under the appearance of compassion had likewise deceived Eve; who incited Abishai to keep Shimei away from David; and Job's wife to stir him up against God. And because in such circumstances nothing is more moving than the voice of love and dear friends—just as Paul also had found when he was to travel up to Jerusalem—so Jesus met Peter with a short answer and spoke earnestly: "Get behind me, Satan, for you are a hindrance to me." There Peter stood ashamed before him and looked down; alas, what is it with man? Well may David say: *Great men fail as well* <note>original: "Groote lieden faelgeren oock"</note>. This seemed a man to build a church upon, and when it all comes down to it, he is of himself no more than another; all that he had was shared with him out of the deep mercy of God. Furthermore, Jesus taught not only Peter, but also all his other present Disciples, by what path he was to be followed.

<header>The Fourth Part / John 7</header>

### MATTHEW 16. MARK 8. LUKE 9.

...loses his life for my sake, he shall find it. For what does it profit a man, even if he were to win the whole world, if he suffers the loss of his own soul? Or what can a man give, with which he may redeem his soul again? For it shall come to pass that the Son of Man shall come in the glory of his Father with his angels, and then he shall reward every man according to his works. Truly I say to you: There are some standing here who shall not taste of death before they see the Son of Man coming in his Kingdom.

### Observation.

This goes entirely against common human understanding: for everyone strives after how he might preserve himself, make himself great, and rescue himself from all crosses and suffering. It also sounded strange in the ears of the disciples—who had set their minds on becoming great masters in this world and reigning with Christ—that they now, together with him, had to enter the path of suffering as the only entrance into life. To deny oneself is to not know or regard oneself, as if one were nothing; so did **Jesus**, who lived not according to his own will, but according to his Father’s will. He brings forth two weighty reasons for this. 1. That even the winning of the whole world is of no use when one neglects one's soul in any part; likewise one knows that neither **Alexander the Great** <note>original: "Alexander Magnus"</note>, nor **Julius Caesar**, nor **Pompey** <note>original: "Pompejus"</note>, nor anyone else had any advantage from their great
<margin>Psalm 49:11. Luke 12:20.</margin>
dominion when they lay gasping their last breath <note>original: "ziel-tooghden," referring to the final struggle for breath at the moment of death</note> and had to die as miserable men; it is then great foolishness to choose that weak and powerless refuge, and to set aside God, who is a firm fortress. 2. That a day shall come in which every person must appear before the Judgment Seat to receive reward according to his works; even if he wished to deceive himself for a time, to stifle the accusations of his conscience, and to hoodwink his soul, he cannot ultimately escape that strict Judge. Finally, **Jesus** wished to provide a proof of that coming glory, and that in a very short time, just as he did for three of his prominent Apostles, as shall follow hereafter <note>referring to the Transfiguration</note>.

### Description of the city of Caesarea Philippi.

**C**aesarea Philippi takes its name from Philip the Tetrarch <note>original: "Vier-Vorst," a literal translation of the Greek "tetrarch," meaning ruler of a fourth part</note> of Trachonitis, a son of Herod the Great, and a brother of Herod Antipas, who had stolen <note>original: "ontboert," meaning to take away or deprive</note> his wife Herodias from him:

It links the physical landscape of the Jordan's source to the spiritual "source" of Christian belief.</meta>

<header>Of the Life of Jesus Christ.</header>

->MATTHEW 16. MARK 8. LUKE 9.<- <insert>John 7.</insert>

For this Tetrarch <note>Referring to Philip the Tetrarch, son of Herod the Great, who ruled the northern regions.</note> has magnificently built up *Paneas* and named the same *Caesarea* after the name of the Emperor *Tiberius*, from which it held these two names: namely, *Caesarea* after the Emperor, and *Philippi* after the founder *Philip*. Its location was near the source of the *Jordan*, twelve miles <note>The original text specifies 12 miles, though the actual distance from Jerusalem is significantly further; the author may be using a different unit of measure or following an older source.</note> from *Jerusalem* toward the North, not far from Mount *Lebanon*.

<margin>Joshua 19:47.</margin>
It is held that this is the same place which was previously named *Leshem*, after the precious stone *Ligure* <note>original: "Ligurius," a gemstone mentioned in Exodus as part of the High Priest's breastplate</note> which was also set in the breastplate of *Aaron*.

<margin>Judges 18:14</margin>
In the Book of Judges the same city is named *Laish*; and having been taken by the children of *Dan*, they named the same *Dan* after their father's name; and as this city was situated at the furthest borders of the Jewish land in the North, and *Beersheba* in the South,

<margin>Judges 20:1.</margin>
so all of *Israel* was characterized by this, that they gathered from *Dan* to *Beersheba*, namely, from one extreme to the other. The district of *Paneas* in which this city was situated was first subject to the rule of *Zenodorus*, and when after his death this was given to *Herod*,

<margin>Josephus, The Jewish War, Book 1, Chapter 16.</margin>
he built there a magnificent temple of white marble in honor of the Emperor *Augustus*, which was a striking building. There lies a high steep mountain, which on one side, by reason of the deep valley, forms a dark cave where the water, which runs down from the high stones, being driven together, becomes a great and unfathomable water; and outside of this cave well up some flowing springs, originating from the water of *Phiale*,

<margin>The Jewish War, Book 3, Chapter 35.</margin>
which always runs around like a wheel; and it was found by the aforementioned Tetrarch *Philip* that this is the beginning and the source of the famous River *Jordan*, which, flowing through the Galilean sea, finally pours itself into the sea *Asphaltites* <note>The Dead Sea</note> or Dead Sea, also named the *Pitch Sea*, because of the wondrous bitumen <note>original: "lijm," literally glue or lime, referring to the asphalt/bitumen found there</note> that it casts out. Thus the *Jordan* on the East side is the border of the Jewish land, so often mentioned in the Holy Scripture. So then, near the source of these rivers was revealed the source of the glorious confessions, which like a fast-flowing water has spread itself over all the world, namely:

<margin>Matthew 16:16.</margin>
That *Jesus* is *Christ*, the Son of the living God; and it is also like an unfathomable fountain, clear and bright in the fruitful lands, but in the Dead Sea of the world, which is corrupted by the *Sodomitic* ashes, there it is without any working power.

<margin>Josephus, Antiquities, Book 20, Chapter 8.</margin>
Now this city *Caesarea Philippi* was later rebuilt by King *Agrippa* and named *Neronia* after the Emperor *Nero*; yet now in our times it is named *Belianus*, as *Raphael Volaterranus* <note>A 15th-century Italian humanist and scholar</note> describes.

### Observation.

<margin>Luke 9:28.</margin>
Luke, who also describes this history, says that it was eight days after the preceding events, which one must reconcile in this way: there were six days between the first and the eighth day on which this glorious manifestation occurred; thus Luke counts the first and last day among them, but Matthew and Mark count the six days in between.
