# Of the Life of Jesus Christ.

*MATTHEW 17. MARK 9. LUKE 9. John 7.*

1. Jesus had (according to *Luke’s* description) gone up this mountain to pray, when this transformation came upon him; <note>The Transfiguration is often depicted as occurring during a moment of intense communion with God.</note> which teaches us that a person is transfigured <note>original: "verklaert," meaning clarified, enlightened, or glorified.</note> when he approaches God through devout prayer; just as happened to *Moses*, <margin>*Exodus 34:33*</margin> who, having spoken with God on Mount *Sinai*, came down with a clear and shining countenance; as *James* very rightly says: <margin>*James 4:8*</margin> Draw near to God, and He will draw near to you.

2. He chooses three from among his Apostles—namely *Peter, James*, and *John*—as special friends, to let them see this glory of His; thereby indicating that He, in His Divine being, is free to distribute His grace to whomever He pleases; the rest He had left below at the foot of the mountain, for He did not wish to reveal this vision to them.

3. His face became shining like the Sun, and His garments white as snow, prefiguring the glorification of all believers in eternal joy; just as He had said: that the righteous shall shine like the Sun in their <margin>*Matthew 13:43*</margin> Father’s kingdom; with which *Daniel* also agrees, <margin>*Daniel 12:3*</margin> <note>The source text cites Daniel 13:13, but this refers to Daniel 12:3, which describes the wise shining like the brightness of the heavens.</note> who attributes this shining to the Teachers. Since everyone now desires to enjoy glory and beauty, take this as a mirror for yourself, and consider what pearls, gold, silver, or jewels could be compared to this; and whether *Solomon’s* glory, which is less than the beauty <margin>*Matthew 6:28*</margin> of the lilies, is in any way relevant here. The Roman conquerors who triumphed in golden chariots are but dung and filth compared to this exceeding beauty.

4. Two men come to Him as witnesses of His Majesty—namely *Moses* and *Elijah*—just as a King is honored by the highest of his nobility; one came on behalf of the Law of God, the other on behalf of the Prophets; these were adorned with the same ornament as their Prince, namely with Heavenly clarity. And behold, in the midst of this glory, they speak of the cross and suffering; one had experienced it under *Pharaoh*, the other under *Ahab*, <margin>*Luke 9:31*</margin> and now their Lord would undertake the same struggle and fulfill the prophecies that they, along with others, had testified to.

5. This was a great assurance in the hearts of the three Apostles; yet it was a strange sight that this joy was tempered by pressure, <note>original: "druck," referring to the heavy spiritual weight or distress felt by the disciples.</note> whereby their hearts being burdened, sleep overcame them, as they saw no way through such a mystery.

6. Having woken and risen as if into a new joy, *Peter* requested to build three Tabernacles there: See here an image of Heavenly glory; they recognize *Moses* and *Elijah* whom they had never seen. They are minded to stay there eternally and never again return to their earthly dwelling. It did not grieve them to erect a Tabernacle for each one: for love is of such a nature that it <margin>*1 Corinthians 15:8*</margin> spares no labor to keep together everything it can embrace. Yet it was all childishness, for the suffering had to be fulfilled first; so eager is man to possess Heavenly joy without suffering, yet he does not understand the entrance to it.

7. A bright cloud surrounds them: They hear a voice: This is my beloved Son in whom

### Reflection.

<margin>
2 Pet. 1:17.
John 1:14
</margin>

MATTHEW 17. MARK 9. LUKE 9. JOHN 7.
The power of Christ in the driving out of the Devil. The people ran from all sides to see what would happen; the Scribes stood like <margin>1 Samuel 19:10</margin> Saul with the spear in his hand, ready to throw it at this David. The Harp <note>The author uses a musical metaphor: Jesus’s voice is compared to the harp played by David to soothe the troubled King Saul, while the Scribes represent the hostile Saul.</note> began to play and gave a swift sound: "I command you, you dumb and deaf Spirit <note>original: "stomme en doove Geeft"</note> (as a Lord and ruler of all) that you depart from him." He was not so deaf that he did not hear this voice clearly, nor so dumb that he did not express through his gestures that it pained him greatly to have to leave; he seemed to burst with envy when he understood that he might not enter there again. When the unclean Spirit leaves of its own <margin>Matthew 12:45</margin> accord or to please the exorcists, he wanders about a bit but returns easily; but when he is driven out by Jesus, he remains away forever. This Spirit wanted to show his nature one last time, just like those who must leave a city and see no chance of retaking it, who destroy and set on fire whatever they can; he cried out, tore, and raved, and tortured him to the point of death, so that many even said he was dead. A person must lie just as still when they die to evil, so that they do not move, and <margin>Luke 9:43</margin> everyone judges them for dead. And then comes the power of Jesus, which raises them up and sets them there alive and healthy. At this glorious work they were all greatly amazed, the Scribes were ashamed, and the Disciples—embarrassed by their failure—waited for their moment and questioned him alone, just as Matthew describes most extensively.

<margin>Joshua 7:2. 2 Corinthians 10. Hebrews 11:30. 1 Corinthians 13:2. Exodus 17:8. 1 Peter 5:8. Acts 13:3. 1 Corinthians 7:5. 1 Peter 5:8.</margin>
...easily weakens the spirit, just as Joshua, seeing his people retreat because of the crime of Achan, lay prostrate upon the earth, defeated and sorrowful; but he was given counsel on how this Curse <note>original: "Ban"; referring to the "herem" or the devoted things that led to Israel's defeat at Ai in Joshua 7.</note> was to be proclaimed, just as Jesus does for his own. Through faith, the mountains and all high rocky cliffs are moved, which otherwise stand in the way and seem unconquerable. All high places that exalt themselves against the knowledge of God fall down like the walls of Jericho, if the Ark of God and the sanctuary are continually carried around them. From this saying of Christ has come the proverb: *to have a faith that can move mountains*, which Paul also mentions, adding that the same is vain if love does not accompany it. Yet this is not to be understood as natural mountains, rocks, or stone cliffs, but Parabolically in a Spiritual sense, just as the power of the Mustard-seed is to be understood: for the working of faith that happens outside of a person does nothing toward the driving out of the evil nature of which Christ speaks here. Furthermore, by this kind of Devil, the old habits of sin are depicted, which are rooted in nature and have clung to a person since youth; these cannot be cast out except by heavy labor, namely through prayer: that is, to lift the spirit up from the earth and to call upon God for help, just as Moses, by lifting his hands, defeated Amalek; and through fasting, that is: the withdrawal of the nourishment <note>original: "boetsel"; literally meaning "patching" or "sustenance," referring here to the things that fuel sinful habits.</note> of sin. For a thing from which the root is taken, and everything by which it is kept alive, must soon wither and perish. Prayer and fasting are profitable for everyone, and are commended to the believers in many places of Holy Scripture.

# The Fourth Part

MATTHEW 18. MARK 9. LUKE 9. <margin>John 7.</margin>
The characteristics of a child are the lessons for the elder: A child is free from 
malice and wickedness: it is free from deceit, from greed, and from 
self-interest: it shares gladly, is obedient under 
its parents, contented, and quickly forgets the harm done to it: and 
it does not yet know of the unrighteousness of the world. And so the 
<margin>1 Corinthians 14:20.</margin>
Lord wants us to be children in malice, knowing nothing of it, 
but rather to be clothed in edifying love; men in understanding, for the 
soul, being purified of evil, increases in wisdom and in simple 
virtue. But it generally goes otherwise; men strive to be 
men in malice, and then they become children in understanding; and they remain 
<margin>Isaiah 65:17.</margin>
so, even if they lived a hundred years. Thus there must be a turning back, 
a laying aside, and a complete change, as Jesus here teaches as 
a necessary lesson to enter the Kingdom of Heaven. Now John, hearing 
the instruction of his master, recounts an example of what they had done 
to forbid others, wanting to know if such an act conflicted 
with humility.

verse
**6** But whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in me to stumble, it would be better for him that a millstone were hung around his neck, and that he were
**7** drowned in the depth of the sea. Woe to the world because of offenses <note>The Dutch *ergernisse* refers to stumbling blocks or things that cause someone to sin.</note>, for it is necessary that offenses come; nevertheless, woe to that man by whom the offense comes.

### Observation.

<margin>Romans 14:13.</margin>
**To cause to stumble:** <note>original: *verergheren*</note> that is to place something in someone's path upon which they trip, or over which they grieve, and whereby their good intention is extinguished, making them worse than they were before. Where this happens, it is against the nature of love, as Paul explains in another place; and this happens through things that one may omit, or things that one may not omit. If one can omit them while maintaining a good conscience, then one must omit them, or else one does not walk according to love. If one cannot omit them, then one is not guilty in this, even if the whole world were offended; for in such a case, Christ took no notice of the offenses of the Pharisees and other ill-willed
<margin>Matthew 15:12.</margin>
men. When he says: *Woe to the world because of offenses*, he makes it known that the world must fall into both parts—both in the giving and in the taking of offenses—and consequently, full of stumbling and destruction it must become, to the great lamentation of weak, anxious hearts who, through their little knowledge, do not know which way to go. Whereupon a horrific punishment also follows for the guilty one, as he is the cause of the destruction of so many souls for whom Christ
<margin>Romans 14:20.</margin>
died, and who are loved by God with such great love. Meanwhile, he also makes known: *That such offenses are necessary*, which the Apostle Paul, explaining in another place, says:
<margin>1 Corinthians 11:18.</margin>
that it is so that those who are tested <note>In the sense of being "approved" through trial.</note> may be made manifest through them. For while
<margin>Psalm 101:7.</margin>
the eyes of the Lord look upon the faithful in the land, he also gives power and strength to those who serve him uprightly, so that in all kinds of tempests and commotions of offenses, they remain standing like a firm fortress. Furthermore, just as he has warned and advised not to place any offense, he also gives counsel to flee the offense that is given, as follows here.

### MATTHEW 18. MARK 9.

### Observation.

<margin>Romans 6:6.</margin> It is well enough known that by the cutting off of hand, foot, or eye, one must not understand any outward members of the body—as if someone should make themselves lame or maimed when they find that through the misuse of these they offended themselves or someone else and were moved to sin. For the outward members are God’s creatures and entirely innocent in the evil. Rather, one must understand this as referring to inner members, which are firmly attached to the "body of sin," of which Paul testifies that it must be crucified; and of which the outward body is an image and expression. Man, then, has two inner eyes: with the one he beholds the good, and with the other the evil. When he is then beguiled or deceived by the beholding of evil, it seems to him that he has received a keen, sharp sight, now having two eyes where before he had only one; and he begins to be full of judgment, and to look at many things wrongly, <margin>Matthew 20:15.</margin> just like the one whose eye had become "evil" against the master of the house because he distributed his penny <note>original: *penningh*; refers to the denarius or daily wage in the Parable of the Workers in the Vineyard.</note> so generously to the last-hired laborers. Now the Lord wants man to pluck out and blind that "sharp sight," which Isaiah calls the "closing of the eyes," and that he should attend to his soul in
<margin>Isaiah 33:15.</margin> simplicity. And if this counsel seems foolish to man, as if he might not use his understanding and wisdom, and therefore did his "sight" a disservice; the Lord answers here: That it is better to enter into life with one eye, than having two eyes to [be cast]...

...to be thrown into hellish fire: for they are nothing but the inquisitive eyes of Adam, <note>A reference to the Fall of Man, where Adam and Eve's eyes were "opened" to sin after eating the forbidden fruit.</note> which bear death and no life, even though eating from that forbidden tree has a beautiful and glorious appearance. <margin>Song of Songs 4:9</margin> The bride in the Song of Songs <note>original: "Cantica"</note> had drawn her bridegroom's love to her and captured his heart with a single eye—that was the eye of love and of noble simplicity. The same must also be understood regarding the hands and feet, for through these is depicted man's worldly activity <note>literally "workability"</note> in which he takes great pleasure and exalts himself, just as the Pharisee did above the Tax Collector. <margin>Luke 18:9</margin> Furthermore, by these members one must also understand the members of the body of Christ <note>Meaning the individual people within the Church community.</note>, of which some (as Paul testifies) are eyes, ears, hands, and feet; and <margin>1 Corinthians 12:11</margin> when such people teach or live in a scandalous way, they must be cut off from the body without respect of person. So too the salt loses its power if one does not strictly guard oneself; and the Lord asks: With what shall one then salt? Since you yourself have become stinking and blameworthy, not purifying yourself of all malice and deceit, how shall you be able to turn away another's evil? For He speaks here of such salt that is accompanied by peace. Such that peace and love must be present to preserve and to heal, just as much as the sharpness of the salt is needed to bite away the impurity of the body. By the immortal worm that eternally accuses the sinful conscience, and the unquenchable fire, the Lord wishes to express the greatness of the punishment, so that one will not think lightly of His words, but take them to heart as words of truth.

### Matthew 18. Mark 9. Luke 9. John 7.

...I say to you truly, he rejoices more over that one than over the ninety-nine that did not go astray. In the same way, it is not the will of your Father in Heaven that any of these little ones should be lost.

### Observation

<margin>2 Samuel 6:19</margin>
It happens very easily that those who appear somewhat greater than others—whether because they have received more wisdom or temporal goods—hold others who are lesser in contempt and secretly despise them, as Michal did to David <note>Michal, the daughter of King Saul, famously despised her husband David in her heart when she saw him dancing for joy before the Ark of the Covenant, viewing his humility as beneath his dignity.</note>: but this does not accord with the Divine love and wisdom of Christ, who always associated himself with the least. And because much evil arises from that contempt, he here presents his own example for teaching: That he came to save that which was lost. Teaching further through the 
<margin>Luke 15:2</margin>
parable of the hundred sheep, with what close attention and fatherly care he stands—like a good Shepherd who loves his sheep—to preserve the very least of them and bring them to his fold <note>original: "hope," likely meaning a place of safety or the sheepfold</note>. He leaves the ninety-nine on the mountains, as those who are kept and protected in the highly exalted Divinity from all misfortune; for there is no surer refuge than to dwell on high, for as Isaiah 
<margin>Isaiah 33:16</margin>
says: *His bread is given to him, and his water is certain.* Meanwhile, the shepherd leaves the mountains of his rest, betakes himself down into the wilderness where there are hedges and thorns, and searches for the lost sheep until he has found and secured <note>original: "ghebonden," literally "bound," referring to the practice of a shepherd securing a sheep to carry it home</note> it. So he also wants us not to love our own spiritual exaltation <note>literally "up-liftedness"</note> so much that we neglect the salvation of our brother, but that we should remember: if we suffer some discomfort, love will repay it with joy when it brings the found sheep into its fold. And besides this, the Father’s will is fulfilled, who does not want one of the least to be lost. Let us consider and remember this in love.

<margin>Matthew 18</margin>
<margin>Mark 9, Luke 9, John 7</margin>
18 ...and a tax collector <note>original: "Publicaen." In the New Testament, tax collectors were often Jewish individuals working for the Roman occupiers and were frequently grouped with "sinners" and social outcasts.</note>. Truly I say to you: whatever you bind on earth, shall also be bound in Heaven; and whatever you loose on earth, shall also be 19 loosed in Heaven. For 20 where two or three are gathered in my name, there I am in the midst of them.

### Observation

The love between brother and brother is strong, and also delicate. It is strong as long as one does not perceive anything that is contrary to the love of God or of one's neighbor. It is delicate—or rather, jealous—whenever any signs are noticed of deviation or a slackening in virtue. Likewise, judgment varies greatly even among people who are of good will; what one judges to be a sin, the other considers to be no sin at all. Similarly, the aim of the one who rebukes is different: some do everything out of a pure love and from the bottom of their heart, whether they choose to endure it or to speak out. Others labor to find something against their neighbor, so as to have material and reason to put their rebuke into action. Others are misled by appearances, because they interpret something further than their brother’s intention actually was, or they catch something from hearsay from other people and build great things upon it. In such a way, the brotherly love which is necessary above all else to remain and increase, stands in many parts in great danger of being withheld <note>The Dutch "verhouden" implies a stopping, withholding, or growing cold of affection.</note>. To preserve this love as much as is possible, the Lord Jesus—as a true shepherd of his sheep—gives here an order on how to act when such a thing occurs: *If your brother sins against you.* By this, he means a sin of which one is well-assured that it is indeed a sin; otherwise, he would not say: <margin>Sirach 19:15</margin> *rebuke him*, but rather *investigate the matter*, as Sirach <note>Referring to the Book of Sirach or Ecclesiasticus from the Apocrypha, which provides practical wisdom on social conduct.</note> teaches in one place. Yet he also speaks of such matters that are not yet known to everyone; <margin>Galatians 6:1</margin> *Rebuke him between you and him alone*: that is, as is explained in another place: *Instruct him with a spirit of gentleness*, always looking at yourself and thinking that you too could fall into that temptation. It may also be that in that conversation your brother can so inform you that the matter is not so bad, or perhaps not a sin at all. And even assuming it was indeed bad enough, he may show himself so repentant that you see yourself satisfied and rejoice with him that a lost sheep has been found. Therefore he says: *If he hears you, then you have...*

you have won your brother: for this is the end <note>The intended goal or purpose.</note> that is aimed at. 

Yet if the confrontation turns out such that you cannot understand one another, or that no turning of the heart and necessary repentance is observed, then do not bring your brother out into the street <note>Meaning: do not make his faults public or humiliate him.</note>, do not increase his wound, but take one or two more with you: namely such as seek the best and are pious of heart. If the matter is doubtful, these can instruct you and mediate the case; if it is certain, they can move the straying person to repentance or, in case of stubbornness, serve as witnesses as to how the matter proceeded—all in order to win the brother. If all this should not help, one should not yet lose heart; <margin>John 11:9</margin> there are twelve hours in the day, a person can change his mind, or the misunderstanding may still lie with the speaker. Therefore more persons must be troubled with it; Tell the Community <term>Gemeynte: The local body of believers or the congregation, rather than a formal institutional hierarchy.</term>: namely, such a community that is one and common with God, where there is understanding to forgive and knowledge to punish, in such a way that the Spirit of God governs the same. Whatever then such a community judges regarding that brother, that also counts with God, since it is one Spirit that leads and governs them; thus, she does nothing here but according to the wisdom of God. 

If that brother does not conduct himself godly before that community, but resists and slanders, then he proves by his actions that he is no true member of the same: for true members love, and do not take sides against one another. Thus he must then be held for what he is, namely: no member, but as a Heathen and an open sinner, who has no inheritance in the Kingdom of God. This binding which happens through the Spirit of God is just as firm with God in Heaven as it is down on earth; such is also the case with the unbinding <note>The restoration or "loosing" of a repentant member.</note>. But a Diotrephes <note>A reference to 3 John 1:9-10, signifying an ambitious leader who loves to be first and expels members unjustly.</note> <margin>John 9, John 8:7</margin> does not have such power, nor does the Pharisaic Spirit, which itself is full of judgment despite a stained conscience, seeking how it might fulfill the Law of Moses in punishing the fallen human.

If this were rightly known, how those minds would bow toward each other, yield and give way to one another, laboring until that unity were bound, just as one turns the strings of a musical instrument <note>original: "Musijck Instrument"</note> up and down until accord is struck; precious, yes, beyond measure precious before God is peace. To such an extent that Christ also further testifies: That He is there in the midst with His Spirit and power, where such united hearts (however few they may be) gather in His name: That is, gather in His essence, there pouring out His abundant graces for growth and...

<margin>24</margin> And when he began to calculate, one was brought before him who owed him ten thousand pounds <note>original: "pondt." In the biblical context, these are "talents," representing an impossibly large sum of money that a common servant could never repay.</note>:

<margin>29</margin> Then his fellow servant fell down, and pleaded with him, saying: Have patience with me, and I will pay you everything.

### Reflection.

Through this parable, Jesus removes the limitation that Peter thought existed in the matter of forgiveness: for he first brings to mind how great the debt is that man incurs before God, namely: **Ten thousand pounds** <note>original: "Thien duysent ponden." While the text says "pounds," this refers to the biblical "ten thousand talents," a sum representing an infinite, unpayable debt</note>, which is put in place of an infinite number; namely, so much that it is impossible to pay. Secondly, he sets before our eyes what right God has over such a person; namely: to sell him and all that is his: that is, to throw him into eternal slavery under the Devil’s power. Thirdly, what a distress comes over man standing before the judgment of God / how humbly and lowly he sings / as long as justice flits before his eyes and is revealed in his conscience: promising much more than he is able to carry out; and all that in order to escape the hands of the Judge. Fifthly / the Lord teaches the unfaithfulness of that same man against such immeasurable goodness / and forgetting the remission of his great sins / he is cruel and unmerciful toward his fellow neighbor / who pitifully begs him for patience; but he, not being satisfied / demands what he has to claim / namely / **one hundred pence**, which do not even come into comparison against the debt that was so graciously forgiven him by the King: being about the six-hundred-thousandth part of those ten thousand pounds. <margin>Bünting, in his *Calculation of the Coinage*, *Travelbook* <note>Heinrich Bünting (1545–1606) was a German pastor and cartographer whose popular book *Itinerarium Sacrae Scripturae* provided readers with maps and explanations of biblical weights, measures, and coins.</note>.</margin> Sixthly / the righteous anger of the King is set before our eyes / over such a wicked and ungrateful servant: for he had not forgiven him for this purpose / that he should live according to his own will / be merry / and walk after his earthly lusts / being simply free of that previous crime; but because he should become a partaker of the good and compassionate nature of his King / and him so

Johann Alsted <note>Johann Heinrich Alsted (1588–1638) was a German Calvinist theologian and encyclopedist</note> maintains that it was a Feast of Tabernacles <note>original: "Looverhutten"; a Jewish autumn festival</note>—not the one mentioned by John in his 7th, 8th, and 9th chapters, but another; namely, the one closest to the aforementioned Passover. Both scholars agree on this: that Jesus preached and traveled for a year longer than is commonly thought, which would make his ministry four and a half years in total. Regarding my own view, although I can accept that Jesus stayed in Galilee for a long period, I nevertheless find it difficult to stretch the time of his travels a full year longer than has been understood by so many learned and investigative men until now. I have therefore followed this middle-path: I prefer to guess that the following journey took place during a Pentecost feast <note>original: "Pinxster-feest"</note>, being seven weeks apart from the preceding Passover, rather than stating something uncertain as a certainty. It also does not necessarily follow that this was a major high holiday. Furthermore, Luke does not clearly state whether Jesus traveled all the way to Jerusalem, or whether, after turning toward the land of the Samaritans, he returned and then sent out his seventy Disciples, as will be discussed in its proper place. Meanwhile, leaving everyone free to hold their own opinion, let us return to the text and the teachings contained therein.

### Reflection.

<margin>Matt. 17:22. Mark 9:30.</margin>
The Lord Jesus, having taught / instilled / and made known to his Disciples for some time / that he must go up to Jerusalem / and there be despised by the High Priests / and be subjected to the death of the cross: So he wishes to prove by deed / that / although he well knew all this / he did not want to shun or flee such a city and people; but willingly gave himself up to fulfill the will of his Father. So now that the time was drawing nearer and nearer, he made himself ready for the journey; set his face toward Jerusalem; just as if he wanted to fulfill the saying of David: <margin>Psal. 40:8</margin> *See, I come; in the book it is written of me, I gladly do your will, my God: and your law I have in my heart.* And the saying in the Song of Solomon: <margin>Song of Sol. <note>original: "Cant." for Cantica Canticorum</note> 5:10</margin> *My friend is white and red:* white in the innocence of his blameless life; red in the readiness of suffering. Let us now observe what met him on this journey. 1. He sent messengers before him: <margin>Num. 20:17.</margin> He did not want to overwhelm or be burdensome to anyone with his followers; but he wanted (as Israel of old) to eat his own bread / and drink his water / he only requested passage through the land of the Samaritans / which was situated between Galilee and Judea: these messengers were presumably / James and John. 2. They did not receive him, that is / they refused him lodging / and what was necessary for it; even though he wanted to pay for it. Luke 2:7.</margin> late in the evening: the nature of the Bethlehemites / who did not receive his dear Mother / with Joseph her husband / in their houses / although she was in the final stages of pregnancy. ### The Fourth Part / Matthew 18. Mark 9. John 7.

<margin>Luke 9.</margin>
could also be; yet Luke goes into more detail than Matthew, which is why his text and order are followed here. Take note then of the following. 1. It happened while they were on the way (whether on the journey there or on the return from Jerusalem): one said to him: **I will follow you.** <margin>Matt. 8:19.</margin> This man was (according to the testimony of Matthew) a **scribe** <term>scribe: a scholar and teacher of the Jewish Law</term>; he showed himself to be quite willing, but the way was unknown to him. It is much easier to read the scriptures and to contemplate the footsteps of the saints than to walk them in deed. The Lord, seeing the unthinking zeal of this man, set before his eyes what he was to encounter on this path, so that he might make his account of it: **The foxes have holes, and the birds of the Heaven have nests,** thereby expressing <margin>Jer. 25:24. Mic. 3:2. Isa. 5:8.</margin> two kinds of men. First: Wicked, cunning deceivers, who know how to manage themselves with such dexterity—living off the sweat and blood of poor people without gaining any shame for it, indeed sitting in much greater honor and dignity than if they were doing good—for the word **holes** signifies a certain hidden crookedness, just as a fox's lair represents, such that they are (as the saying goes) <note>original: "voor geen een gat te vangen en zijn" - a Dutch idiom meaning someone is so slippery or cunning that they cannot be caught or pinned down.</note> not to be caught by a single hole. Second: **High-flying spirits**, who under the cover of **Religion** play the master here, engaging in it and also obtaining great advantages, even the riches of this world, making their nests in high-reaching trees, sufficiently protected from all peril. These have (according to the sound of His word) all rest and comfort, the opportunity to dwell therein, to lay eggs, and to bring forth young. But the **Son of Man**, who through his humiliation is subject to all misery, **has nothing**, much less a nest or a secure place where he may lay his head, claim it as his own, and possess it in peace under the protection of others: for having given up all things, he became poor in this world, and is also <margin>2 Cor. 8:9. Luke 2:7. and 9:53. Luke 13:29. Matt. 27:34. John 19:23.</margin> rejected by everyone, and driven away whenever it pleases them, denied land and place. As has been shown not only in this preceding example of the Samaritans, but from his youth upward, and so it shall remain until he, as everyone’s prey, shall be stripped even of life itself. And such are also his followers who faithfully tread in his footsteps; there is not one among them who must not make the same account.

2. To another he said: **follow me**; This man sought delay: **Lord, allow me first to bury my Father.** It seemed a necessary family duty, yet it displeased the Lord. One is obliged to submit all things, to honor and love Father and Mother, but when God <margin>Matt. 4:20.</margin> calls, one must regard nothing, leave everything, and follow him, just as the Apostles did with their sheep <note>The author uses "schaepkens" (little sheep), likely a metaphorical reference to the Apostles' livelihoods or literal flocks before they were called.</note>. What then of the rest? All things will settle themselves: **Let the dead,** who do not feel the life of God in them nor believe that it exists, **bury their dead** (whom they regard as dead and of whom they have no hope, except to be glad for the earthly inheritance), burying them as grandly and expensively as they wish, erecting **Tombs** and **Pyramids** to enjoy an immortal name among men.

### Observation.

There was no ingratitude / no persecution / no hatred nor envy so great / that it could turn Jesus away from his customary compassion for the poor people / who were scattered like sheep without a shepherd. He looked upon the Harvest in the field / how everyone was diligent in cutting their corn / binding it / and bringing it home before the rain. He noticed that at such a time there were hardly enough laborers to be found / because of the great haste everyone had to preserve their fruits. All of this he applies to the Harvest of the Gospel / and the abandoned Jewish Field / where much corn was in danger of being lost. Thus, he sent out more Laborers than before / to gather that Harvest / so that he might come as a faithful and caring Master of the House <note>original: "hups-Vader" — an archaic term for a householder or head of a family</note> / and bring the prepared sheaves into his barn:
<margin>Exod. 16. 1.</margin>
He wished not only to gladden the spiritual Israel with twelve Fountains, but also with seventy Palm trees <note>This refers to the oasis of Elim in Exodus 15:27, where there were 12 wells and 70 palm trees, often seen by early commentators as a prefiguring of the 12 Apostles and 70 Disciples.</note>:
<margin>Num. 11. 17. Baron. An. 33. Num. 13.</margin>
choosing from the group of his Disciples the number of seventy; or as some ancients firmly believe / seventy-two, according to the number of the chosen Judges / appointed by Moses over Israel: which number was subsequently maintained among the Jews / so that they also had, in the time of Christ, seventy-two Elders, whom they called the Sanhedrin <term>Sanhedrin: the supreme council and tribunal of the Jews</term>, or the Great Council.
<margin>Baron. An. 32. Num 6. Luc. 24. 17. Baron. An. 109 Num. 1.</margin>
What Names these men had, the Evangelist does not express / but says only that they were others than the twelve / who had been found previously. When Jesus presented these things to the Disciples, he at the same time recounted as examples those places that had despised him and his Apostles, showing no improvement according to the requirements of the offered grace, and how miserably it would yet end for them, saying: *Woe to you, Chorazin, woe to you, Bethsaida,* <margin>Matt. 11:21. Lam. 1:1. Jer. 9:1.</margin> and that with a sorrowful and sighing heart; just as the Prophet Jeremiah foresaw the fall of Jerusalem and voiced a mournful lament over it. It is to be believed that he often looked upon these places (in which he frequently stayed) in their ruined state—the houses burned, the walls overthrown, the people slain—just as later followed through the war of the Romans <note original: "krijgh der Romeynen">The First Jewish-Roman War (66–73 AD), which led to the destruction of Jerusalem and surrounding towns.</note>. He compared the fall of these cities to the destruction of Sodom, and to the fall of the opulent cities of Tyre and Sidon, which had entirely fallen into ashes for the sake of their sins; just as happened to Babylon and other wanton cities, <margin>Fol. 36v.</margin> as we have treated more broadly in its proper place. 3. But most of all, he grieved for the corruption of their souls, that they let such beautiful offered grace pass them by; a grace which those of Sodom and Gomorrah, as also those of Tyre and Sidon, had never been permitted to have; and therefore they would also be more tolerable on the day of judgment than these, who willfully did not want to see. In this, we notice the wonderful wisdom of God, that he distributes his gifts with distinction and punishes with distinction; seeking much from those to whom much is entrusted, <margin>Luke 12:48</margin> and demanding much from those to whom much is given. Returning again to his messengers, he says: *He who hears you hears me*: and that for this reason, because his Spirit spoke through them. Many indeed claim for themselves the power of these words, but are often estranged from his Spirit; and where the Spirit of Christ is not, there these words do not apply: for by the word *me*, he gives to understand that he must be there with his Spirit and Essence, as Paul also teaches: *he who despises you, despises no man, but God, who has given his holy Spirit in you.* <margin>1 Thess. 4:8</margin> And where God gives his Spirit, there it is evident by the fruits.

These seventy Disciples having been sent out, a great part of the summer thus passed by, and meanwhile the <term>Scenopegia<note>The Greek term for the Feast of Tabernacles or Sukkot, a week-long Jewish autumn festival commemorating the dwelling of the Israelites in booths during the Exodus.</note></term> or Feast of Tabernacles began to approach, which was one of the three annual Feasts in which everyone had to appear in Jerusalem. For the start of this Feast, Jesus made no preparations yet, and was therefore exhorted by some of his kinsmen out of a sense of presumption, as John describes.

<margin>Leviticus 23:34. Josephus, Antiquities, Book 3, Chapter 10.</margin>
This Feast of Tabernacles <note original: "Feest der Loover-hutten">Literally the 'Feast of Leafy Huts,' known in Hebrew as Sukkot.</note> was instituted by God in memory of the fact that the children of Israel had been strangers in Egypt and wandered for forty years in the wilderness. The first day of this Feast was on the fifteenth day of the seventh month, called Tishrei <note original: "Thisri"></note>, corresponding with our eighth of October; this day was very holy, and no servile work might be done on it. Huts were erected from all kinds of beautiful green branches: such as from citrons <note original: "Citroenen">Referring to the Etrog, a citrus fruit used in the holiday ritual.</note>, myrtles, palm trees, brook willows, peach trees <note original: "Persic-bomen"></note>, and others of like sort. This Feast lasted eight days, and the last day was the most glorious of all. A great multitude of people gathered from all sides to observe it annually within Jerusalem. Seeing then the brothers of Jesus that everyone was preparing for this Feast, and that he, contrary to his custom, still held himself quiet, they sought to exhort him to set out <note original: "optreckingh">The journey up to Jerusalem.</note>; which proceeded not from a godly diligence—for this was not necessary—but from a bold presumption, making themselves masters over him, just as the brothers of David, Joseph, and others also did in their time: for commonly

This Feast of Tabernacles <note>original: "Feest der Loover-hutten," literally "Feast of Leafy Huts," commonly known as Sukkot.</note> was instituted by God in memory of how the children of Israel had been strangers in Egypt and wandered for forty years in the wilderness. Furthermore, Jesus rejoices in consideration of the wisdom of God, who had locked away this mystery from the clever and the wise of this world, and revealed the same to the little ones, and the simple, who are not wise in themselves, but humble, bowing at the feet of Jesus to learn from him the way of wisdom:
<margin>Matt. 11:25.</margin>
of which more has been spoken in its place. 5. And after he had thanked his Father for this, standing turned away from his Disciples, he then turns back to them, as if having another great secret to reveal, saying: Blessed are the eyes that see what you see. He spoke this not of their outward eyes, with which they beheld his body—for the Scribes and Pharisees saw that as well—but of the inner eyes of the mind, with which they received the light of God through his Heavenly teaching. They saw fulfilled that which the ancients hoped for; and that was what many Kings and Prophets had longed for. The blind Didymus <note>Didymus the Blind (c. 313–398 AD), a famous Alexandrian theologian who lost his physical sight but was renowned for his spiritual "vision" and learning</note> was, through his inner
<margin>Eusebius Book 11 Chapter 7.</margin>
<margin>John 19:34, 37.</margin>
<margin>Psalm 36.</margin>
sight, far more Blessed than those who, seeing Jesus outwardly, pierced his side. Thus, it is such eyes that Jesus speaks of here: of which David testifies when he says: In your light we see that light. And this happens through the eyes of the understanding. Now when the time was fulfilled that Jesus should go to the Feast of Tabernacles <term>Feast of Tabernacles: also known as Sukkot, a major Jewish festival involving the building of temporary shelters to remember the Israelites' journey through the wilderness</term>, he made himself ready to visit that Feast with his Disciples in a quiet ascent, when the greatest crowd of the people, and also his unbelieving brothers, had already gone up, as John describes.

<vocab>
<term>Parable</term> (Gelykenis): A moral story used by Jesus to illustrate spiritual truths.
<term>Samaritan</term> (Samaritaan): A member of a group historically marginalized by the religious elite, here representing Christ's compassion.

<term>Priest</term> (Priester): A high religious official who, in the parable, passes by the wounded man.

<term>Christ</term> (Christus): Though not in the verse, he is the "Samaritan" in this interpretation.
<term>Beast</term> (Beest): The animal (usually a donkey) used to carry the wounded man to safety.

eyes upon the earth, he saw deserts, wild forests, and thorns: if he looked along the way, there was no one he perceived to comfort him: if he attempted to stand up, all his limbs were broken and paralyzed; who shall help him? 2. **The Apparent Help**; he saw a Priest coming; he felt some refreshment as this man came nearer, his hope grew, but what was it? Upon arriving, the Priest looked at him; he preached and promised great things, yet they were nothing but words; he let him lie there and went his way. After that came a Levite; this man had many ways of religious service, seemed very devout, and made a display of great knowledge, yet he was not the true Master Physician <note>original: "Medicijn-meester"</note>; he also looked at him, but went away without offering any help: All hope was now lost, since such men show no mercy—indeed, they increase the pain and make the wound strike deeper, pointing out his imprudence and grieving the heart more than comforting it; from where shall help now come? 3. **The Restoration**; he saw a Samaritan approaching: Oh, this stranger shall not help me! Thus was Divine love the ointment and perfect healing against the poison of the evil spirits and the deadly stings of the one who has been a murderer from the beginning <note>A reference to Satan; see John 8:44.</note> and who casts man into unspeakable misery.

With this parable the Lord *Jesus* gave this Scribe—being a Jew—no small thing to understand: how vain was their boast...

### Observation.

In the middle of the Feast (that is, namely, on the fourth day: for the Feast lasted eight days <note>The Feast of Tabernacles, or Sukkot, is a week-long Jewish harvest festival</note>), Jesus went up into the Temple, a place where an exceedingly great multitude was gathered; where minds were conflicted, driven to and fro, and where shortly before people had spoken doubtfully of Jesus. He did not go to sit hidden in a corner, but showed himself to everyone publicly: teaching his usual teachings, which opened the mystery of the scripture as if with a key. 1. From this arose a wonder; a common failing among people, that they fall into wonder rather than into improvement. They ask among one another: How does this man know the scripture, having never studied <note>original: "niet gheleert," referring to the fact that Jesus had not attended the formal Rabbinic schools</note>? For the scriptures were in the custody of the Scribes <term>Schrift-geleerden: scholars who interpreted and taught Jewish law</term>, where the common man was not allowed: and they knew of what lineage he was, and in what manner he was raised. 2. Jesus, to take away this wonder from them, makes it known that he did not need to fetch such things from the place where they thought: but that all such things were given to him from the Father through a Divine power. My teaching is not mine, to wit, insofar as I am a man, and would have to present the same in a human manner; but his who sent me; so that it is a Divine teaching descended from above, like a flood of living water. And this teaching is just like light, in that it brings testimony of itself; not that one needs many reasons of proof to establish this or that, but it is a clear and uncontradictable truth; which truth those find in themselves who take and receive it. The teaching of the Scribes may be called into doubt; they refute one another: The Sadducees are against the Pharisees, and again both these against the Essenes <note>The author highlights the internal divisions between the major Jewish sects of the Second Temple period</note>. But as far as my teaching is concerned: if anyone wants to live the same, he shall immediately find that it has a certain power. Testifying that it is from God, and not of myself, that I should invent or devise anything to draw you, to move you, or to make you understand something only through words, as is the nature of false Prophets: <margin>1 Kings 22:24</margin> for these become upset if one does not honor them enough; seeking glory from that which they produce skillfully; and with that glory one can also appease and satisfy them, or otherwise they become irreconcilably disturbed: all of which is far from me, since the disobedient person harms no one but himself. 3. <margin>John 5:1.</margin> Further, Jesus attempted to take away their gathered anger, which they wrongly held against him because he had previously made a man healthy there on the Sabbath: recounting how the Law of Moses is not broken by circumcision, which often happens on the Sabbath. Saying: Why do you seek to kill me? This he spoke regarding the plots of the Pharisees,

### Observation.

The most gracious Lord, having given a glorious testimony and brought the counsel of the Pharisees into confusion, withdrew to the **Mount of Olives**, a place where he retired in devotion with his disciples, and which was also located near **Bethany**, so that he could easily visit his dear friends. Meanwhile, the Pharisees, continuing to lay snares for him through some clever traps, devised a scheme through which they firmly imagined they could cause Jesus to fall into one thing or another: either to speak guiltily against the Law of Moses, or—against his own teaching, which always spoke for mercy and forgiveness of sins—to pronounce the sentence of death upon a sinner who was sufficiently distressed and struck in spirit, seeing herself at the ultimate point of her life.

<margin>Gen. 38. 2 Sam. 12:11. Hist. of Susanna.</margin>
2. They then brought a woman who was found in **adultery**. A sin that was subject to sharp punishment, as the examples of **Tamar**, of **David**, and of **Susanna** <note>The author cites these biblical and apocryphal figures—Tamar (Genesis 38), David (2 Samuel 12), and Susanna (from the Book of Daniel/Apocrypha)—as historical precedents regarding sexual sins and accusations.</note> can teach us. They took advantage of the time while he was teaching; and the listening crowd was drinking in the Kingdom of Heaven, the love of God, and his abundant mercy. They make a circle and place this woman in the middle, so that everyone might see and hear how Jesus would be caught in a bind <note>original: "in de klem," a Dutch idiom meaning to be trapped or stuck in a dilemma.</note> through their cleverness; but see here the wisdom of God: "Master, this woman was found in adultery." With this, they first incriminated themselves, for what woman had more unbecomingly strayed into adultery than the **Jewish church**? <note>The "Jewish church" (Jootſche kercke) is used here as a period-typical theological term referring to the religious community of Israel, often metaphorically described as a spouse to God in early modern commentary.</note>

<meta>This page continues the reflection on the story of the woman caught in adultery from John 8, moving from the accusations of the Pharisees to the internal conviction of their consciences and Jesus’ final act of mercy.</meta>

The fourth Part / Matt. 18. Mark 9. Luke 10.

## JOHN 8.

<margin>Jer. 2:20. Ezek. 16:32.</margin>
Jeremiah compares them <note>The religious leaders or the people of Israel who had gone astray.</note> to a wild and raging she-camel; Ezekiel to an unclean prostitute who runs after her lovers with money in hand, showing terrible unfaithfulness toward her lawful husband, who had raised her from a foundling and brought her to honor. Furthermore, they themselves were consorting in their hearts with their secret and hidden sins, just like the villains in the story of Susanna <note>A reference to the apocryphal story where two elders falsely accuse Susanna of adultery while they themselves were driven by lust.</note>, as their desires drove them. 3. See now what Jesus does: He bent down and wrote with his finger in the earth, signifying thereby that they should look within themselves and notice what the finger of God pointed out on the tablets of their hearts—whether they themselves were free of the very things they charged this woman with. It is to be believed that through this writing, their own ugliness was revealed to them in no small measure, making their consciences tremble. But these people, boldly overlooking their own faults and staring fixedly outside themselves at this woman, hoping to achieve their purpose, continued questioning him. 4. The all-knowing Lord—who can search the hearts and kidneys <note>original: "herten en nieren"; a biblical expression for a person’s innermost thoughts and emotions.</note>—knowing how miserable the internal state was, stood up, saying: "He among you who is without sin, let him throw the first stone." The law of Moses was not forbidden from being carried out, but the man could not be found who would start first; one looked at the other, each knowing where the shoe pinched <note>A common idiom for knowing where one's own guilt or trouble lies.</note>. And Jesus, to further unsettle the conscience, wrote again with bold strokes into their hearts, bruising those hard stone rocks with the hammer of his piercing word so that they could no longer endure the pain; nor did they dare to remain standing out of shame. They removed themselves like accused men from the company, one after the other; the eldest and most prominent, who had started the game, first, and the others following after, once their Goliath <note>Likely referring to their pride or their leading argument which had been defeated.</note> was defeated. <margin>1 Cor. 1:17. Isa. 29:14.</margin> See how little power human schemes have, and how the wisdom of the wise is made into foolishness, and the understanding of the prudent into nonsense through the wisdom of God.

5. Jesus, standing up again and seeing this army had departed, asked the woman (who was waiting fixedly for the outcome): "Where are your accusers?" For it is reasonable that the accusers be present above all things when they bring someone before the court. But finding no one, he asks again if anyone had condemned her? Far from it; the stones had fallen from their hands, feeling that it would cost them dearly. <margin>2 Sam. 12:5.</margin> David was changed just as quickly when he had first condemned the sheep-thief with great zeal, only to hear that *he* was the man <note>Referring to the prophet Nathan's parable which led King David to recognize his own sin with Bathsheba.</note>; no human is so strict that he is not merciful to himself. "Neither do I condemn you": for how would it be possible that I, who proclaim the mercy of God to all people, would be more cruel than those strict avengers of the Law of Moses, who had come here with the intent to practice justice? If they let the matter rest, how shall I pursue it? <margin>Ezek. 18:23.</margin> Finally, proving that he had come to seek the lost, not desiring the death of the sinner but that he be converted and live, he spoke to the woman: "Go and sin no more": for that is all that God seeks from mankind.

It concludes with an explanation of Jesus' mercy as a fulfillment of God's desire for repentance rather than punishment.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discourse following Jesus' declaration as the "Light of the World." It focuses on the debate between Jesus and the Pharisees regarding the validity of his testimony and the nature of spiritual versus worldly judgment.</meta>

<header>The Fourth Part / JOHN 8. Matt. 18. Mark 9. Luke 10.</header>

...following [his] steps, they shall be freed from all works of darkness and feel the light of life within them; which shall always lead them on an indubitable path of truth, so that no one needs to remain in error, nor limp on both sides. <note>original: "op beyde zijden te hincken." A biblical idiom from 1 Kings 18:21, meaning to waver between two opinions or to be indecisive.</note> 2. The Pharisees, consumed with envy and blinded in their souls, accused him of presumption because he testified of himself. And truly, they did not know how great the difference is between the testimony of light—which makes known what it is through its own rays—and the verbal testimony of a man, which he gives concerning himself so that he might be esteemed and known for what he is not; which is a lie and an ambitious impulse. And so they themselves persisted in seeking fame and honor from men, according to their fleshly disposition: Therefore the Lord says, *Even if I testify of myself, it is nonetheless true,* because it is done not according to the flesh, but according to the truth of the Spirit: For I am entirely certain in all my matters, knowing my origin, lineage, and where I am going. But you judge according to the flesh, and therefore your judgment is false: you look upon my person and human being, which appears lowly in your eyes, not knowing that I have come from eternity and return to the same. I judge no one in that manner; my eyes see further than yours. Whenever I judge, whether it be regarding myself or someone else, it does not happen according to human appearance (as you think), but according to the invisible essence in which the truth reveals itself: <margin>John 4:24</margin> God, who is a Spirit and judges all things according to his truth, is my wisdom, light, and discernment of judgment, who is so united in me that I am never without him. Therefore, when you look upon me according to the grasp of your understanding, as a man alone in his human being, you judge poorly and do not understand my testimony. <margin>John 5:33</margin> My testimony is true of itself; to this is added the testimony of my Father, who has openly testified of me by a voice from Heaven; and still does the same daily through his works before everyone's eyes. <margin>Deut. 17:16</margin> And that is (according to your Law) enough, which is satisfied with two witnesses, even if they were but mortal men. When the Jews heard these words, they again took them in a fleshly manner, saying: *Where is your Father?* for they thought that the Lord spoke of someone who could be pointed out with a finger. Therefore he rightly answers: that they know neither him nor his Father, nor can they know them, since their judgment was too coarse and their intellectual eye too blind. Jesus spoke all these things by the Offering Box; <note>The "treasury" mentioned in John 8:20.</note> which still stood as a witness over the blindness of their ancestors, who indeed thought they saw, yet had killed Zacharias the son of <margin>1 Chron. 24:21</margin> Jehoiada, <note>Referring to the priest Jehoiada who created the first chest for temple contributions in 2 Chronicles 24.</note> the finder and first establisher of this Offering Box. And although they were now well-inclined through that same blindness to seize Jesus, nonetheless this did not happen; the power of God restrained their intent, because his hour of suffering had not yet come.

<header>The Fourth Part /</header>

**JOHN 8.** ->centered text<- **Matt. 18. Mark 9. Luke 10.**

**Jesus** having proved that **God** was not their Father / he now points out as if with his finger who their Father is / for they could not exist without a Father : saying : The Father from whom you come is the **Devil**. That might well have brought terror to their hearts / but they did not believe it : for the **Devil** has no knowledge of himself / otherwise he would shudder at himself ; as they say the **Basilisk** does. <note>The Basilisk was a mythical serpent-king in medieval lore, believed to be so lethal that its glance could kill. It was often said that if a Basilisk saw its own reflection in a mirror, it would die of its own terror or poison.</note> The Lord adds the proof: you wish to do according to your Father’s lusts. They proved by their deeds / that the **Devil’s** will and their own will were one ; as one as **Christ** was with **God** / so one were they with the **Devil** ; and his desire was their desire :
<margin>Micah 2:1.</margin>
they plot on their beds what deceit they shall employ / and go about evil deeds. 3. For further proof, he describes the character and nature of the **Devil** :
<margin>Gen. 3:4 and 4:5.</margin>
He is a murderer from the beginning, murdering the souls of the first parents in Paradise ; he drove **Cain** to the murder of his brother / and other following examples. He did not remain standing in the truth, but fell out of it / and departed willingly ; just like these **Jews** / at first they seemed to side with **Christ** / and immediately thereafter they picked up stones from the streets in anger. The reason : In him there is no truth : for if it had been in him / then he would surely have remained in the truth ; and it would not have been possible to fall out of it. When he speaks a lie, he does not borrow it from others / as he must borrow the truth ; but he speaks this from himself , and he does nothing more gladly ; he laughs about it / and is joyful in his wickedness : For he is a Father of the same ; just as a father brings forth his own likeness / which is also evident in animals / that in the springtime they are joyful to the highest degree / because their time for procreation has come. So does the **Devil** / whenever he finds an opportunity to sow his lies ; he does nothing more gladly. 4. He proves from this : that / although the **Devil** was a liar / they nonetheless inclined their ear toward him : but that they did not believe him / who spoke the truth; by which they confirmed / that they were children of lies.

### Reflection.

<margin>1 Sam. 12, 3.</margin> The Lord Jesus offers his blameless life as a witness to the truth dwelling within him / for as the tree is / so are the fruits. In this manner, Samuel presented his innocent life to the children of Israel / showing that he had taken no man’s ox / donkey / nor any gift.
<margin>Jer. 15, 10.</margin> Jeremiah showed that he had neither taken nor lent money upon usury; <note>In the 17th-century context, "usury" (woecker) referred to the charging of interest, which was often viewed as a moral and social transgression.</note>

Abraham was indeed dead in appearance; but in truth he lived for God. Are you greater than our Father Abraham? You speak of an eternal life / and they are dead: what do you make of yourself? Jesus proves / that he did not praise himself in that regard: It is my Father who praises me, through signs and wonders / testimony from Heaven / conviction in the hearts / and the testimony of John. <margin>John 5:33.</margin> You say this one is your God; yet you have no knowledge of him / as was evident both outwardly and inwardly; for (at best) they sought nothing other than the glory of this world and a high-minded, fleshly existence: which, according to their own feelings, was subject to death / after which nothing more was to be expected.

### Reflection.

Nothing was more intolerable to the Jews than when Jesus began to give testimony of his eternal **Divinity**; they could tolerate that he went about as a **Prophet**, or was praised as a renowned Master in Israel; but to be higher or greater than their father **Abraham**—who was said to have been glad and joyful in his day, as if he were already present in being—this they could not suffer. They asked therefore with an agitated spirit: *You are not yet fifty years old, and have you seen Abraham;* who has now (they meant to say) been gone for a good two thousand years? What presumption is this? Even **Moses**, though a Prophet, never claimed such a thing for himself. Now, if the Lord had added to this: "Men, listen; you must understand me to mean that Abraham saw my coming in a prophetic way, and rejoiced in the Spirit that such a descendant would arise from his lineage; I do not mean to say that I am so old, or was in existence in the time of Abraham." If he had said that, they might have been able to digest his words to some extent. But when he added: *Verily, verily I say unto you: Before Abraham was, I am,* that was unbearable; for from this it appeared not only that he was in the time of Abraham, but even before him, and thus it would ultimately follow that he was eternal with God, through whom all things originally came to be and were brought forth. This seemed like a work of madness to them, for they saw a man of middle age standing before them who spoke these words: the Son of **Joseph** the Carpenter, as they supposed. Immediately they had stones in hand to throw at this blasphemer of God. By this example we are taught to what a tempestuous blindness man falls when he proceeds according to his own imagined fantasy. And it is to be feared that even today, Jesus is often driven out of the Temple of the heart by fleshly wisdom, which is an enemy of his holy, Divine being. The Jews were quick to pick up stones when things did not go according to their liking:
<margin>2 Chronicles 24:20.</margin>
for not only did they help **Zechariah**, the son of **Jehoiada**, to his death with stones,
<margin>Josephus, *Antiquities*, Book 14, Chapter 3.</margin>
but also a certain **Onias** <note>This refers to Honi the Circle-Drawer, a Jewish miracle-worker described by the historian Josephus.</note>, a pious man who (according to the testimony of **Josephus**) could unlock the Heavens to obtain rain; because he would not sing their tune <note>Meaning: because he refused to pray for the side of the conflict they supported during a civil war.</note>, they stoned him to death with a mad mind in the time of King **Aristobulus**. So also did Jesus: He saw a man who was born blind. This man he had chosen / not only to show a miraculous and never-before-heard Miracle / but at the same time to set an image of the whole human race; and especially the Jewish Nation / with whom he had to deal. It appears from the History / that Jesus paused a while with this man; as if standing in reflection / in order to hear the judgment of his Disciples in the meantime; who, being busy searching out the works of the Lord / looked upon this blindness as a heavy and particular punishment / asking immediately: Master, who has sinned, this man or his parents? The blind man himself could not have sinned before his birth / unless they understood along with the common Jews: That souls were punished in other bodies according to their merits; <note>This refers to the "transmigration of souls" (gilgul), an idea present in some Jewish thought of the era, suggesting a soul might be punished for sins committed in a previous life.</note> be it with blindness / deafness / or similar misfortune. ...saw a change in him; he had just been sitting there begging, and now he joyfully abandoned that trade <note>The original Dutch uses 'ambacht' (trade/craft), suggesting that begging had become the man's full-time occupation.</note>, having been helped by the light. Those who are enlightened by the power of Christ no longer need to beg for alms: for they are now placed on the path of light and know where they must go. They were amazed: "Is this the man?" Some said yes, some no; but he himself openly confessed that he was the man. But look, a wonder! He could see. He spoke with the neighbors, who investigated the matter; but he did not know his healer. So it is in the first stage of enlightenment: there is some sight, but not yet as it should be; for to know God is perfect righteousness.

<margin>1 Corinthians 13:12</margin>
It is an exceeding grace to know God in His holy being. At present (says the Apostle), I know imperfectly, but then I shall know even as I am known—thereby expressing perfect joy. As long as one does not know Jesus, one cannot show others where He is. The neighbors of the blind man ask for Jesus, yet not from a right vision; rather, they held the Sabbath to be desecrated. They knew as little as their Masters <note>A reference to the religious authorities/Pharisees.</note> that the powers of Christ perform their greatest work on the Sabbath, when all things are in rest and silence. They led the blind man to their Synagogue; there they sat like sharp-sighted people, yet with thick scales before their eyes <note>original: "dicke schellen voor haer oogen" — a reference to spiritual blindness, similar to the scales that fell from Saul's eyes in Acts 9.</note>, groping with their hands

<margin>1 Peter 1:9</margin>
for the way: "How did you obtain this sight?" Thus they did not know the way of light, nor the means to enlighten anyone; they were like those who see a good and genuine piece of gold and will not believe it came from a genuine gold mine. The miracle is wonderful, the work is good, but [they say] the man is not of God. So many a person still exists who, when they see things that should make them fall silent in awe, say: "The works are indeed good, but the faith and virtue are not." See how far a person can be warped by their preconceived prejudices <note>original: "inghenomen partij-schap" — refers to being blinded by partisan bias or sectarianism.</note>. As the senses drifted through one another like clouds of vapor, one guessing this and another that, they asked the blind man himself. He spoke according to his straightforward knowledge: "He is a Prophet"—that is, a man of God, a true Teacher, who is not a sinner as you think, but who has received these powers from God, who works all good. Convinced by the present deed, these people nonetheless willfully refused to see, and were of those of whom the Prophet Isaiah <note>original: "Efaias"</note> had said:

<margin>Isaiah 6:10</margin>
"They have closed their eyes." Thus they began to think of ways to bring this matter into doubt.

### Observation

<margin>Proverbs 17:12</margin> The wise Solomon does not say in vain: It is better to meet a bear robbed of her cubs than a fool in his folly. These "bears" <note>A metaphorical reference to the hostile religious authorities.</note> were anxious that this "cub" <note>The truth of the miracle.</note> had been snatched from them; they hold their heads to the wind, sniffing and searching to tear apart whomever they find; they have sharpened their teeth, the ban is ready, should anyone dare to confess the truth; they summon these innocent parents before their judgment seat as if they were fishing for the truth, yet meanwhile, those summoned must watch what they say.

<margin>Josephus, *The Jewish War*, Book 2, Chapter 12.</margin> These parents, knowing the severity of their ban <term>ban|a decree of excommunication from the religious and social community</term>, and how they would be cast out of all fellowship, did not wish to oppose these fools in their folly, by which they might get the noose around their necks; yet they nevertheless gave enough indication by their words that the matter was true in itself, and that they need not doubt it: *We know that he is our son, and that he was born blind, but how he now sees, we do not know, or who has opened his eyes, we also do not know.* The confession was very good; on their side, their son had nothing but blindness; sight he had obtained—but how? Or from whom? Unknown; it serves to God’s glory when one sees one's own misery and claims no virtue for oneself, even though one shares in the benefit. These parents then directed these people to the most direct path, saying: *He is old enough, ask him.* These people knew this well: but these [authorities] sought to use their great status to make them afraid and to cause doubt in the matter; not being able to do this, they began to press him again, as follows.

### Reflection.

<margin>Heinrich Bünting in the *Harmony of the Gospels* <note>Heinrich Bünting (1545–1606) was a German theologian and cartographer famous for his "Travel Book through the Holy Scriptures," which attempted to synchronize the chronologies and locations of the Gospels.</note>.</margin>
Whether this discourse followed immediately upon the preceding history / or whether some time had elapsed between the two / we cannot know for certain: It is also not probable what Heinrich Bünting suggests / that the stories and discourses of these four chapters of John / namely the seventh / eighth / ninth / and this first part of the tenth / each occurred in a separate month; although it can be admitted / and is not unlike the apparent truth / that they are distinguished from one another by some period of time. Now we come to the reflections on these words of Christ: Seeing that God in former times had portrayed the coming of his Son through various figurative ways of speaking / and made it known to the forefathers; such as by the name of a <margin>Isaiah 9:5.</margin> Father <note>The OCR text reads "Dader" (Doer), but in the context of the titles for Christ in Isaiah 9:6, it is almost certainly "Vader" (Father).</note>, King, Prince, Hero, Bridegroom, and more of the like: So he has also done the same under the name of a Shepherd, and described his Office and deeds under that title; accordingly, his believers are also portrayed under the name of Sheep and Lambs. > He shall feed his flock like a shepherd: He shall gather the lambs in his arms, and carry them in his bosom, and lead the ewes.

<margin>Ezekiel 34:2.</margin>

<margin>Ezekiel 34:11.</margin>
> I myself will now take charge of my flock, and seek them, just as a shepherd seeks his sheep when they have strayed from his flock: and I will deliver them from all places where they were scattered; at the time when it was dark and gloomy. ->Of the life of Jesus Christ.<-

*JOHN 10. Matt. 18. Mark 9. Luke 10.*

...sacrificed himself, in order that he might reconcile his sheep to God, and deliver them from the hooks of the Wolf, who roared most terribly, and laid snares for this good Shepherd everywhere, <margin>*Mat. 4. 3.*</margin> both through temptations, assaults, struggles, and trials, as well as through the senseless hirelings among his servants, over whom this Shepherd nevertheless triumphed in the end, snatching the prey from his teeth.

Regarding the second: Hirelings are those who, for their temporal gain, honor, ease, or pleasure—which they aim for—undertake to pasture the sheep, as the <margin>*Micah 3. 5.*</margin> Prophet says: *They preach that things will go well when one gives them something to eat, but if one puts nothing in their mouths, they preach: there must be a war.* <margin>*Rom. 16, 17.*</margin> Of these Paul also says: *That they served not the Lord Christ, but their own belly.* These cannot withstand the resistance of the Wolf; for since they love not the sheep but their own profit, they flee easily and abandon the sheep to their fate, which the faithful shepherd does not do, <margin>*1 Sam. 17. 34.*</margin> of which *David* gave an example when he killed the Lion and the Bear, and delivered the flock from their teeth. Furthermore, Christ is also an inward faithful Shepherd, who remains with the heart in all need and difficulty; but the hired or assumed pleasures do not deliver in time of need, but vanish in the time of distress, like ice before the sun.

Regarding the third: The knowledge between him and his own is firm on both sides, and they are as inseparable from one another as God is inseparable in himself. <margin>*Rom. 8. 35. 38.*</margin> Of this Paul says: *Who shall separate us from the love of God? Tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or hunger, or nakedness, or peril, or sword?* And further he testifies that he is certain that such cannot happen. This is then a firm comfort for the believers, that they know—however much they are despised, mocked, and disregarded by the vast majority of men—that they are nevertheless known to God in secret; from this it also follows that they do not judge lightly, nor fear anyone’s judgment, since they rest in this: <margin>*2 Tim. 2. 19.*</margin> that God knows his own; it also comforts them in all kinds of distresses that they encounter in this world.

Regarding the fourth: There were at that time still many hidden among the Gentiles <note>original: *Heydenen*; nations other than Israel</note> who loved a Godhead with upright hearts, though they did not yet know it, and ran wild like wandering sheep, <margin>*1 Pet. 2. 25.*</margin> who were afterwards converted to the Shepherd and Bishop of their souls, and thus brought into one sheepfold, among whom were: <margin>*Acts 8. 26 and 10. 1. and 16. 14. 30.*</margin> The Chamberlain of Queen *Candace*, who was baptized by Philip. Likewise *Cornelius*, *Lydia*, the Jailer <note>original: *Stock-meester*; the keeper of the prison stocks</note>, *Gaius*, *Aristarchus*, and many others who would be innumerable.

Regarding the last: Christ here makes it well known that he did not lose his life as other men lose theirs, but that according to his Divine being he retained such power to take it up again, just as he gave it up willingly and unforced; for it is manifest that he offered up his Spirit much earlier than the necessity of <margin>*Mark 15. 44.*</margin> human [death] forced him: *Pilate* marveled that he was so soon dead,

The fourth Part /

<margin>JOHN 10</margin> <margin>Matt. 18. Mark 9. Luke 10.</margin>
from which it appeared that he had given it <note>that is, his life</note> up willingly, and that it had not been taken from him by force; he also says that his Father loves him for this reason; namely, because he gave himself up not out of a hatred for life, but for his sheep, so that he might take his life unto himself again; for otherwise, the giving up of his life—had it remained lost—would not have benefited his sheep. Thus, this was the perfect will of his Father, with whom he was one; accordingly, it was also his will in the Divine essence. The origin of this was the love he bore for his sheep for their salvation. These arguments, as they were obscure and incomprehensible to the Jews, again stirred up an uproar and division among them, as is to be seen in the following.

<margin>19</margin> But then there arose a discord again among the
<margin>20</margin> Jews because of these words. Some said: He has
<margin>21</margin> the Devil, and is mad, why do you listen to him?
Others said: These are not the words of one pos-
sessed. Can the Devil also open the eyes of the blind?

## Observation.

<margin>2 Pet 1. 9.</margin> Discord arises from the uncertainty of feeling, where man imagines he has certainty; for then he lashes out at strange things, like a blind man who gropes for the way with his hand; only where there is light can one see the path one must travel, and all discord stems from that lack. It was then so situated with these people that, being clouded by the mist of the Pharisees, they did not know what they were saying. Sometimes they seemed to agree and believe; at other times they broke out in slander and knocked down everything they had built up. 1. Thus, there were some mixed among these people who pulled the rope of the Pharisees <note>An idiom meaning they followed the Pharisees' lead or sided with them</note>; these cried out according to the <margin>Matt. 12. 24. / Mark 3. 22. / John 7. 20. and 8. 48.</margin> instruction of their Masters: *He has the Devil, and is mad*: and according to their perverted understanding, it was indeed so: for Christ speaking of himself as a Door, as a Shepherd, likening his own to Sheep, and others to Wolves, even Thieves and Murderers—these were all words without meaning if no Divine light is added, from which these people were very far removed. 2. There were also others who took heed of the words themselves, and how the reasoning was bound together, being moreover moving and piercing; these, considering how great a distinction there is between these excellent expressions and the Devil's vain gestures and <gloss>mockery</gloss> <note>original: "schumperie," meaning derisive or empty babble</note>, refuted the first group, saying: *These are not the words of one possessed*, since they are of an entirely different scent.

<summary>This page discusses the division among the Jews following Jesus's discourse on the Good Shepherd, contrasting those who dismissed him as demon-possessed with those who recognized the divine authority in his words and miracles.</summary>

A third sort / turning their eyes to the **Miracles** of **Christ** / which had never before been heard of or seen / brought those forward as witnesses, saying: Can the **Devil** also open the eyes of the blind? what can you say to that? have you heard of such a thing? just as we know / that the man born blind was so miraculously enlightened that even the <margin>John 9:7.</margin> **Pharisees**, investigating the matter, were confounded by it: So one cannot say with truth / that such a powerful **Teacher** and wonder-worker has the **Devil**. And thus this crowd, milling among <margin>Isa. 57:20.</margin> each other like a roaring sea / went away again without having settled the matter; So miserably are the people tortured and led astray <note>original: "om den tuyn geleydt," a Dutch idiom meaning to be deceived or led down the garden path</note> / when one looks to men, whom one trusts with the matter, and when one does not purely take one's refuge in **God** / to be enlightened in the soul.

## Historical continuation.

<margin>John 10:22.</margin> The **Evangelist** **John** does not relate where **Jesus** went after the ending of this **Feast of Tabernacles** <note>The Jewish autumn festival of Sukkot</note> / for that which he relates immediately following / occurred at the **Feast of Dedication** <note>The winter festival of Hanukkah</note>, which came about a quarter of a year after the aforementioned **Feast of Tabernacles**, and it is not likely that **Jesus** stayed so long in **Jerusalem** / but much more likely <margin>Matt. 19:1. Mark 10:1.</margin> that he now traveled to that region / which **Matthew** and **Mark** mention / namely / across the **Jordan** <note>The region known as Perea</note> / leaving **Capernaum** and the lands of **Galilee** / so that he might plant his **Evangelical** teaching everywhere there; And so that he might approach the city of **Jerusalem** all the more / where he would fulfill his passion in due time. He did not, however, stay constantly in one place across the **Jordan** / but sometimes traversed the land according to his old custom / then had his principal residence there / as he previously did within **Capernaum**; all of which will be shown in the following part.

<margin>John 6:5. Matt. 14:22. Matt. 15:21. Matt. 17:1. Mark 9:13.</margin> Let us take a little heed of the preceding: How **Jesus** showed his glory / through the feeding of so many thousands; through helping the **Canaanite** **Woman**; the healing of the mute / deaf / lame / and blind; through the transfiguration on mount **Thabor**; and the driving out of the unclean **Spirit**; how he shows his patience toward the **Pharisees** / who constantly follow him / rebuking him for the unwashed hands /
